Preface

The books that shaped how I build software have one thing in common: they are a body of knowledge you can read from the first page to the last. EMF: Eclipse Modeling Framework explained not only how to generate code from a model, but why a model is worth having and what it buys you once you have one. The C4 model for visualising software architecture gave boxes and lines a vocabulary small enough to remember, a stark contrast to no vocabulary at all or UML, BPMN and other complex notations, which are so huge that it is almost the same as having no vocabulary - the point at infinity. Neither is a reference manual. Both are arguments, made one chapter at a time, with enough "how" to make the "why" concrete.

Two books about programming languages shaped how I build software too, from the side of the code. Bjarne Stroustrup’s The C++ Programming Language, in its third and special editions, teaches its key features together with the design techniques they exist to support, gives its last part to design, and ends each chapter with numbered advice. Bruce Eckel’s Thinking in Java teaches a way of thinking rather than a syntax; Eckel put it on the web while he was writing it, gave its early editions away, and let what readers sent him shape the editions that followed.

This book tries to do the same for the Nasdanika SDK Runtime - thinking in models and JVM (not just Java).

The runtime is the part of the Nasdanika SDK you install first and build everything else on. It gives you models written as text in a language called Xcore and handled by the Eclipse Modeling Framework (EMF), a capability framework through which code finds what it needs by asking for its type, telemetry that is part of the code rather than bolted on, volumes that present anything as files, and a command line assembled from whatever modules happen to be present. It is influenced by EMF but has nothing to do with the Eclipse IDE. It speaks OpenTelemetry but keeps telemetry local, as a model, next to the models it describes. It is built on the JDK and adds as little as it can. Those choices have reasons, and the reasons are most of what this book is about.

Who this book is for

Architects who want more structure with less effort. If you have ever tried to keep a domain vocabulary, an architecture or a portfolio in office documents, a wiki and a drawing tool, you know the problem: structure is expensive, so it decays. The runtime is my answer to making structure cheap enough to keep. You do not need to write Java to get value from the first part of this book, and the parts that are about code explain what the code makes possible before they show it.

Java developers who want an observable, testable foundation with few dependencies, and who are curious what modeling looks like when it does not require an IDE.

Researchers and R&D teams, in a company, a lab or in the open, who need to try an idea before anyone will provision infrastructure for it. The runtime needs a JDK and nothing else: a solution built on it runs in one JVM, on a laptop, a single virtual machine or the free tier of a CI service, with no cluster, database server or message broker to set up and ask permission for. It also keeps the record a researcher wants: listings that are tested code, telemetry kept as a model next to the results (Chapter 13), and a snapshot of exactly which modules ran (Chapter 22), so that an experiment can be repeated and its result explained. Academic research is mostly done in Python, and this book does not try to change that; it is for the research and development that happens where the JVM already is, or where one machine has to be enough.

When releases are archived on Zenodo, add the concept DOI here and in the colophon, so that a result can cite the version of the runtime it ran on.

Collaborators. If you want to contribute to Nasdanika, or build on it, this is the map. It says what exists today, what is a sketch, and what is planned.

Me. "The faintest ink is better than the strongest memory." A design that is not written down is re-derived, slightly differently, every time it is needed.

AI assistants. A coding assistant working on a Nasdanika project is grounded in what it is given. This book is written to be given: the terms are used consistently and defined in Appendix D, the rules of thumb are collected in Appendix C, and every listing is code that compiles. If you are an assistant reading this, start with Appendix C.

What this book assumes

This book does not start from zero, and it is not an introduction to modeling or to Java. It assumes you have seen the problems it is about: a definition that lives in a schema, a wiki and three spreadsheets, a diagram nobody trusts, a question about your own systems that nobody can answer. You do not need to write Java to read the first part, but you will meet terms like EMF and metamodel there. Appendix D defines them, and an assistant can take you further than I could here.

My sister, who knows modeling a bit, says of this material человек с мороза не поймёт: someone walking in from the cold will not get it. She is right. If the problems are not yet yours, the book will keep until they are.

How this book is organized

Part I explains the problem the runtime addresses, the principles it follows, how it is built with an AI assistant, why some organizations will resist it, and how its parts fit together. Part II covers the common module: models with EMF, generic types at run time, reactive flows on the JDK, and the capability framework. Part III is about telemetry: how the runtime instruments itself, how to watch work while it runs, and how telemetry becomes a model. Part IV introduces volumes, the runtime’s file abstraction, and serving them over HTTP and WebDAV. Part V shows how commands are contributed by modules and wired by generic types. Part VI tours the models that ship with the runtime: the Groovy DSL for authoring, the core model, Meta, the JVM model, the models that generate the web, user interfaces assembled from views chosen by the class of what they show, and diagrams: drawn in Draw.io, laid out with ELK, and drawn as SVG. Part VII is the roadmap and the vision. The appendices are references: modules, telemetry names, rules of thumb, a glossary, and how this book is built.

Like "Beyond Diagrams", this book is more a menu than a recipe book. Architects can read Part I and the first section of each later chapter, which says what a capability is for, and skip the listings. Developers should read the parts in order, because each builds on the previous one, and run the examples as they go.

In a martial art, techniques are learned one at a time and then put together in forms, as words are put together in sentences. Most chapters of this book teach techniques: a volume, a flow, a capability, a model. The examples that combine them, from the command followed end to end in Chapter 5 to the stories of the Nasdanika Body of Knowledge (Appendix F), are forms. Both differ from the mainstream the way one school of kung fu differs from another.

My kung fu teacher (Where the opinions come from) says: "I teach you my kung fu so that it becomes your kung fu." Students differ, heavier or lighter, taller or shorter, and each practices what they are taught in the way that fits them. This book is offered the same way. Its techniques have worked for a practitioner working alone or in a small team; take the ones that fit, adapt them, and make them your own.

The Nasdanika Zephyr Books

This book is the why, the what and a high-level how of the runtime. It shows enough of each module to make its purpose concrete, and stops there. The depth is in the Nasdanika Zephyr Books: in-depth technical manuals, one per module, or per small group of modules that are used together, for the modules that need more than a chapter. If this book is the menu, the Zephyr Books are the recipes.

The model is IBM Redbooks. They are technical guides written by practitioners, IBM specialists working with partners and customers, and they are free. They cover what a product is for, the scenarios it serves and, step by step, how to put it to work, which is more than a reference manual does.

A Zephyr Book does the same for one module of the runtime. It goes deeper into the how: every form and option, the extension points, and the errors and how to read them. Where the module calls for it, it goes deeper into the why and the what as well, with the use cases the module was built for, which a chapter of this book can only name. It stands on its own: a reader who starts with a Zephyr Book does not need this one, so where the two touch, the Zephyr Book repeats what it needs. The chapter that introduces a module points to its Zephyr Book.

These are available with this edition:

  • Matching and Wiring, for the common module of Part II. Its why is that most of software development is matching parts and checking that they fit, and that the runtime matches at run time on the generic declarations the compiler has checked, with the compiler’s rules. Its how is a chapter per package: types, adaptation, capabilities, flows, resource sets and telemetry.

  • Telemetry Model, for the telemetry model of Chapter 13: traces, log records and metrics exported from the OpenTelemetry SDK as EMF models, kept next to the models they describe, with the changes a unit of work made to models recorded in the spans that made them.

  • Volumes and Content, for the volume module of Chapter 14 and Chapter 15: a small SPI for trees of files wherever they live and a re-readable abstraction of bytes, models stored in volumes through EMF, and anything presented as files served over HTTP and WebDAV, in one trace with its clients.

  • Harness, for the harness module of Chapter 15: an HTTP server that is up while code runs against it, the code’s requests and the server’s work in one trace, recorded as a model.

  • Declarative Command Lines, for the cli module of Chapter 16 and Chapter 17: command lines assembled from contributed picocli commands that find their parents and sub-commands by generic types, mix-ins, overriding, the runtime’s commands and the launcher, and the pipelines the approach makes possible.

  • Groovy DSL, for the groovy module of Chapter 19. The user’s side is the language rule by rule: call forms, references and name resolution, loading other resources, prototypes, saving, diagnostics and telemetry. The developer’s side is binding the DSL to a metamodel of your own, with handlers, capability factories and resolvers. Its use cases are models kept as scripts, models derived from diagrams and spreadsheets, and scripts that write themselves back when they are saved.

  • Meta Model, for Meta of Chapter 21: a language-neutral type system, a vocabulary written down once in a text syntax with documentation as structure, drafted with an AI assistant for the people who own the words, and projected to glossaries, Ecore, TypeScript and the tool schemas of agents.

  • JVM Model, for the JVM model of Chapter 22: what a Java virtual machine can name, from layers and modules down to methods and parameters, identified the JVM’s own way so that builds, coverage, profiles and traces join on it without a mapping.

  • HTML and Bootstrap Models, for the web models of Chapter 23: HTML as an EMF model with a generator that writes it, and Bootstrap 5 with Bootswatch themes as a model of what components mean, expanded to HTML for static pages and used in React components.

  • TypeScript and React Models, for the web models of Chapter 23: TypeScript’s declaration surface and React’s components, hooks and JSX as EMF models, with generators that manage imports and write code a browser runs with no npm and no build step.

  • Walk-throughs with Playwright, for the playwright module of Chapter 23: browser sessions in the server’s trace, with steps as spans, the server’s work as their children, screenshots and narration recorded in the steps, and an optional video of the session that the trace explains.

  • Diagram Model, for the diagram model: diagrams as data, built, stored as YAML, converted from Draw.io and mapped to the models they depict. With the Draw.io Model book, it is the mapping of diagram elements to model elements that makes a diagram the source of a model.

  • Diagram Layout with ELK, for automatic layout of the diagram model with the Eclipse Layout Kernel, with diagrams of Ecore models generated, laid out and rendered with React Flow and Draw.io.

  • Draw.io, for the drawio and drawio-playwright modules of Chapter 25: diagrams that people draw and programs read. Its why is the visual communication continuum, from a picture to a diagram that is documentation, configuration or the source of a model. Its how is the Java API for Draw.io documents, pages, layers, nodes, connections, properties, links and styles, and rendering pages with Draw.io’s own viewer as images and videos. Its diagrams are PNG images with the diagram embedded: a reader sees a picture, Draw.io opens the same file for editing, and the book’s tests load it as the document the next listing works on.

  • Draw.io Model, for Draw.io documents as an EMF model on the diagram and presentation models: loaded into a resource set from .drawio files and exported images, read, changed, generated and saved, with a diagram of the running JVM generated, laid out with ELK and drawn by Draw.io’s viewer.

  • SVG Model, for SVG as an EMF model: the subset of SVG that generated diagrams need, with a diagram laid out with ELK and written as SVG, every shape a link.

  • Presentation Model, for the presentation model of Chapter 25: decks, slides, masters, shapes, text, tables, connectors and speaker notes as an EMF model on the diagram model, because a slide is a diagram.

The rule of this book holds for them. Every listing in a Zephyr Book is included from the module’s own tests, and a warning fails the build, so a Zephyr Book that no longer matches its module does not build.

Each Zephyr Book is on its module’s page on the runtime site, runtime.sdk.nasdanika.org, as a PDF and as a single HTML page. It is also on Maven Central, attached to its module’s artifact with the classifier book: org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime:groovy:pdf:book:2026.11.0 is the PDF of the Groovy DSL book, and html in place of pdf is its HTML. The test sources that the listings come from are attached the same way, with the classifier test-sources, so the whole test behind a listing is one download away. The Zephyr Books are also on Leanpub, in a bundle with this book. Printed versions of this book and its Zephyr Book can be ordered on Lulu. An assistant can follow the same division as a person: this book to find a module and understand why it exists, its Zephyr Book for how to use it, and its test sources for the complete code.

The name is borrowed, not invented. Redbooks are named after the color of their first covers. Nasdanika’s color is blue, and a blue book is taken: by Kelley Blue Book for cars and, in programming, by the Smalltalk-80 "Blue Book" of 1983. So the books are named after the Bootswatch theme they are styled with, Zephyr, which is blue and is also the theme of the runtime’s site. A name that describes a look promises nothing else, which is what a series name should do: a reader who has one Zephyr Book knows how the next one will look and how it will read. The books have nothing to do with the Zephyr real-time operating system, a project of the Linux Foundation.

Conventions

I write in the first person. "The author" is ten times more letters than "I", and a book about doing more with less effort should not waste them. "You" is the reader, whether you write the code or decide what gets built.

Code listings are included from the book’s example modules, in the runtime repository under doc/book/examples. Each module is a small Maven project, built and tested before the book is rendered, so a listing that no longer compiles stops the build instead of misleading you. The examples use the org.example namespace for Java packages and modules, as your own code would use yours. Numbered markers in a listing, such as <1>, are explained in the list right below it.

Status labels say how far along something is: AVAILABLE means it is in Nasdanika SDK Runtime 2026.11.0 and the book shows it working; SKETCH means a model or an interface exists without the behavior around it; PLANNED means it is designed, on the roadmap, and not built yet.

Versions

This edition describes Nasdanika SDK Runtime 2026.11.0, built with Java 25 and Maven 3.9.16 or later. The runtime’s version is a calendar version: year, month, patch.

Feedback

The book is developed with the runtime, in github.com/Nasdanika-SDK/runtime. Issues and pull requests against the manuscript in doc/book/manuscript are welcome, and so are questions: a question is a section that is missing.

Where the opinions come from

The runtime is opinionated, and you are entitled to know where its opinions come from.

I trained as a physicist, with a master’s degree in plasma physics. I was taught Fortran, and Quasic, a small interactive language for programming laboratory hardware. The rest I taught myself: Pascal, assembler and machine code, Basic, Object Pascal in Delphi, C++, Java and JavaScript, and XML with XPath and XSLT. Between them they cover most of the distance from the machine to the model, and working with an assistant, as Chapter 3 describes it, is one more level up.

I learned to think in shapes and connections, and in signals moving along them, long before I learned UML. As a teenager I built electronic devices: amplifiers, radio receivers and my first computer. I read and drew schematics, and laid out my own printed circuit boards, by hand and later in OrCAD, and etched them with ferric chloride and zapon varnish. As a physicist I designed scientific devices in AutoCAD, and a workshop built them as drawn. A schematic, a board layout and a CAD drawing are not illustrations: they are what the thing is made from. So ERwin for databases and UML for software came easily; they were drawings to build from too.

Software gave me more drawings that run. I programmed Lego Mindstorms robots, first in the visual language that comes with the kit, where a program is blocks wired together, and then in Java with leJOS. A robot is event-driven by nature: it waits for a sensor to fire and reacts while its motors are still turning, and that shaped how I build software. At work I built integrations in TIBCO BusinessWorks, where a process is drawn as activities and transitions and deployed as drawn, and modeled business processes in TIBCO Business Studio. In all of them the drawing was the program, not a picture of it. The North Star of this runtime, work drawn as a graph and executed as drawn (Chapter 26), is the same idea once more. When I wrote about the executable graphs of earlier Nasdanika releases, the metaphor I reached for was a printed circuit board with processors soldered to it (Executable (computational) graphs & diagrams, Concurrent Executable Diagrams).

From 1989 to 1992 I was also trained as a platoon commander, in the military department of my university, and commissioned as a lieutenant in the reserve. Two things from that training stayed with me. One is maps: reading them, and drawing a plan of defense on one, another drawing to act from. The other is Article 17 of the Combat Regulations of the Ground Forces, Part III, for the platoon, the squad and the tank (Voenizdat, 1990), which was drilled into our heads. On receiving a combat mission, a platoon commander must:

  1. understand the mission: the task of the company as well as the platoon’s own, which targets on the platoon’s front the senior commanders' weapons will engage, the tasks of the neighbors and how to coordinate with them, and the time to be ready;

  2. assess the situation: the enemy, the platoon and the units attached to it, the neighbors, the terrain, the weather, the season and the time of day;

  3. make a decision: how to accomplish the mission, the tasks of the squads and of the attached units, and how the platoon will be commanded;

  4. reconnoiter the ground;

  5. issue the combat order;

  6. organize coordination, support and command, and prepare the people, weapons and equipment for combat;

  7. check that the platoon is ready, and report it to the company commander at the set time.

It works well beyond a platoon: I have explained it to my children, and they know my version of it by heart. I later recognized it in project management and in the TOGAF Architecture Development Method, and the loop of Chapter 3 has the same shape.

The training met its first real test in a computer game. In the late 1990s I played a lot of Command & Conquer, a real-time strategy game; I never cared for Doom. At first I lost badly, and it stung: I had been trained for this. A short while later I could not understand how I had ever lost so badly. Doom puts you in one body and asks for reflexes. A real-time strategy game gives you a map and units that act on their own: you set them a task, watch, correct and decide again. That is the work of directing an assistant, decades before there were assistants to direct. Against the usual advice, I later had my children play it, for the strategic and spatial thinking it trains.

Looking back, it is one path. As a child I spent hours with Lego, long before Mindstorms; a cousin of mine holds that it trains spatial thinking, and I agree. Then came schematics and circuit boards, maps and Command & Conquer. Now I play Go, which is older than chess and has far more possible games. At home we play Harmonies, a board game in which a landscape is built tile by tile. Chinese has a word for a lifelong practice like this, dào, the way, which Japanese reads as dō, as in judo, kendo and bushido. Mine is a way of seeing structure: things, the connections between them, and how they will change; modeling is where it led.

The other way I have kept is a martial one, since about 1989. Wushu as a student, aikido in the 1990s, and after ten years without practice in the United States, Kenpo and Modern Arnis: I had taken my son to the classes, realized how much I had missed it, and joined the adult group, where the oldest student after me, past forty, was fifteen. Then came ninjutsu, and now Praying Mantis kung fu, tai chi, and the broadsword and the long sword.

My teacher explains every technique he teaches and shows its applications. Some techniques are counter-intuitive at first and take as much effort of the mind as of the body, and once the application is understood, repeating a drill for the hundredth time is not boring: each repetition is an exercise in seeing what the technique is for. He also talks about small moves. A master wins with moves that a casual observer does not see: no more motion than the situation needs, and all of it to the point. That is efficiency and effectiveness together, more with less, and it is what I look for in software: a loop over an array instead of a database (Chapter 4), a few thousand lines of Xcore instead of hundreds of thousands of lines of Java (Chapter 3), the JDK before a library (Chapter 2). And he says that kung fu is "eating bitter", chī kǔ: hours of practice that nothing replaces, ten thousand of them, he says, to master the long sword.

Ten thousand hours is also the number Malcolm Gladwell made famous. In Outliers he tells how Bill Gates got time on a computer as a schoolboy, when almost nobody could, and spent every hour on it that he could find. Opportunity and hours, at the moment a technology is new. The PC was such a moment, and Chapter 3 tells what my mother made of it. Assistants are another, and this book is what my hours with one have produced so far.

I taught myself from books, and in Khabarovsk, in the Far East of the Soviet Union and then of Russia, books about computers were scarce. A few bookstores had a few of them; on business trips to Moscow I found more. The first computer store I visited in the United States was a Micro Center, and I went straight to its books section, which held more computer books than I had ever seen in one place. A colleague who came with me was surprised: "Oh, you are still reading…​" He had read his computer books in college and did not expect to need more.

Scarcity leaves habits behind. Mine is to assume that I do not know enough yet and that somebody has done this before, and to find out who, and what they learned. That is the first step of every design in this runtime.

Physics taught the same habit, with a story that I was told when I was in the university. A student wrote his diploma thesis on computing an integral by numerical methods. An old academician who happened to attend the defense opened a table of integrals and asked why the student had computed numerically an integral that has a closed form. The student got a C, the lowest passing grade, out of pity. The computation was correct; the work was not needed, and an hour in the library would have shown it.

Later I learned the name lawyers give to what that student skipped. I prepared two patent applications myself, for the automated build and deployment system my team had built, and a patent application is judged against the prior art: everything published before it that already does what it claims. The examiner searches for it, so you search first, and you learn to read what others have done as the measure of what you have. The applications were abandoned when the team left the company; the habit stayed. It is the reason for the next section, which is the prior art of this runtime in my own work, and for the table in Chapter 2 of what the runtime borrows from the work of others.

Plenty of books did not mean plenty of fluency, though. When I came to the United States I assumed that every developer knew UML, and I was wrong. Chapter 3 argues that fluency in modeling, and in technologies such as EMF, was scarce for twenty years and is not anymore. I take the end of a scarcity seriously, because I have watched one end already, in the aisles of a computer store.

Prior art, first-hand

The runtime is new; most of its ideas are not. I have built nearly every one of them at least once before, in large organizations, for a real problem and under harder constraints than the runtime has now: 32-bit address spaces, no assistant, and teammates who had never heard of EMF. This section is the record, so that you can judge the claims the book makes against what they come from. The organizations, the commercial products and the people are left unnamed; the problems, the numbers and what I built are as they were.

Before EMF

One of my first projects in the United States integrated a mainframe through a screen-integration product. It was meant to be used by mapping the input and output fields of every screen in its user interface and then writing Java against its API, one integration at a time. There were dozens of screens with hundreds of fields. Instead, I worked out the product’s file formats and described the screens, and the flows between them, in XML. Then I wrote an interpreter for that XML: it received a request from the message bus, navigated the screens, entered and collected the data, and sent the result back, with XSLT for transformations and Java handlers for what XSLT could not do. The same XML generated an HTML view of every screen, which people who knew the mainframe could read without knowing the product. They and the developers wrote flows, and I tested and deployed them. It was an executable model, documentation as code and inner source, years before I had a name for any of them.

At that time people could log in to application servers and change them by hand, and source control labeled files one at a time instead of committing a set of files together. Environments drifted apart: a logging library’s jar had the same name on every server and a different size, timestamp and digest on many of them. I wrote a scanner that walked folders, and the archives inside them, computed a digest of every file and of every directory from the digests of its contents, and compared two scans as an HTML report. It was a Merkle tree; I learned the name some twenty years later.

The team had also bought a commercial code-review tool. It was expensive and hard to use, and I was responsible for it. So I matched the part of it we used with an open source project of my own, Hammurapi. It parsed Java sources with an ANTLR grammar into a hand-made model of the language, with cross-references resolved down to method calls and bytecode consulted where it was available, and its inspectors navigated the model rather than matching patterns in the text. On a 32-bit JVM a large code base did not fit in memory, so the model was held with soft references. The reviews ran in the automated build, which checked the code delivered by outside contractors before anybody had to read it.

Later, as the integration architect of a call-center modernization, I had to talk to a mainframe in a binary format that carried no metadata: two bytes of element identifier, two bytes of length, then the bytes of the value. The client code had to know what each identifier meant. There were about 250 message tables with 18,000 element types, and they changed every month. What we were given was XML generated from the mainframe’s C header files: a metamodel of the mainframe, although nobody called it that. I wrote a generator that turned it into Java codecs streaming between the binary format and XML, and regenerated them when the tables changed.

Models of what already exists

My path with EMF started in 2008, in an R&D team. The first model was of decisions: which technology to use, and when, decided with a formal method by several experts (Chapter 4 tells the rest of that story).

The second kind of model I kept building was of things that already existed and that nobody could see whole. A customer-interaction framework drew processes as activities mapped to Java methods, with transitions between them and processes calling processes. After several years one project had about 800 of them, and nobody knew which were still used. I loaded them into a model, found the entry points in the configuration, resolved the references and reported the processes and the Java code that nothing reached.

I have modeled the code base of a visual integration platform three times, in two organizations, over fifteen years. The first time the model generated documentation for the whole code base, with a diagram of every process, and ran automated reviews in the manner of Hammurapi. The second time it was an inventory, to estimate a modernization. The third time it was an engine that executed the processes from the model directly (Direct semantic execution).

In 2012 the task was a monolith: about fifteen thousand classes in a thousand packages and two and a half million lines of code, with two hundred packages in a single dependency cycle. On our diagrams those packages were drawn red, and we called it the black hole. A commercial dependency analyzer gave a first look and stopped there. We built an Ecore model of Java that went beyond reflection to call trees, field references and inheritance in both directions, populated it from bytecode with ASM, and browsed it in a web application with class and sequence diagrams generated by PlantUML; it held about two million objects. An instrumentation tool recorded call trees at run time, to catch what reflection hid from static analysis, and an Eclipse plug-in extracted into a new module only the code traceable from chosen entry points, down to the individual members of a class. It all ran on a 32-bit JVM.

In the same R&D years I exposed a banking domain model as JavaScript APIs generated from an EMF model, because writing them by hand would have been slow and error-prone. The generated code loaded classes, data and templates on demand, worked synchronously or with promises, and measurably reduced network traffic compared to the approach then in use.

Models of how work is done

For a cloud migration, the software delivery process was a drawing of about a hundred activities. I built a diagram editor backed by a model of what is done, by whom, in which phase and with what resources, and migrated the drawing into it. For the same effort I built a generator of starter solutions. A developer filled out a form in the browser, the form was committed to a repository as YAML, and the commit started a build that generated the code, pushed it to the developer’s repository, started its first build and wrote the identifiers of the cloud resources it created back into the YAML. It was a Git-driven workflow before I called it that. It also taught me a lesson that Chapter 3 returns to: the generator’s specifications were EMF models saved as XMI, and my teammates, who did not know EMF, edited them in a text editor.

The developer-experience work that followed modeled the delivery process as journeys: directed graphs of activities, nested without limit, performed by roles using tools and consuming and producing deliverables, kept as YAML and Markdown in source control and generated into documentation with clickable diagrams. Next to it, documentation as code generated and federated the sites of more than sixty components from their own repositories.

The organization as a model

The largest model I have built joined three sources in a bank: the people directory, with tens of thousands of people and their reporting lines; the inventory of thousands of applications, with their owners, tiers and dependencies; and tens of thousands of source repositories, with their commits, files and Maven dependencies. Joining them was most of the work, because the same person had different identities in each. Once joined, the model answered questions that had needed a project each: who owns what technology, rolled up the reporting hierarchy; which organizations contribute to the same repositories; which languages the code is written in; and, from an organization-wide dependency graph, where code could be reused and which vulnerable libraries sit closest to the attack surface.

What carried over

None of these is the runtime. Each was built for one organization and one problem, on the platform of its day, and each ended when its project did. What they share is a shape, and the runtime is that shape built once, in the open, with the organization-specific parts left out.

Part I: The Why

Why the runtime exists, the principles it follows, how it is built with an AI assistant, why most organizations will resist it, and how its parts fit together. No code is needed to read this part; it is the argument the rest of the book makes concrete.

Chapter 1. More structure with less effort

Glass is a curious material. It is a solid, it holds its shape, and you can build with it. Look closely, though, and there is no crystal inside: the atoms have short-range order, each one sitting sensibly next to its neighbors, and no long-range structure at all. It is a liquid that stopped moving before it got organized.

Most enterprise knowledge is glass. Every team has its documents, its diagrams, its spreadsheets and its wiki pages, and each of them makes sense locally. Step back and there is no structure that connects them. The definition of a customer lives in a database schema, a JSON Schema, a partner’s XML Schema, a Java class, a Confluence table and three spreadsheets, and nothing relates them. Each is a projection of a model that nobody ever wrote down.

This chapter is about what structure is for, why there has been so little of it, what changed recently that makes it fixable, what kind of structure lasts, and what the Nasdanika SDK Runtime is in that picture.

1.1. What structure is for

"Life, at its core, is a self-sustaining, autocatalytic process," writes the biologist Alexander Markov in Birth of Complexity (Рождение сложности, 2010; my translation). An autocatalytic process makes the things that speed it up, so the more it has grown, the faster it grows. Business works the same way. A company does some things better, faster or cheaper than others, sells the difference as a margin, and puts the margin into doing them better still. An enterprise is a group of stakeholders and resources devoted to a mission, and structure is worth exactly what it adds to the effectiveness and efficiency with which the mission is pursued.

Life also shows what happens without structure. About three and a half billion years ago, microbial mats divided labor between layers of bacteria and archaea, which exchanged the products of their work and signaled to each other with chemicals. They did well for billions of years, then lost the lead to organisms with nervous systems, which carry a signal across a whole body in a fraction of a second. Enterprise IT is still a mat: each group works from its own playbook, often a tribal one, nobody has the whole picture, and improvement stops at the edge of a group. Glass and the mat are one observation, made by physics and by biology: order that is only local. Structure that connects the groups is the nervous system.

1.2. Structure has been expensive

We are managing twenty-first century complexity with twentieth century tools. Office documents were designed to be printed. Wikis were designed to be edited by anyone, which is exactly why nobody owns what they say. Drawing tools produce pictures: a box on a diagram looks like a system, and nothing about it says which system, who owns it, or whether it still exists.

None of this is news, and the industry has tried to fix it more than once. I learned UML in the 1990s, when it was going to be how software was designed. By the 2010s I had concluded that it was dead in the enterprise, and I was not alone. Simon Brown observed in the C4 model book that many teams "have already thrown them out in favour of much simpler 'boxes and lines' diagrams". The reason was not that structure is useless. The reason was cost.

Modeling came with a tax. The tools were desktop applications with their own repositories, their own licenses and their own learning curves. The open source alternative, the Eclipse Modeling Framework, was excellent and lived inside an IDE: to use a model you installed Eclipse, configured a workspace and generated code with a wizard. Catalogs and ontology platforms moved the tax to a server you rent, with an administrator who owns the whole graph. Every one of these asks people to adopt something before they get anything back.

So people rationally chose less structure. When a model costs more to keep than it pays, a spreadsheet wins, and the spreadsheet is the real competitor of every modeling tool. It is free, everybody can use it, and it never asks anyone to adopt anything.

The price of that choice is paid later, and by somebody else. Ask three people what the third measure on a list in some system prompt means and you get three answers. Ask who owns the definition and you get silence, then a suggestion that some other team may know. The knowledge exists. It lives in people’s heads, and it leaves when they do. An assistant cannot be fed it either.

Volume is not what makes structure expensive; complexity is. When I joined a bank’s people directory, application inventory and source repositories into one model (Prior art, first-hand), a conventional web application already reported on much of the same data, from about fifty relational tables. It handled the volume well. It could not keep up with the questions, because every new question needed a new join, a new table or a new screen, and the reports it could not produce were produced from the model instead.

1.3. What changed

Four things changed, and together they make structure cheap enough to keep.

The JDK grew up. Virtual threads became final in Java 21, so blocking code no longer costs a platform thread, and the main reason for reactive libraries disappeared. java.util.concurrent.Flow has been in the JDK since Java 9, the HTTP client since 11, ScopedValue since 25, and a class file API since 24. Many of the libraries an enterprise application drags along were written before the JDK had the feature. The reasons to take those dependencies expired; the dependencies did not. A runtime that starts today can say "if the JDK can do it, use the JDK" and mean it.

EMF works without Eclipse. EMF itself never needed the IDE; the tooling around it did. Today a model is a text file in Xcore, generated by a Maven plugin in any build, edited in any editor, and checked into Git next to the code. The twenty years of engineering in EMF (reflection, serialization, notifications, change recording, cross-resource references) come without the workspace.

OpenTelemetry standardized signals. Spans, log records and metrics have one API, independent of where they end up. Code can be instrumented once, and whether the signals go to an operational backend, to a console, or into a model that is kept forever is decided by whoever runs it.

A new coworker arrived. AI assistants are capable, and they see only what they are given: meeting notes, wiki pages, a deck from three years ago. They cannot absorb tribal knowledge at the coffee machine. An assistant grounded in a declared, versioned, owned model answers from it and can cite it; an assistant given a database schema and a wiki export infers, and inference is not a chain of custody. At the same time, assistants are good at the mechanical part of modeling: they draft a model from a description, a human corrects it, and correcting is much cheaper than authoring.

There is an old camping joke about two friends who meet a bear. One of them starts lacing up his running shoes. "You cannot outrun a bear!" "I do not have to outrun the bear. I only have to outrun you." Businesses do not have to outrun AI either. They have to harness it: ground it in their own terms, systems and rules, so that people and assistants speak the same language. The harness is structure.

1.4. Small, formal, composable

Cheap structure is necessary but not sufficient: structure also has to last. It lasts when it has the three properties that keep code and its libraries alive while the documents around them rot: it is small, formal and composable. Take away any one of them and the failure is familiar. Small and formal but not composable is the monolithic repository of an enterprise architecture tool. Small and composable but not formal is the wiki that drifts the day it is written. Formal and composable but not small is the canonical enterprise data model that nobody updates.

The runtime is built to make all three cheap. Micro-models keep structure small (Chapter 2), Xcore keeps it formal (Chapter 7), and models that reference each other across repositories, with capabilities and commands that find each other by type, keep it composable (Chapter 10, Chapter 17).

1.5. What the runtime is

The Nasdanika SDK Runtime is the set of modules everything else in the Nasdanika SDK runs on, in one repository, released as one unit. The analogy I use is the Java runtime, rt.jar and its successor, the JDK’s module image, or the runtime of an integration platform: the part you install first and build on.

It is built on three things, which I call the "pure Nasdanika" foundation: the JDK, EMF core and the OpenTelemetry API. All three are small, stable and standard, and any module may assume them. Anything beyond them has to justify itself.

On that foundation the runtime provides:

  • Models as the API. Data and operations are defined as text in Xcore, the build generates Java from it, and EMF does the rest: models are typed and documented, can be saved as XML (XMI), JSON, YAML or binary, and can be called by name, so an operation is also a tool a command line or an agent can call (Chapter 7).

  • A capability framework. A piece of code says what it needs, and the framework finds it among the modules that are present. It asks by type, down to the generics: Supplier<Library>, something that supplies a library, and Supplier<Catalog> are different things to ask for (Chapter 10).

  • Telemetry as part of the code. The runtime’s own operations report what they do through the OpenTelemetry API, as spans and log records, with a separate record for each unit of work, such as a command run. You can watch them live with no OpenTelemetry SDK and no backend, or save them as a model next to the models they changed (Chapter 11).

  • Volumes, a small abstraction of files, so that a model, a running JVM or a remote system can be presented as files, loaded as models, served over HTTP or mounted as a drive over WebDAV (Chapter 14).

  • A command line assembled from contributions. Modules contribute commands, and each command finds its parent by type, so adding a dependency adds commands (Chapter 16).

  • Models that ship with it: a core model for identity, documentation and provenance, Meta as a language-neutral type system, a JVM model, a telemetry model, and models of HTML, Bootstrap, TypeScript and React that make the web a generation target (Part VI).

1.6. What it is not

It is easier to place something by what it refuses to be.

Not Eclipse. There is no workspace, no plug-in registry, no update site, no OSGi. Modules are standard Java modules (JPMS) and Maven artifacts. The influence of EMF is everywhere; the IDE is nowhere.

Not Spring. There is no container that owns object lifecycles, no classpath scanning, no XML or annotation configuration of beans. Services are registered in module-info.java, and capabilities are resolved on request.

Not a modeling tool. There is no diagram editor in the runtime. Models are authored as text (Xcore, a Groovy DSL, YAML), harvested from what already exists, or drawn in tools people already use, and the runtime loads them.

Not an observability backend. It does not compete with Grafana or Datadog. Operational telemetry is sampled, retained for days and forgotten; the runtime is for the small fraction of signals worth keeping, resolved against a model, for years.

Not a platform you rent. There is no server. Models live in Git and in Maven repositories, reference each other by URI, and are owned by whoever publishes them. Everything runs locally, in a container, or in a CI pipeline, as the same artifact.

Not all or nothing. You take the modules you need. A Java program that wants a volume over a directory depends on the volume module and nothing else above the foundation.

1.7. Who gets what

Architects get structure at the cost of a text file. A vocabulary in Meta is one source for a generated glossary, a JSON Schema for a tool call, a TypeScript package for a user interface, and a lookup an agent can be grounded in (Chapter 21). A running system can describe itself: a JVM snapshot shows what an assembly became after its modules were resolved, which no build file says (Chapter 22). Telemetry kept as a model is evidence of who changed what, in the course of what work, years after the fact (Chapter 13). Because models are files in Git and artifacts in Maven repositories, teams own their parts and reference each other’s, and nobody administers the whole.

Developers get a foundation that is small, observable from the first line, and tested. The examples in this book depend on the runtime and on JUnit; the runtime depends on the JDK, EMF, the OpenTelemetry API and a handful of libraries that do something the JDK does not.

Subject-matter experts get their words written down precisely without learning a notation: an assistant drafts a vocabulary from what they say and hand over, the build checks its structure, and they correct its meaning (Section 21.9).

Agents get typed models instead of prose, operations that are tools by construction, and file systems they already know how to use.

1.8. A short tour

The rest of the book explains how each piece works. Here is what a few of them look like from the outside, using the output of the book’s examples.

The first program in Chapter 6 builds a one-class metamodel at run time, saves an instance as XMI, JSON and YAML, and does nothing else. Run under a publishing OpenTelemetry instance, with no SDK and no backend, this is what it prints:

> Save a book
  > ResourceSetContributor.configure
    Contributed uri-handler ...ClassPathURIHandlerFactory$1
    Contributed contributor ...XMIResourceFactoryContributor
    Contributed contributor ...JsonResourceFactoryContributor
    ...
  < ResourceSetContributor.configure
  > Resource.save
    Saved file:/tmp/watch-it/book.xmi: 230 bytes
  < Resource.save
  ...
< Save a book

Nobody instrumented that program. The runtime’s resource set configuration, resource factories and URI handlers report what they do through the OpenTelemetry API, and whoever runs the program decides where it goes.

The command line example in Chapter 16 contributes a library command and a few sub-commands. The runtime’s own save command was written long before that example and knows nothing about libraries, yet it appears under library, because the library command offers what save declares it needs: something that supplies a collection of EMF objects.

nsdk
  launcher
  hello
  library
    books
    export
      csv
      markdown
    save

And the recording example in Chapter 13 edits a library inside a span, with the OpenTelemetry SDK exporting to the telemetry model. Reading the saved traces back as a model, the change is in the span that made it:

Curate the shelf
  * created Library 'A Modeler's Shelf'
  Resource.save (2059 bytes)
  Correct the year
    * Book 'Domain-Driven Design'.year = 2004
    Resource.save (2059 bytes)

That last output is the point of the whole runtime in miniature. "Somebody changed the year of a book" is a log line. "In the course of the work named 'Correct the year', this attribute of this object changed to this value", with the work, the object and the attribute all being model elements you can navigate and query, is structure. It cost one line of code: Changes.record(…​) around the edit.

1.9. Where this is going

The runtime is a seed. Its North Star, explained in Chapter 26, is agentic work on models: executable graphs whose activities include AI agents, operating on bounded, typed models, with transactional safety and state saved to Git, runnable on a laptop, in a container or in a CI pipeline as the same artifact. Several capabilities on the way there are useful long before it, and they are what this book is mostly about: models without an IDE, telemetry without a backend, files without a file system, and a command line without configuration.

The next chapter states the principles the runtime follows. They are short, and every later design decision traces back to one of them.

Chapter 2. Principles

A runtime is a long series of small decisions. Most of them are made under time pressure, by whoever happens to be writing the code, and the result is consistent only if the decisions follow from a few rules that everybody knows. This chapter states the rules the Nasdanika SDK Runtime follows, with the reasoning behind each one. Later chapters refer back to them by name.

2.1. Pure Nasdanika: the JDK, EMF core and the OpenTelemetry API

The foundation of the runtime is three things:

  • The JDK, currently Java 25.

  • EMF core: org.eclipse.emf.common, org.eclipse.emf.ecore and org.eclipse.emf.ecore.xmi.

  • The OpenTelemetry API: io.opentelemetry.api and io.opentelemetry.context, not the SDK.

I call this "pure Nasdanika". Any module may depend on all three, common does, and code that uses only them counts as foundational. All three are small, stable, and standard in their space, which matters more than any feature they have: a platform team can approve "Java, EMF and the OpenTelemetry API" in a meeting, while "Java, EMF, Reactor, Netty, Jackson and two vendor SDKs" is a review.

Everything beyond the foundation is justified per module. emf-json brings Jackson because EMF JSON is implemented on it. groovy brings Groovy because it is a Groovy DSL. The command line module brings picocli and JLine because they are what a command line is made of. None of them is allowed into common. The one exception made so far is geantyref, a tiny library with no dependencies that common uses to match generic types, wrapped behind the runtime’s own Types class so that no public signature mentions it (Chapter 8).

2.2. If the JDK can do it, use the JDK

Occam’s razor, applied to dependencies: a third-party library earns its place by doing something the JDK does not do.

Concern The usual choice The runtime’s choice

HTTP client

Netty, vendor SDKs

java.net.http.HttpClient

HTTP server

Netty, servlet containers

com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer on virtual threads

Asynchrony

Reactor Mono and Flux

Blocking code on virtual threads; java.util.concurrent.Flow

Ambient context

Thread locals, frameworks

ScopedValue, and the OpenTelemetry Context

JSON

Jackson data binding

org.json where JSON is a wire format; EMF JSON where it is a model format

Logging API

SLF4J and a backend

The OpenTelemetry Logs API, correlated with spans; where a log record goes is decided by whoever runs the unit of work

Most of the libraries in the middle column were written before the JDK had the feature. Reactor and Netty solved a real problem: a blocked platform thread was expensive, so non-blocking I/O and reactive composition were the only way to serve many concurrent requests. Virtual threads removed the cost. The reasons to take the dependency expired; the dependencies did not.

Blocking code is also better code for the work the runtime is heading toward. An agentic loop is sequential: call the model, run a tool, call again. On virtual threads that reads as it runs, the OpenTelemetry context propagates through straight-line code with no hooks, spans nest the way the code nests, and stack traces are readable. Reactive operators pay off for fan-in and fan-out pipelines, and the runtime keeps Flow for those (Chapter 9).

There is one refinement. Where the runtime consumes something, it uses the JDK’s API. Where it implements something many times, it prefers a small interface of its own. File systems are the example: NIO is how the runtime reads existing file systems, and Volume, an interface with five methods in the shape of Go’s io/fs, is what it implements over a directory, an in-memory tree, a running JVM or a remote system (Chapter 14). Implementing an NIO file system provider is a large job; implementing a volume is an afternoon.

2.3. If Xcore can model it, model it

Data and APIs are Xcore classes and operations, not hand-written Java beans and interfaces.

A model is more than a data structure. It is documented, so a generated site explains it to people. It is serializable, to XMI, JSON, YAML or binary, so a snapshot is a file you can diff and commit. It is reflective, so a viewer can show any object without code written for its class, and a query language can traverse it. And with operation reflection turned on, every operation can be invoked by name with arguments, which means an operation is already a tool: it has a name, parameters, types and documentation, which is everything a tool declaration for an agent needs.

The cost is a code generator in the build. Chapter 7 shows that this cost is now one Maven plugin and a text file, which is the change that made the principle affordable.

2.4. Telemetry is part of the runtime

Instrumentation is not an add-on that somebody remembers to do later. Every runtime module that does something worth knowing about reports it through the OpenTelemetry API, and modules wrap the JDK APIs they use so that instrumentation is the default. Four conventions make that consistent:

Spans for operations, log records for what happens in them. A span has a duration; a log line, a measurement or the progress of a long-running operation is a log record emitted through the OpenTelemetry Logs API, correlated with the current span. Span events are not used, because OpenTelemetry is moving events onto the Logs API.

One OpenTelemetry per unit of work. A unit of work is a command, a request or a test. It builds or is handed an OpenTelemetry instance and makes it current, the way it would make a span current, and everything instrumented underneath reports to it. GlobalOpenTelemetry is never used. This is what lets one command save its own telemetry next to its own output, while another, running in the same JVM, sends its telemetry somewhere else.

Console output is a subscriber, not a second API. Progress bars and live trees subscribe to the same span and log events that a model exporter or a backend receives (Chapter 12).

Every signal is precious. Mainstream observability collects everything cheaply, samples, and forgets within days. The runtime is for the opposite end: deliberate collection, indefinite retention, and every signal resolved against a model, so that "who changed what, in the course of what work" can be answered years later (Chapter 13). The two are complementary: the same instrumentation can feed an operational backend and a model at once.

2.5. Services before capabilities

The runtime has two ways for code to find other code, and the rule for choosing between them is simple:

  • When the lookup is by type alone, such as every EPackage or every resource set contributor, it is a Java service, registered in module-info.java and found with java.util.ServiceLoader.

  • When there is a requirement object for providers to interpret ("a renderer for this format", "a contents handler for this file name"), or when resolving one thing requires resolving others, it is the capability framework (Chapter 10).

ServiceLoader is a dozen lines of JDK and costs nothing. The capability framework is more powerful and has a cost: a resolution, a pump, memoization, telemetry. Using it where a service would do is the kind of generality that makes a codebase hard to read.

2.6. Declaration is registration

The runtime avoids strings that name types and configuration files that list classes. What a module contributes is declared in its module-info.java (provides CapabilityFactory with …​), and what a contribution provides and needs is declared in Java types the compiler checks.

A capability method’s generic return type is what it provides, and its parameters are what it needs. A command’s @Parent field says, by its generic type, which parents it can work under. An adapter method’s return type says what an object can be adapted to. One class can declare many such members behind a single entry in module-info, and a refactoring tool renames them like any other code.

The honest caveat goes with it: objects carry no type arguments at run time, so what is matched is always a declaration, never an instance. A method declared to return Supplier<Library> is matched as one, whatever it actually returns.

2.7. Micro-models and nano-models

Models rot the way applications do: they accrete concepts until every consumer pays for every concept. The answer is the one the industry found for applications and for code: decompose along concerns, and make the dependencies explicit. Microservices decompose deployment, Java modules decompose code, and micro-models decompose meaning.

A micro-model is a small model with a single concern, explicit dependencies on other models, and no knowledge of its consumers, in a module of its own, so that it is versioned, released and adopted on its own. Extension happens at the edge: a model extends the models below it, and they never learn about it. Meta and the JVM model are micro-models.

A nano-model is smaller still: one of several models in one module, because they are reused and changed together. The core model and its kind package are two nano-models in one module; telemetry, traces, logs and metrics are four in another. The Xtext Maven plugin generates every .xcore file under its source root in one go, so a nano-model costs one file. One model per project was an Eclipse convention, and nothing in the runtime needs it.

A new module, rather than a new file, is justified by a dependency the others do not want, a different set of consumers, or a different maturity. The telemetry exporters need the OpenTelemetry SDK, so they are a module of their own, while the four telemetry models share one.

The size of a model has a budget, and the budget is attention. Code hides its implementation behind an interface; a model hides nothing, because its concepts are its interface. So a model should fit in the head of the team that maintains it, and its core concepts should fit in one diagram that a newcomer understands in a quarter of an hour. A model whose diagram outgrows a page is two models. The same budget makes a model fit in the context of an AI assistant (Chapter 3).

2.8. One identity per module

Every module has one path in the repository, and every name it has is derived from that path.

Identity Rule

JPMS module and root package

org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime. followed by the path with / as ., dropping a trailing model segment: models/telemetry/model is org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.models.telemetry

Maven coordinates

Group org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime followed by the parent path, artifact the last segment: org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.models.telemetry:model

Namespace URI of a model

The model’s page: runtime.sdk.nasdanika.org/models/telemetry, and a child path for each further model in the module, such as …​/models/telemetry/traces

Documentation page

runtime.sdk.nasdanika.org/ followed by the path

One rule means any identity can be computed from the others, and someone who has seen one module knows where to find the next. It also removes name and version clashes with the older Nasdanika organizations by construction: nothing in the runtime shares a Maven group, a module name or a package with them, so the old and the new line can sit on one machine during a migration.

2.9. Pull, don’t push

The runtime grows from a seed, one increment at a time, and modules from the older Nasdanika code base come in when an increment needs them, not before. Each increment has to state the capability it adds, the demonstration that shows it, what it pulls in, and that a clean clone builds.

Pulling a module is not moving it. Its core comes in as a small library, and each integration becomes a separate adapter that is pulled only when something needs it. common started empty: a helper enters it when a second module needs it and no JDK feature replaces it. That keeps common from becoming the place things go because they have nowhere else to go.

The same rule shapes how documentation and sites are produced. A site is not pushed out by a generator that knows every page; it is pulled from a model presented as files, by whatever reads it: a static copy, an HTTP server, a WebDAV mount, an agent (Chapter 15).

2.10. Local first, federated, no server

Everything the runtime does runs on a laptop, in a container and in a CI pipeline, as the same artifact. There is no central server and no administrator of the whole.

Models are files in Git and artifacts in Maven repositories. They reference each other by URI, the way a class references a class in another jar, and URI handlers load them transparently from wherever they are. A team owns its vocabulary and publishes it; another team references it without either coordinating a release. A published version is what it was, so "what did this mean last quarter" is an install, not an archaeology project.

This matters most where data cannot leave the building. Local telemetry, local models and local agents are the configuration that a regulated organization can approve.

2.11. Say what is stuck

A failure that does not say what failed is a mystery, and mysteries are expensive. The runtime prefers reports to guesses:

  • The pump that drives capability resolution and transformations fails at once when nothing can progress, with a list of what was waiting for what, including the path of a dependency cycle (Chapter 9).

  • A capability loader can be given a listener that explains, line by line, which factories were asked about a requirement, which declined, and what each produced (Chapter 10).

  • Command wiring fails with the types a command needed and what its parent offered, and asking for help never fails on wiring (Chapter 17).

2.12. Humans at both ends

Draw software development as a line from intent to operation. AI is taking the middle of that line: writing code, writing tests, translating between formats. It pushes people out to both ends.

To the left is intent: deciding what things are, what words mean, who owns which fact. That is modeling, and it is why the runtime makes models cheap.

To the right is assurance: knowing what the system actually did. Assurance means checking what ran against what was intended, and that check is only as good as the evidence. Telemetry per unit of work answers "what did this command or this agent turn do?". A JVM snapshot answers "what actually runs?". Live observation answers "what is it doing right now?", for the person who has to decide whether to stop it.

When intent and evidence are both models, assurance is a query instead of a meeting.
