With the principles stated, the next chapter tells how the runtime is built, by one engineer and an AI assistant, and why that changes which technologies are practical.

Chapter 3. Built with an AI assistant

The runtime’s repository was created on 29 September 2026. This edition describes it twenty-six days and 59 commits later. By then it held about 40,000 lines of Java and 24,000 lines of tests in 395 test cases, 8,800 lines of Xcore from which EMF generates about 449,000 lines of Java, and 2,600 lines of Groovy. Part of it was migrated from earlier Nasdanika repositories rather than written from scratch, and the migration was work too: new packages, new identities, new conventions.

One person did this work, with an AI coding assistant. This chapter is about how, because the how is part of the argument of the book. The runtime is built on technologies that most organizations have kept at arm’s length for twenty years, for a reason that no longer holds.

3.1. Binding decisions

My favorite definition of software development comes from a talk by Ivar Jacobson that I heard around 2006. This is how I remember what he said: software development is the process of binding decisions to make them executable. A design starts as a space of open questions, and development binds them one by one, at design time, at build time, at deployment and at run time, until what is left can run.

The definition does not say who binds. For most of the history of software, people bound every decision, and compilers and builds checked that the bindings were consistent. An assistant now binds some of them: a name, a data structure, a library, a way of handling errors, the shape of an interface, and now and then one that matters a great deal. That is the real change, more than the speed, and it makes the traceability of binding paramount: which decision was bound, by whom or by what, in the course of what work, and on what evidence.

The runtime makes binding traceable at both times. During development, a decision is written down before the code that binds it, in the loop described later in this chapter; changes to models are recorded in the spans that made them (Chapter 13), and markers record where an element came from (Chapter 20). During execution, the runtime binds late and says how: a capability loader can explain which factories it asked about a requirement, which declined and what each produced (Chapter 10), command wiring that fails names the types a command needed and what its parent offered (Chapter 17), and a JVM snapshot records how modules and services were bound when an assembly started (Chapter 22). Late binding without a record is magic; with a record, it is a decision that can be reviewed.

3.2. Who does what

The division of labor settled quickly, and it is worth stating plainly, because it is easy to get wrong in both directions: an assistant is neither an autocomplete nor a colleague who can be left alone.

Intent comes from experience. I decide what the runtime is for, which problems are worth solving, and in what order. That judgment comes from decades of building software and of watching what works and what does not, in projects of every size. The principles of Chapter 2 are such lessons, written down. Documentation is part of the model because I have watched documentation drift away from what it describes wherever the two were kept apart. The JVM model snapshots what runs because I have seen dependency trees that bore little relation to it. Telemetry is a model kept with the work because telemetry kept for a week cannot answer the question asked a year later.

Research comes from the assistant. Every design starts with a question: who has done this before, and what did they learn? The volume interface of Chapter 14 was compared with Go’s io/fs, Python’s fsspec, Visual Studio Code’s file system provider, Hadoop’s FileSystem, Apache Commons VFS and Eclipse EFS before a line of it was written. The polymorphic user interface of Chapter 24 was set against Naked Objects, EMF.Edit, JSON Forms and Django’s admin. When I believed an idea was new, the research often found that it was not, which is better news than it sounds: an idea with twenty years of precedent is easier to adopt and to defend than a novelty, and the precedent shows where the pitfalls are. The assistant checks claims as well as designs: a claim about what a regulation requires was checked against the text of the regulation and narrowed in the draft.

Implementation comes from the assistant. Changes that would take a person weeks take hours. The pumped publisher, the transformer and the capability loader were rebuilt as one engine, with tests, in a day (Chapter 9). Telemetry per unit of work went into the runtime’s core classes, with tests, in another (Chapter 11). Mechanical work that is tedious and error-prone for people, such as renaming packages across modules, aligning identities, migrating a module from an older code base and regenerating models, is fast and consistent for an assistant.

Assurance stays with people, and with the build. I review designs, read diffs and decide. The build checks the rest: every module is tested, every listing in this book is compiled and tested, and a warning in the manuscript fails the build. Writing this book was also a review of the runtime: describing what the code does exposed where it did not do what it should. A command tree was assembled only in part, two families of dependencies were out of step, and names had drifted. Each became an editor’s note in the first draft, and each was fixed in the next session.

The division is older than assistants: when I designed scientific devices, I drew them, my boss reviewed the drawings and a workshop built the devices as drawn; an assistant does the workshop’s part, from intent and models instead of drawings.

The routing of work is older than software, too. When I bought my first PC, in 1996, my mother thought I was crazy. Then she saw an opportunity in it and built a writing business that fed our extended family for several years. Each writer in the family specialized in a field; my mother took the orders and routed each one to the writer whose field it was. She never called it orchestration, but that is what it was: one who understands the request and knows who is good at what, and specialists who do the work. Multi-agent systems are built the same way today, and the part my mother played is the part that stays with people.

3.3. One level up

Development with an assistant, as this chapter describes it, is the same activity as development without one, a level of abstraction higher: further to the left on the line from intent to operation (Chapter 2), closer to the why and the what than to the how.

Without an assistant I write code, and the compiler tells me where I got it wrong: a typo, a reference to a type that does not exist, a generic type that does not fit. In my C++ years I loved templates, and they were one of my nightmares: a small flaw in a design, and I spent hours sifting through pages of compiler errors to find it.

With an assistant I write intent, and the feedback is about the intent. The assistant tells me the prior art of an idea, how my idea differs from it, what the difference is worth, and what to watch for and improve. Like the compiler’s, the feedback comes in minutes and costs little, so I can afford to be wrong early, at the level where being wrong is cheapest.

The feedback is not a proof, though. A compiler that accepts a program has checked it; an assistant that agrees with an idea has only not found a reason to disagree. So the decision stays with me, and the compiler and the tests still check everything below it.

3.4. The mainstream filter

For two decades EMF was hard to propose in most large organizations, and not because it did not work. Technology choices there pass through a filter that is rarely written down: will an average developer on an average team be able to work with it? A technology that fails the filter is "too complex", however much it would save. The mainstream framework, which in the Java world means Spring, passes by definition, so it wins by default. It is a fine framework; the problem was never the choice, but a filter that left room for only one.

The filter was rational. The cost of a technology includes the cost of everyone who has to understand it, and people fluent in EMF were few. The price of the mainstream choice was paid elsewhere, and quietly: in the effort of explaining what needed to be done, in reviewing whether it had been done right, and often in doing it yourself. It also produced judgments that sound odd side by side. Two hundred lines of Xcore were too complex; fifty thousand lines of AI-generated TypeScript were a great achievement. The first measured the cost of understanding; the second measured output.

This is not a criticism of developers. Fluency follows exposure, and organizations exposed their people to what the market used most. It is a description of an economy in which fluency was scarce.

I paid that price myself. The specifications of a code generator I built for a cloud migration (Prior art, first-hand) were EMF models saved as XMI. My teammates did not know EMF, so they edited the XMI in a text editor, and the generator worked anyway. The obstacle was not the model but the format it asked people to read. If the mountain will not come to Mohammed, Mohammed must go to the mountain: since then I keep models in formats people already read and write, YAML, JSON and Groovy scripts (Chapter 19), with EMF behind them.

3.5. When fluency is not scarce

An assistant is fluent in Xcore, EMF, OpenTelemetry, the Java module system, picocli and Groovy, and in Spring and React as well. It does not tire of explaining, and it does not need things explained to it twice. The premise of the filter, that a technology must be within reach of every developer working unaided, loses its force when nobody works unaided.

Two questions take its place.

Is it the right abstraction? Mendeleev is said to have compared burning petroleum as fuel to heating a stove with banknotes: a valuable resource spent on low-value work. An assistant writing the boilerplate of a framework is the same trade. Its leverage compounds when it works a level or two higher: on models that generate the routine code, on languages that remove the need for it, on user interfaces that render themselves from the model. In this runtime, 8,800 lines of Xcore generate about 449,000 lines of Java, and people review the 8,800. Xcore is the concise, high-level representation; the generated Java is the verbose, low-level implementation. Xcore is declarative with occasional operations - much smaller human review surface and "attack surface" for errors.

Can the result be checked? What an assistant produces must be checkable, cheaply, by people and by machines. That is a design constraint, and it explains much of this book: typed models instead of maps of strings, generic types that the compiler checks (Chapter 8), declarations instead of registration code, tests for every module, listings that compile, telemetry kept as models (Chapter 13), and changes recorded in the spans that made them, so that what an agent did can be reviewed and reverted.

Understanding still matters; it moves. It moves from the mechanics of a framework, which the assistant carries, to the meaning of the model, which only the people who own the domain can judge. That is where the experienced engineer, the architect and the domain expert spend their time, and it is a better use of it.

Fluency can be borrowed from an assistant; judgment cannot. Judgment grows the way any expertise does, by what psychologists call deliberate practice: practice aimed at what one cannot do yet, with feedback, and often with a teacher who explains (Ericsson, Krampe and Tesch-Römer, 1993). My kung fu teacher calls it eating bitter (Where the opinions come from), and nobody can eat it for you. What an assistant changes is the price of the practice, not the need for it. Its feedback comes in minutes (Section 3.3), and the hours it saves on the mechanics of a framework can go to practice at the level that matters: the model, and whether it is right.

3.6. Fall back to the keep

In The Two Towers, when the outer wall of Helm’s Deep is breached, the defenders fall back to the keep of the Hornburg, the innermost and strongest part of the fortress; in the film the order is shouted along the wall: "Fall back to the keep!"

The analogy is not literal. Assistants are not the enemy; they are allies, and very capable ones. But the shape of the situation is similar. Assistants now hold most of the outer wall: they write code, tests and documentation faster than people can read them. What people keep is the place from which they can still check what was built, and the stronger that place, the more of the work can safely be given to the assistants.

I think the JVM is a better keep for people than Node.js. Its declarations are checked by a compiler and kept in the class files, so a person or a program can read what a part claims to provide and rely on the claim, and the runtime matches parts on those declarations with the compiler’s rules (Chapter 8). And with JavaScript as a generation target (Chapter 23), falling back to the keep gives up nothing in the browser.

There is also the matter of where the systems already are. In my experience, in the enterprises I have worked in and with, Java has been at least twice as common as Node.js for systems in production, and about an order of magnitude as common as Python. I measured it once. Scanning the tens of thousands of source repositories of one bank (Prior art, first-hand), I counted about twice as many Java files as JavaScript files, with all of JavaScript’s extensions counted, and about ten times as many as Python files. That is one organization, and it counts files rather than systems in production, so it is evidence, not research: I know of no public study that measures it, and developer surveys measure something else, the languages developers use, by which JavaScript and Python are ahead of Java. Both can be true at once, since many developers write some JavaScript and some Python, while the business logic (e.g. microservices) of large organizations, in my experience, run disproportionately on the JVM - comparing to JavaScript and Python and excluding mainframes.

3.7. How the work flows

The work runs as a loop, and every turn of it leaves something written down.

  1. Intent. A few paragraphs of what I want and why, often ending with a request for an assessment.

  2. Assessment. The assistant agrees or pushes back, finds prior art, and names risks and alternatives. I decide.

  3. Design. The decision is recorded: a design document, or a section of the roadmap saying where the work lands (Section 3.8).

  4. Increment. Code, tests and documentation change together, and the build is green from a clean clone.

  5. Observation. Using the result, and reading its telemetry, produces the next intent.

A few rules keep the loop honest, and they serve people and assistants alike:

  • One source of truth per fact: one identity rule, one model, and generated code that is never edited by hand.

  • Everything is compiled and tested, the listings of this book included.

  • Failures say what is stuck, which helps an assistant find a cause as much as it helps a person.

  • Small models. A micro-model, one concern in one module (Chapter 2), fits in an assistant’s context as well as in a person’s head.

  • Documentation anchored to the model. A micro-wiki (Chapter 20) gives every model element a documentation file of its own, so people and assistants know which file to edit when they learn something about an element.

  • Status labels. What is available, sketched or planned is marked, so that neither people nor assistants mistake a design for a feature.

3.8. Gradient ascent

The loop turns on a roadmap, and keeping the roadmap is one of the most valuable things the assistant does.

I have used Jira, and it is good at what it was made for: a unit of work with an owner, a status and a history. It is not good at what a project like this one needs most, which is ideas that depend on each other. A new idea rarely stands alone: it revises two earlier decisions, makes a third unnecessary and changes the order of the next five steps. A tracker records such links as "relates to", keeps the reasoning in comments, and orders the work by a rank field. What I need to know is not the rank of an item but the best next action: the step that brings the most value for the time and effort it costs, given everything already decided.

The runtime’s roadmap is a single Markdown document, started on 19 September 2026. A month later it held about 72,000 words, more than this book, in 32 dated sections, each written in answer to an intent of mine. A section has a regular shape: the decision, the assistant’s assessment of it, the prior art, what it revises in earlier sections, and where it lands in the order of the work. Nothing is rewritten silently. When a decision supersedes an earlier one, the earlier section stays and the later one says which of them wins, so the roadmap is also the history of how the plan changed and why.

In that sense the roadmap is a log, as a database keeps one: entries are only appended, a later entry overrides an earlier one, and what is true now is what the log says once all of it has been read. And like a log, it has to be compacted from time to time, for the same reason an assistant compacts a long conversation: the reader has a limited context, and the more the log grows, the more of that context goes to finding out what still holds. The first compaction came on 25 October, when the roadmap had reached about 89,000 words. A new document became the plan of record: the decisions still standing, one line each with a link to the section that argued it, the ranked list of next steps, and new dated sections after them. Unlike a conversation’s summary, this one lost nothing: the old document stays as it was, as the record of why each decision was made, and the new one starts where it ends.

The assistant maintains it. When I bring an idea, it reads the roadmap, places the idea among the decisions already made, says what the idea revises and what it makes unnecessary, and proposes where it lands and what to do next. I decide, and the decision becomes a section. Kept by hand, a document like this would be a job of its own, and it would drift within weeks. Kept by an assistant, it costs minutes per idea and stays consistent, because the assistant reads all of it each time it is asked.

The order that comes out of it is a gradient ascent, the mirror image of the gradient descent that trains neural networks: from where the work stands, take the step that climbs steepest, the most value per unit of effort, then measure the slope again. Value includes what a step makes cheaper later, not only what it delivers now, and the slope changes after every step, because every step changes what the next one costs and what it is worth.

For its first nine days, the plan of record was a migration in one piece: move the models of the older Nasdanika code base into a new core, then build on it. On 28 September it became a seed crystal instead: start from one small working core and grow it one increment at a time, each adding a capability that a demonstration shows. An epic that would have delivered nothing until it ended, a slope of zero for weeks, became a climb that delivers something at every step, and code that no increment needed was never migrated, which settled the size of the migration better than any analysis would have. Four days later the route turned again: the North Star stayed, and the capabilities useful without language models, such as telemetry, volumes and the JVM model, moved ahead of the ones that need them, because they gave developers something to use now for a fraction of the effort.

Gradient methods have a known weakness: they climb the nearest hill, which need not be the highest. The North Star is the guard against it (Chapter 26): a step that climbs steeply in another direction is not admitted, and the rule for an increment is that test, written down.

The roadmap is the least formal artifact of the project, and deliberately so. It is where decisions are bound first, in prose, while binding them is still cheap to undo; designs, models and code bind them further and become formal as they do. What keeps the prose useful is not a schema but a reader that reads all of it every time.

3.9. What the assistant does not do

  • Decide what matters. The North Star, the order of the work and the trade-offs are mine (Chapter 26).

  • Know what is not written down: the constraints of an organization, the history behind a decision, the people involved. An assistant sees what it is given, which is why grounding it in models matters (Chapter 1).

  • Own the consequences. A person signs off on what ships.

  • Be right every time. An assistant can be confidently wrong, as people can. Types, tests, reviews and failing builds catch it, and the same habit of research that finds prior art also catches my mistakes: claims of novelty, a misremembered fact, a requirement read too broadly.

3.10. This book

This book was written the same way. I described what it should be and for whom; the assistant read the runtime’s code, my stories and the roadmap, wrote the examples first and the prose around them, built the PDF and looked at its pages. I review, correct and decide. The examples are modules of the runtime’s build, so the book cannot claim what the code does not do without the build saying so. In that sense the book is code: if an example does not build, neither does the book.

It is also small, measured the way an assistant measures text. This edition is about 56,000 words, listings included, or roughly 100,000 tokens: about a tenth of a context window of a million tokens. An assistant will rarely load all of it, and does not need to. It looks things up the way an engineer does: a term in the glossary, a convention in the rules of thumb, the chapter about the module it is changing, and the example module a listing comes from, which the manuscript names in each include. A book grounds an assistant well when it is small enough to hold whole and structured enough not to have to. The same holds for the books around it: this book is one of the Nasdanika Body of Knowledge, whose layout and reading order are the subject of Appendix F.

Writing the book reviewed the runtime, and reading it reviewed my thinking. Graham Wallas recorded a child’s question in 1926, and E. M. Forster attributed it to an old lady a year later: "How can I tell what I think till I see what I say?" Working with an assistant gives the question a second reading: how can I tell what I think till I see what it makes of what I have said? Reading the drafts of this book, I kept having the same reaction: this is what I meant, and I never quite put it like that. For years I had written about what makes structure last, a story at a time, and an assistant put it in three words: small, formal, composable (Chapter 1).

Recognition is a check, but a weak one, because a fluent summary can feel right without being right. A distillation earns its place when it can be tested, and this one can: take away any one of the three words and you get a failure I have seen many times.

The next chapter is about the organizations the runtime is built for: what an assistant amplifies in them, and why many of them will resist an approach like this one.

Chapter 4. Against the grain

The previous chapter is about how the runtime was built. This one is about the organizations it is built for, and why many of them will resist it. An assistant amplifies the way of working it is given: it makes a faster horse faster, and it lets people who never owned their code produce more of it. The sections below describe five patterns I have watched for years, with the names others have given them, and what the runtime does about each.

4.1. Faster horses

Steve Jobs liked to quote a line he credited to Henry Ford, although nobody has found it in anything Ford said or wrote: if he had asked his customers what they wanted, they would have said a faster horse. Developers given AI tools often ask for a faster horse. They speed up the tasks they know, such as boilerplate, mappings between formats and tests for code that should not exist, when the tasks themselves should be rethought. Modern trains do not have stokers with ergonomic shovels. They do not have stokers.

A smaller count is not a weaker system either. In the third presidential debate of 2012, answering the charge that the Navy had fewer ships than in 1916, Barack Obama said: "Well, Governor, we also have fewer horses and bayonets, because the nature of our military’s changed." Lines of code, services and boxes on a diagram count the stokers, not the train. The question to ask before giving a task to an assistant is not how to do it faster but whether it should be done at all; in this runtime the answer is often a model and a generator (Chapter 7, Chapter 23).

4.2. Owning the result

An assistant raises the stakes of ownership. Somebody has to see the big picture and own the why, the how and the assurance of what ships, and with an assistant that somebody did not type most of it. Owning what you did not type takes evidence: what changed, in the course of what work, at whose request, and how to undo it. That is one of the reasons the runtime keeps telemetry as a model and records changes down to single attributes, in the spans that made them (Chapter 13): "the assistant did something" becomes a list of changes to review and, if need be, to revert.

Tools do not create ownership where the organization of work does not. For decades much of the industry has separated deciding from doing: the people who write the code are not the people who decide why it is written, and neither answers for how it runs. Teams measured by tickets closed and staffed by the hour learn to stay inside their tickets. Given AI tools, they produce more code, faster, that they do not understand and do not want to own.

The same separation produces a pattern I have watched more than once. An architect with better AI tools than the team generates tens of thousands of lines in a language of their own choosing, with no regard for what the team knows or for what the organization uses for that kind of component: TypeScript, so that the user interface and the business logic share one code base, for a team of Spring developers in an organization that builds its server side in Java and Spring. There is a demo, a round of applause from the business,the code is handed over, and the architect moves on to the next team. The developers are left to work out what they now own, and to take the blame if it fails. The same pattern deploys a vector database for a similarity search over fifty vectors, which a loop over an array answers in microseconds. The database costs money and does nothing a loop would not, and the person who chose it does not pay for it; what they get is another box on a diagram and a line in the resume.

These patterns have names, which is some comfort: it is not only me who sees them. Nassim Taleb calls what the architect lacks skin in the game: making decisions without bearing their consequences. Choosing a technology for how it looks on a résumé, or on a diagram, rather than for the problem has been defined and measured as résumé-driven development (Fritzsch and others, 2021).

Where people do not contradict those above them, which students of culture call high power distance, an organization learns only what its leaders already believe. John Maxwell calls this the law of the lid: an organization rises no higher than the ability of the person who leads it (Maxwell, 1998). If the boss has mastered addition, whoever computes 1 + 2 + …​ + 99 + 100 as n(n + 1) / 2 will be flogged. Legend has the young Carl Friedrich Gauss do exactly that in a Brunswick schoolroom in the 1780s, writing 5050 on his slate while his classmates were still adding, under a schoolmaster known for his cane; that schoolmaster, at least, recognized the answer. To my surprise, I have crossed paths with several people in the twenty-first century who epitomize the law. Nokia is a studied case: interviews with 76 of its managers and engineers found middle managers who feared their superiors and peers and kept bad news from the top, and top managers who, with a rosier view of the company’s technology than the facts supported, underinvested in what came next (Vuori and Huy, 2016). Aviation met the problem in the cockpit and answered it with crew resource management, which trains first officers to challenge captains, and with checklists that ignore rank. The software equivalent is evidence anyone can query: a junior engineer who can point to the decision record and the trace does not have to contradict a superior. When intent and evidence are both models, assurance is a query instead of a meeting (Chapter 2).

None of this is a failing of the tools, or of people who work the way they were taught to. It is what happens when the people who bind decisions are not the people who live with them. The runtime cannot reorganize a company, but it can keep the binding visible and keep ownership where it belongs. Decisions are recorded before the code, changes are recorded in the spans that made them, and generated code is the output of models the owning team works with: the web models of Chapter 23 let a team of Java developers own a React application as Java code and models, without a second code base in TypeScript.

4.3. Stories are not source code

This section is speculation, and I label it as such.

Agile, as many large organizations practice it, works like a virtual machine. Stories are its instructions: small, uniform, prioritized, and executed by teams sprint after sprint. The machine compiles intent into running software, which is what an AI assistant does as well. What it does not keep is the source. Ron Jeffries described the card of a user story as "a token representing the requirement", with the requirement itself carried by conversation; in the machine, the card is all there is. The why, the vocabulary and the whole that the stories are parts of are in nobody’s repository.

Armies, which nobody accuses of loose hierarchy, settled this long ago. In the combat regulations I was trained on (Where the opinions come from), the first duty of a platoon commander who receives a mission is to understand it: the task of the company as well as the platoon’s own, the tasks of the neighbors and how to coordinate with them, and the time to be ready. The US Army asks the same of its platoon leaders, who must understand the situation and the commander’s intent one and two levels above their own (Field Manual 3-21.8, 2007). A story card carries the platoon’s task and leaves out the level above and the neighbors.

That has always been the tension between architecture and agile as practiced: architecture is about the source, and the machine ships only bytecode. I am not alone in seeing the machine: Martin Fowler named it the Agile Industrial Complex, which imposes process on teams in the name of agility, and John Cutler described teams that crank out features without measuring their effect as a feature factory.

AI assistance as this book describes it pulls toward the source: intent and models at the left end of the line (Chapter 2), compiled by an assistant and checked by the build. A machine built to turn stories into code competes with the assistant at what the assistant does best, and I expect the tension to grow. None of this is an argument against agility. The Agile Manifesto values individuals and interactions over processes and tools; much of what is practiced in its name inverts that.

4.4. When a question becomes answerable

Most of what I describe in Prior art, first-hand made a question answerable that had not been: which processes are dead, which packages tie a monolith into a knot, who owns an application, on what grounds a technology was chosen. While a question cannot be answered, nobody is accountable for the answer. Once it can be, somebody is. An answer arrives with three costs that have little to do with the technology that produced it, and knowing them in advance saves disappointment.

It moves decisions. In 2008 I built a model for choosing technologies with the Analytic Hierarchy Process: a hierarchy of criteria, several experts weighted by their expertise in each branch of it, alternatives compared in pairs, and the consistency of each expert computed. It worked, and it went no further, because using it would have changed who decides and how. That is an old pattern. Simple formal methods have been matching or beating unaided expert judgment since Paul Meehl reviewed the evidence in 1954, and experts have resisted them for as long; Kahneman, Sibony and Sunstein retell the history in Noise (2021). Organizations also gather information they do not use, and use information to justify decisions already made (Feldman and March, 1981), and a formal procedure can be kept as a ceremony, apart from the work it describes (Meyer and Rowan, 1977). I have taken part in more than one technology evaluation whose result was known on the first day.

It shows what was not visible. The metaphor I use is glasses. A nearsighted person complains that they cannot see well enough to do what needs to be done. Given glasses, they see every detail, and with it everything that needs doing, and they may well put the glasses away. Economists call it information avoidance: people avoid information that would oblige them to act, or that they expect to dislike, even when it is free (Golman, Hagmann and Loewenstein, 2017).

It changes the work. Seeing more means more to fix, and generating what was written by hand removes work that people were hired, and teams were sized, to do. On one project there was a concern that we did not have enough people to build all the integration processes we needed in time. I proposed generating the starter processes from the same metadata that already generated our codecs; the answer was that the people were already allocated. Nobody was being unreasonable: a plan was in place, and in many organizations a manager’s standing is measured by the size of the team, the bureaucrat William Niskanen modeled as maximizing a budget (Niskanen, 1971).

When I told my wife about such episodes, she used to say: everybody is busy, everybody gets paid, the economy works. She is right, and it is the most important fact about them: the arrangement is stable. The runtime cannot take these costs away. What it can do is make answering a question cheap enough for one team to answer its own, for its own use, before anybody else has to agree to anything.

Confirm with my wife that she is comfortable being quoted. Check the citations against the sources: Meehl (1954), Noise (2021), Feldman and March (1981), Meyer and Rowan (1977), Golman, Hagmann and Loewenstein (2017), Niskanen (1971).

4.5. Failing conventionally

A traditional enterprise will most likely reject an approach like this one, and not because it does not work. It goes against the grain of how the enterprise is organized in the middle, where survival pressure is low and everybody does the same thing. The mainstream filter of Chapter 3 is one form of it. Keynes saw it in investors in 1936: "Worldly wisdom teaches that it is better for reputation to fail conventionally than to succeed unconventionally." Information technology has its own version: nobody ever got fired for buying IBM, a saying in print since at least 1978. Sociologists call the result institutional isomorphism: organizations in a field come to resemble each other, and under uncertainty they copy whoever looks successful (DiMaggio and Powell, 1983). Biologists would call it an evolutionarily stable strategy: once most of a population follows it, a rare alternative cannot displace it, because the alternative does worse while it is rare, even if a population that followed it would do better.

I cannot change the payoffs of an organization, so the runtime was designed to pay off while it is rare. Its foundation is the JDK, EMF and the OpenTelemetry API, which a platform team can approve in a meeting (Chapter 2). It needs no server and no platform, and one team can take one module without anybody else adopting anything (Chapter 1). A strategy that pays off only when everybody adopts it cannot invade; one that pays off for a single team can.

The next chapter puts the runtime on one page: its modules, how they depend on each other, and what happens when a unit of work runs.

5.2. Three planes

It helps to sort what the runtime does into three planes, with two seams between them.

Figure 2. Three planes and the volumes between them

The data plane is raw data where it lives: files on disk, a running JVM, a Git repository, Jira, a Maven repository, a cloud provider’s API. The semantic plane is models loaded from that data, typed, with cross-references resolved, in a resource set. The presentation plane is how people and programs see the models: HTML pages, a React UI, Markdown for an agent, plain text for a console.

Reads flow up. A volume presents data as files, and EMF loads resources from those files through a URI handler; or a loader reads an API and builds a model directly. A representation turns model objects into pages or files, and another volume presents those for serving, copying or mounting. Writes flow down, through commands, with telemetry and change recording on the way.

The planes explain why the runtime has volumes at all. A volume is the seam between the data plane and the semantic plane, and again between the semantic plane and channels such as HTTP, WebDAV or a directory. The same five-method interface serves both seams (Chapter 14).

Figure 3. Another view of the planes and volumes

An example

This example is partly built. The Jira model exists, and I have used it to snapshot Jira and give the snapshots to an AI assistant, but that was before the volume module existed. A Jira volume does not exist yet; it will be built on demand, and should be straightforward.

Take a Jira story, and suppose a Jira volume presents it at jira/MYPROJECT/issues/ISSUE-123/index.json as JSON, and at index.xmi next to it as XMI. Neither file is stored anywhere: reading either one makes a REST call to Jira and materializes the issue in that format. Related objects, such as the project, its components, users and linked issues, are relative URI references, and EMF loads their resources on demand, when a reference is followed.

Because Jira is a volume, its content can be copied to a directory or a zip archive like any other files. Take a snapshot today and another in a month, load both, and compare them with EMF Compare to see what has changed.

Because the issue is an EMF object in the semantic plane, it can reference semantic elements that did not come from Jira: a Git commit, a file on disk, or an object from any other system that is also loaded as a model.

Going up, the same issue has representations in different formats: an HTML page, a Markdown or AsciiDoc document, a diagram, or any other format the presentation plane supports. Those representations reach people and agents over different channels: a web browser, a file system mounted over WebDAV, or a directory they are copied to. For example, copy the AsciiDoc representations to a directory, then generate a PDF from them or give them to an AI assistant for analysis or enrichment. AsciiDoc carries more structure than plain text or Markdown, such as document attributes, cross-references and typed blocks, and it might be better suited to AI-assisted analysis and enrichment.

Who the planes are for

The planes say where things are, but not why the presentation plane has so many formats: HTML and Markdown, SVG and Draw.io, a PDF and a JSON file. The answer is a vocabulary older than the runtime, from ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 and TOGAF, which the Nasdanika enterprise model puts in one diagram. Figure 4 is a lighter version of it.

Figure 4. Stakeholders, views and the planes

A stakeholder is anyone with an interest in a system: a business owner, a risk officer, an engineer, and also an agent or a program. Stakeholders have concerns, the things they need to know or decide. A view addresses concerns. It is made of representations, such as a section, a table or a diagram, and a representation represents elements of the semantic plane: objects in the models of several semantic domains, many Ecore models in one resource set. A view sent to stakeholders is a message, delivered over channels: a directory, HTTP, WebDAV, MCP, a printed book. One view goes over many channels, and a channel carries many views.

Formats sit between representations and channels. A representation is available in several formats: a table as Markdown, AsciiDoc or HTML, a diagram as SVG or Draw.io. A channel accepts some formats and not others: a browser takes HTML, an agent takes Markdown, a printer takes PDF. A human stakeholder who wants a table gets it as HTML in a browser or in a PDF; an agent gets the same table as Markdown.

The enterprise model defines an enterprise as a group of stakeholders and resources devoted to a mission (Chapter 1). Views exchanged as messages are how the mission is pursued, which gives two measures: effectiveness, whether a view addresses the concern it is for, and efficiency, what it costs to produce, deliver and understand. Formats are about efficiency. That is why the runtime has a format for every reader. SVG is for people reading a page or a book: it is static, embeddable and needs no viewer. Draw.io is for people who edit, because the picture is also its source. Markdown, or the model itself, is for agents. Each format serves some stakeholder over some channel.

The vocabulary also says what a document is: a view whose sections are representations. A document generated from a model and a document written by hand are the same kind of thing, and a Markdown file loaded as a model is a view that can be rendered again, in another format, for another stakeholder. And it describes the polymorphic UI (Chapter 24) from the outside: given a viewpoint, which names the concerns to address and the representations that address them, a format and a channel, it builds a view. Viewpoints and stakeholders can be kept in catalogs, like any other model: a Sankey chart for "where does the money go", a property table for "who owns what"; business, risk and technology stakeholders.

It is also the first model an effort needs. A project charter names the stakeholders, a communications plan says what each of them receives and how, and a quality management system, such as the one Article 17 of the EU AI Act requires, covers communication with authorities, customers and other interested parties.

The runtime’s design follows this vocabulary, but the enterprise model is not part of the runtime yet. It is PLANNED as a nano-model of the core module (Chapter 20), so that stakeholders, concerns, formats and channels become types, and a view can be asked for by them. It is introduced here because it explains much of what follows.

5.3. How the pieces find each other

Nothing in the runtime is wired by hand, and nothing is configured in XML or YAML. Four mechanisms, from the simplest to the most capable, connect the parts.

Java services. A module declares in module-info.java that it provides an implementation of a service interface, and java.util.ServiceLoader finds every provider on the module path. Resource set configuration uses services: EPackages, URI handlers, adapter factories and `ResourceSetContributor`s (Chapter 7). So does the capability framework itself, to find capability factories.

Capabilities. A capability factory is a service that interprets requirements. A requirement is a type, possibly generic, with optional payloads: "a Function<Library, String> for the markdown format". Factories may raise their own requirements while satisfying one, and the loader resolves the whole graph, once per requirement, with cycle detection (Chapter 10).

Adaptation. An object can declare, with annotated fields and methods, what it can be adapted to, by generic type and with optional context. Adaptation answers "can this thing give me what I need?" without either side knowing the other’s class (Chapter 8).

Wiring. A command declares, by generic type, what it needs from its parent and which sub-commands it takes. Commands contributed as capabilities are matched to parents by those declarations, and the parent is adapted to what the child needs just before it runs (Chapter 17).

Each mechanism builds on the previous ones. Commands are capabilities; capability factories are services; wiring is adaptation.

5.4. One command, end to end

To see the parts work together, follow one command through a distribution: nsdk library save shelf.xmi, which saves the library the library command supplies to a file. Figure 5 shows the main steps.

Figure 5. One command, end to end

  1. The launcher builds a unit of work. It creates a directory for this launch’s telemetry, builds an OpenTelemetry SDK whose exporters write traces, logs and metrics as models, and makes it current. If a TRACEPARENT environment variable is set, by a CI step for example, the launch continues that trace. Everything that follows reports to this instance and to no other (Chapter 18).

  2. The capability loader assembles the command tree. It asks for root commands; the root command’s factory produces nsdk, and every command factory on the module path is asked whether its command fits under nsdk, then under each command added so far. The library command fits under nsdk because it declares the root command as its parent. The runtime’s save command fits under library because it declares that its parent must supply a collection of EMF objects, and library declares an adapter that does (Chapter 16). Each command arrives with its own sub-commands and mix-ins attached, so what the loader returns is the whole tree.

  3. picocli parses the arguments against that tree and finds nsdk library save with one positional parameter.

  4. Wiring injects parents. After parsing, from the root to the executed command, each command’s @Parent members are filled by adapting its parent. save receives a supplier from library; nothing is loaded yet (Chapter 17).

  5. The command executes in its own span. save calls the supplier, which loads or builds the library inside `save’s span, so the cost is attributed to the command that needed it. It creates a resource set, which is configured from services in a span with a log record per contribution, and saves the resource in a span with the byte count, while the URI handler logs progress for large streams (Chapter 11).

  6. The unit of work ends. Closing the SDK exports what is pending, and the exporters save traces.yml, logs.yml and metrics.yml in the launch’s telemetry directory, with log records nested in the spans they were emitted in (Chapter 13).

Nothing in that sequence was configured. The commands are present because their modules are on the module path, the wiring follows from their declared types, and the telemetry is there because the runtime’s code reports through the OpenTelemetry API to whatever instance is current.

Resource sets configured from services, all resource formats, generic type matching and adaptation, the flow utilities, the pump and the transformer, the capability framework, runtime telemetry with live publishing, telemetry and change recording as models, volumes over directories with HTTP and WebDAV serving, commands as capabilities with generic wiring, the launcher and the bootstrap, the Groovy DSL, the core, Meta, JVM, telemetry, HTML, Bootstrap, TypeScript and React models with their generators, Meta’s text syntax, validator, glossary and agent skill, the harness and browser walk-throughs with video, the Draw.io API and rendering with Draw.io’s viewer, the diagram, Draw.io and SVG models, and layout with ELK.

SKETCH

The file model; the presentation model; the reflective operations of Meta’s Object; Meta’s facets, recorded as annotations until the core model has them; the JVM model’s loaders (the book shows a minimal one).

PLANNED

Everything in Chapter 26: the polymorphic UI in React, representations and views over mounted volumes, the inference and tool models, MCP, query languages, executable graphs with state in Git.

Part II: Foundations

The common module and the habits the rest of the runtime is built on: models without an IDE, generic types matched at run time, reactive flows on the JDK, and the capability framework that finds what code needs.

Chapter 6. Getting started

This chapter gets the runtime onto your machine, builds a first program against it, and shows that the program is observable before you have done anything to make it so. The program is small on purpose: one metamodel with one class, one instance, three files. Everything else in the book builds on the same few steps.

6.1. What you need

  • A JDK for Java 25. The runtime is compiled with --release 25. Any distribution works; the examples were built with Eclipse Temurin.

  • Maven 3.9.16 or later. The build enforces the version.

  • Git, to get the source.

  • An editor. The runtime does not need an IDE, and nothing in it is specific to one. Eclipse, IntelliJ IDEA and VS Code all import the Maven projects as they are.

6.2. Building the runtime

Until the runtime is published to Maven Central, you build it and install it into your local Maven repository:

git clone https://github.com/Nasdanika-SDK/runtime.git
cd runtime
mvn clean install

The first build downloads the dependencies and runs every module’s tests, including the book’s examples, and renders this book. Two properties shorten it:

mvn clean install -DskipTests              # compile and install, run no tests
mvn clean install -Dasciidoctor.skip=true  # everything but rendering the book

Update this section when 2026.11.0 is on Maven Central: readers then need only the BOM import shown below, and building from source becomes the section for contributors.

6.3. A first project

A project that uses the runtime imports its bill of materials, which manages the versions of the runtime’s modules and of the libraries they use, and then depends on the modules it needs without versions. The examples share the import in their parent pom.xml:

Listing 1. Importing the runtime’s bill of materials (doc/book/examples/pom.xml)
<dependencyManagement>
	<dependencies>
		<dependency>
			<groupId>org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime</groupId>
			<artifactId>bom</artifactId>
			<version>${project.version}</version>
			<type>pom</type>
			<scope>import</scope>
		</dependency>
	</dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

The first example depends on two modules: common, which brings EMF and the OpenTelemetry API with it, and emf-json, which adds the JSON and YAML formats.

Listing 2. Dependencies of the first example (start/pom.xml)
<dependencies>
	<dependency>
		<groupId>org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime</groupId>
		<artifactId>common</artifactId>
	</dependency>
	<dependency>
		<groupId>org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime</groupId>
		<artifactId>emf-json</artifactId>
	</dependency>
</dependencies>

Every runtime module is a named JPMS module, and so is every example. The module declaration says which runtime modules the code uses:

Listing 3. The module declaration (start/src/main/java/module-info.java)
module org.example.start {

	requires org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.common;

	// JSON and YAML resource factories. Service binding would resolve the module
	// anyway, because it provides a service common uses; requiring it says so.
	requires org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.emf.json;

	exports org.example.start;

}

The comment in the listing points at something worth knowing early. emf-json contributes its resource factories as a service that common uses. When the JVM resolves modules, it adds every observable module that provides a service a resolved module uses, a step called service binding, so emf-json would be in the running program even without the requires. I require it anyway, because a dependency that is visible in the declaration is one less surprise. Service binding comes back in Chapter 22, where it is one of the things a snapshot of a running JVM shows and no build file does.

6.4. A first model

EMF models are usually generated from Xcore, which Chapter 7 covers. The first program builds a metamodel at run time instead, which needs no generator and shows what a metamodel is: a package, containing classes, containing typed features.

Listing 4. A one-class metamodel built at run time (start/…​/FirstModel.java)
/**
 * A one-class metamodel: a book with a title and a year.
 */
public static EPackage libraryPackage() {
	EcoreFactory ecore = EcoreFactory.eINSTANCE;

	EPackage library = ecore.createEPackage();
	library.setName("library");
	library.setNsURI("https://example.org/start/library");
	library.setNsPrefix("library");

	EClass book = ecore.createEClass();
	book.setName("Book");
	library.getEClassifiers().add(book);

	EAttribute title = ecore.createEAttribute();
	title.setName("title");
	title.setEType(EcorePackage.Literals.ESTRING);
	book.getEStructuralFeatures().add(title);

	EAttribute year = ecore.createEAttribute();
	year.setName("year");
	year.setEType(EcorePackage.Literals.EINT);
	book.getEStructuralFeatures().add(year);

	// A package lives in a resource whose URI is its namespace URI, so that instances
	// reference their class as https://example.org/start/library#//Book
	new ResourceImpl(URI.createURI(library.getNsURI())).getContents().add(library);
	return library;
}

The last statement puts the package into a resource whose URI is its namespace URI. That is how EMF expects packages to live, and it matters as soon as instances are saved: an instance refers to its class by the URI of the class, and a package that is in no resource produces a relative reference that cannot be resolved when the file is loaded again.

With a metamodel in hand, the program creates an instance and saves it three times:

Listing 5. Saving one book in three formats
/**
 * Saves one book as XMI, JSON and YAML.
 *
 * @return The saved files
 */
public static List<Path> save(EPackage library, Path directory) throws IOException {
	ResourceSet resourceSet = NasdanikaResourceSet.createAndConfigure(); (1)
	resourceSet.getPackageRegistry().put(library.getNsURI(), library);   (2)

	EClass bookClass = (EClass) library.getEClassifier("Book");
	EObject book = EcoreUtil.create(bookClass);                           (3)
	book.eSet(bookClass.getEStructuralFeature("title"),
			"Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs");
	book.eSet(bookClass.getEStructuralFeature("year"), 1985);

	List<Path> files = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
	for (String extension: List.of("xmi", "json", "yml")) {              (4)
		Path file = directory.resolve("book." + extension);
		Resource resource = resourceSet.createResource(URI.createFileURI(file.toString()));
		resource.getContents().add(EcoreUtil.copy(book));
		resource.save(null);
		files.add(file);
	}
	return files;
}
1 A resource set configured from services: every EPackage, URI handler and ResourceSetContributor on the module path is applied to it. This is the one line that makes everything else in the runtime available to EMF.
2 Packages registered as services are found by namespace URI. This one was built at run time, so it is registered by hand.
3 EcoreUtil.create makes an instance of a class without generated code. Features are set and read reflectively.
4 The file extension selects the resource factory: xmi is the default, json and yml were contributed by emf-json.

The three files hold the same object:

Listing 6. book.xmi
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="ASCII"?>
<library:Book xmi:version="2.0" xmlns:xmi="http://www.omg.org/XMI"
    xmlns:library="https://example.org/start/library"
    title="Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs" year="1985"/>
Listing 7. book.json
{
  "eClass" : "https://example.org/start/library#//Book",
  "title" : "Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs",
  "year" : 1985
}
Listing 8. book.yml
---
eClass: "https://example.org/start/library#//Book"
title: "Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs"
year: 1985

Loading is the mirror image: a resource set, the package registered, and getResource with the file’s URI.

Listing 9. Loading a book and reading its title reflectively
/**
 * Loads a book saved by {@link #save(EPackage, Path)} and reads its title reflectively.
 */
public static String title(EPackage library, Path file) {
	ResourceSet resourceSet = NasdanikaResourceSet.createAndConfigure();
	resourceSet.getPackageRegistry().put(library.getNsURI(), library);
	Resource resource = resourceSet.getResource(URI.createFileURI(file.toString()), true);
	EObject book = resource.getContents().getFirst();
	EStructuralFeature title = book.eClass().getEStructuralFeature("title");
	return (String) book.eGet(title);
}

That is a complete EMF program: a metamodel, an instance, three formats, and reflection, with no generated code and no configuration.

6.5. Watching it run

The program above contains no telemetry code, and it is observable anyway. The runtime’s resource set configuration, resource factories and URI handlers report what they do through the OpenTelemetry API, to whichever OpenTelemetry instance the unit of work made current. To see it, make one current that publishes what it receives, and subscribe:

Listing 10. Watching the first program (start/…​/WatchIt.java)
public static void watch(PrintStream out) throws IOException {
	PublishingTracerProvider tracerProvider = new PublishingTracerProvider(
			TracerProvider.noop(), (1)
			Runnable::run,         (2)
			1024);
	try (PublishingOpenTelemetry openTelemetry =
			new PublishingOpenTelemetry(OpenTelemetry.noop(), tracerProvider)) {
		openTelemetry.subscribe(new Printer(out));                   (3)
		try (Scope scope = Telemetry.makeCurrent(openTelemetry)) {   (4)
			Path directory = Files.createTempDirectory("watch-it");
			Telemetry.inSpan(                                         (5)
					Telemetry.tracer(openTelemetry),
					"Save a book",
					null,
					span -> FirstModel.save(FirstModel.libraryPackage(), directory));
		}
	}
}
1 The tracer provider the events come from wraps the no-op provider: no OpenTelemetry SDK is involved.
2 Runnable::run delivers each event on the thread that produced it. That makes the output deterministic, which suits a console and a test. The default delivers on virtual threads instead.
3 A subscriber that prints span starts, span ends and log records, indented by nesting. It is twenty lines; the listing is in the example.
4 The instance is current until the scope closes. Everything instrumented in between reports to it.
5 The program’s own work runs in a span named for what it does, so that the runtime’s spans nest under it.

The output, with the long class and file names shortened:

> Save a book
  > ResourceSetContributor.configure
    Contributed uri-handler ...ClassPathURIHandlerFactory$1
    Contributed uri-handler ...ModuleURIHandlerFactory$1
    Contributed contributor ...BinaryResourceFactoryContributor
    Contributed contributor ...GzipBinaryResourceFactoryContributor
    Contributed contributor ...XMIResourceFactoryContributor
    > Contribute To Resource Set
    < Contribute To Resource Set
    Contributed contributor ...JsonResourceFactoryContributor
    ...
  < ResourceSetContributor.configure
  Created ...XMIResourceImpl for file:/tmp/watch-it/book.xmi
  > URIHandler.write
  > Resource.save
    Saved file:/tmp/watch-it/book.xmi: 230 bytes
  < Resource.save
  < URIHandler.write
  Created ...JsonResource for file:/tmp/watch-it/book.json
  > URIHandler.write
  > Resource.save
  < URIHandler.write
    Saved file:/tmp/watch-it/book.json: 145 bytes
  < Resource.save
  ...
< Save a book
Done

Three things in that output say a lot about how the runtime is built.

The resource set’s configuration is visible: which URI handlers, factories and contributors were applied, and from which classes. When a format you expected is missing, this is where you find out that its module was not on the module path.

URIHandler.write and Resource.save are siblings, not parent and child. The stream is opened before the resource starts saving into it, and a stream is not a lexical scope, so its span is not made current. In the JSON case the stream span ends before the save span does, because the JSON resource closes the stream itself.

And nothing here needed an OpenTelemetry SDK. The SDK is what samples, batches and exports spans; the API is all instrumented code ever sees. Chapter 11 shows how to add the SDK when you want spans exported, and Chapter 13 how to export them as models.

mvn -pl doc/book/examples/capability -am verify

Most examples are tests: each test method is one scenario, and its assertions say what the scenario produces. That is deliberate. A test is the shortest program that shows both what to write and what to expect, and it keeps working.

Chapter 7. Models: EMF without Eclipse

Everything the runtime defines is a model, and every model is EMF. This chapter explains what EMF gives you, why it no longer needs Eclipse, and how a model goes from a text file to generated Java, registered with resource sets, saved in any of six formats and loaded from a module. The example is the library model that the rest of the book uses as its domain.

7.1. Why EMF

A model is a typed graph. Its nodes are objects of classes, and its edges are references, some of which are containment: a library contains its books, a book refers to its authors. The classes, their attributes and their references are themselves described by a model, the metamodel, and EMF’s metamodel of metamodels is called Ecore.

That sounds abstract until you list what a typed graph buys once a framework handles it for you, which EMF has done for more than twenty years:

  • Reflection. Any object can be asked for its class, and any feature can be read and written by name, without generated code. A viewer, a serializer, a query engine or a diff tool written once works for every model.

  • Serialization. XMI, and with the runtime JSON, YAML and two binary formats.

  • Resources and URIs. Objects live in resources identified by URIs, and resources live in resource sets. A reference from one resource to another is a URI that is resolved lazily, when it is followed, which is what lets models reference each other across files, repositories and the network.

  • Integrity. Containment means one owner. Opposite references are maintained in both directions. Multiplicities are declared and checked.

  • Notifications and change recording. Every change to an object is a notification, and a change recorder can capture a set of changes as a model of its own, which Chapter 13 turns into an audit trail.

  • Operations. Classes declare operations, and with operation reflection an operation can be invoked by name with a list of arguments.

The last item matters more every year. An operation with a name, typed parameters and documentation is a tool, in exactly the sense an AI agent or a command line needs. Defining an API as model operations means it is documented, invocable and discoverable by construction.

7.2. Why not Eclipse

For most of its life, EMF lived inside the Eclipse IDE. To define a model you installed Eclipse with the modeling tools, created a workspace and a plug-in project, drew or typed an Ecore model, and generated code with a wizard that wrote plugin.xml, MANIFEST.MF and a generator model next to it. The output was an OSGi bundle meant to run inside Eclipse.

None of that is EMF. EMF core is a set of plain jars on Maven Central, and the runtime uses them as plain jars: named JPMS modules on the module path, with no OSGi, no workspace and no plug-in registry. The modeling tools were the problem, and two things replaced them:

  • Xcore, a text syntax for Ecore models with operation bodies, which reads like a small programming language and diffs like code.

  • The Xtext Maven plugin, which generates Java from Xcore in any Maven build, on any machine, in CI, and in editors that are not Eclipse.

So a model is a source file in a Maven module, generated by the build, and committed with the code. I described the journey of getting there in "The Architectural Stalker", about liberating useful artifacts from the Eclipse zone; this chapter is the result.

7.3. Ecore in one page

Concept Ecore In the library model

A namespace for related types

EPackage, with a namespace URI and a prefix

library, example.org/library

A type of object

EClass, possibly abstract, with supertypes

Library, Author, Book

A value-typed property

EAttribute, typed by an EDataType

Book.year, an int

A link to other objects

EReference: containment or cross reference, single or many, with an optional opposite

Library.books (containment), Book.authors (cross reference, opposite Author.books)

A fixed set of values

EEnum with literals

Genre

Behavior

EOperation with parameters

Library.publishedBefore(int)

An instance

EObject

a particular book

A unit of storage

Resource, identified by a URI

shelf.library

A working set of resources

ResourceSet, which resolves URIs between them

the resource set a command creates

7.4. A model in Xcore

Here is the library model. It extends NamedElement from the runtime’s core model, so every library, author and book has a name, a stable identifier, documentation and provenance markers without declaring them (Chapter 20).

Listing 11. The library model, header (library/src/main/resources/org/example/library/library.xcore)
@Ecore(nsURI="https://example.org/library", nsPrefix="library")
@GenModel(
	modelDirectory="/library/src-gen",
	featureDelegation="Dynamic",
	complianceLevel="25",
	suppressGenModelAnnotations="false",
	copyrightFields="false",
	operationReflection="true",
	importOrganizing="true"
)
package org.example.library

import org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.models.core.NamedElement
Listing 12. The library model, classes
/*
 * A collection of books and the people who wrote them.
 */
class Library extends NamedElement {

	contains Author[] authors

	contains Book[] books

	/*
	 * Books published before the year.
	 */
	op Book[] publishedBefore(int year) {
		val result = new org.eclipse.emf.common.util.BasicEList<Book>
		for (book : books) {
			if (book.year < year) {
				result.add(book)
			}
		}
		result
	}

}

enum Genre {
	FICTION
	SCIENCE
	HISTORY
	TECHNOLOGY
}

/*
 * A person who wrote books.
 */
class Author extends NamedElement {

	refers Book[] books opposite authors

}

/*
 * A book. The name is the title.
 */
class Book extends NamedElement {

	String isbn

	int year

	Genre genre

	refers Author[] authors opposite books

	/*
	 * Cited books. No opposite: getReferrers() finds who cites a book.
	 */
	refers Book[] cites

}

A few things in the header are worth understanding, because they are where most first attempts go wrong.

@Ecore gives the package its namespace URI and prefix. The namespace URI is the package’s identity: it is how serialized instances name their classes, how a resource set finds the package, and, by the runtime’s identity rule, where the model’s documentation page lives.

@GenModel configures the code generator:

  • modelDirectory says where generated Java goes, and its first segment must be the name of the Maven module’s directory: /library/src-gen for a module in library/. The generator resolves that segment as an Eclipse project name, and under Maven a mismatch produces a successful build with no generated code at all. If src-gen comes up empty, look here first.

  • complianceLevel="25" lets the generated code use the Java version the runtime targets.

  • featureDelegation="Dynamic" makes generated getters and setters go through EMF’s dynamic feature storage, which keeps generated classes small and lets a base class intercept feature access.

  • operationReflection="true" generates eInvoke, so that operations can be called by name.

The import brings in NamedElement from the core model, which is resolved from the module’s compile class path when the model is generated. Comments in /* */ before a class or feature become its documentation in the generated model. Operation bodies are written in Xbase, a Java-like expression language; the body of publishedBefore compiles to the loop you would expect.

7.5. Generating with Maven

The model module declares two plugins. Their configuration is inherited from the runtime’s parent pom.xml, so the module’s own declaration is two lines each:

Listing 13. Generation plugins (library/pom.xml)
<build>
	<plugins>
		<!-- Generates Java from src/main/resources/**/*.xcore into src-gen -->
		<plugin>
			<groupId>org.eclipse.xtext</groupId>
			<artifactId>xtext-maven-plugin</artifactId>
		</plugin>
		<!-- Adds src-gen as a source root -->
		<plugin>
			<groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId>
			<artifactId>build-helper-maven-plugin</artifactId>
		</plugin>
	</plugins>
</build>

The inherited configuration of the Xtext plugin registers three languages, in an order that matters: Ecore and GenModel support first, because Xcore models reference them, then Xcore itself. Its source root is src/main/resources, where the .xcore files live:

Listing 14. The Xtext plugin’s configuration, an excerpt of the runtime’s parent pom.xml
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.eclipse.xtext</groupId>
  <artifactId>xtext-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>2.44.0</version>
  <executions>
    <execution>
      <id>generate-xcore</id>
      <phase>generate-sources</phase>
      <goals><goal>generate</goal></goals>
    </execution>
  </executions>
  <configuration>
    <languages>
      <language><setup>org.eclipse.xtext.ecore.EcoreSupport</setup></language>
      <language><setup>org.eclipse.emf.codegen.ecore.xtext.GenModelSupport</setup></language>
      <language><setup>org.eclipse.emf.ecore.xcore.XcoreStandaloneSetup</setup></language>
    </languages>
    <sourceRoots>
      <root>${project.basedir}/src/main/resources</root>
    </sourceRoots>
  </configuration>
</plugin>

The build helper plugin adds src-gen as a source root, so mvn compile generates and compiles in one step. The model’s dependencies are the model it extends, the runtime’s common module for the services the module contributes, and two small libraries that generated code and Xbase operation bodies use:

Listing 15. Dependencies of a model module (library/pom.xml)
<dependencies>
	<!-- NamedElement and the rest of the core model, which this model extends -->
	<dependency>
		<groupId>org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.models</groupId>
		<artifactId>core</artifactId>
	</dependency>
	<dependency>
		<groupId>org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime</groupId>
		<artifactId>common</artifactId>
	</dependency>
	<!-- Used by generated code and operation bodies written in Xcore -->
	<dependency>
		<groupId>org.eclipse.xtext</groupId>
		<artifactId>org.eclipse.xtext.xbase.lib</artifactId>
	</dependency>
	<dependency>
		<groupId>org.eclipse.emf</groupId>
		<artifactId>org.eclipse.emf.ecore.xcore.lib</artifactId>
	</dependency>
	<dependency>
		<groupId>org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime</groupId>
		<artifactId>emf-json</artifactId>
		<scope>test</scope>
	</dependency>
</dependencies>

The runtime commits generated sources. Generation is deterministic, the diff of generated code is a useful review of a model change, and an editor without Maven integration still sees every class. After editing a .xcore file, run mvn generate-sources in the module and refresh the editor’s view of the project.

The generated API is what you would write by hand if you had the patience: an interface and an implementation class per model class, a factory and a package singleton.

Listing 16. The generated API at work (library/src/test/java/…​/TestLibrary.java)
LibraryFactory factory = LibraryFactory.eINSTANCE;
Library library = factory.createLibrary();

Author evans = factory.createAuthor();
evans.setName("Eric Evans");
library.getAuthors().add(evans);           // Containment: the library owns its authors

Book ddd = factory.createBook();
ddd.setName("Domain-Driven Design");
ddd.setYear(2003);
ddd.setGenre(Genre.TECHNOLOGY);
ddd.getAuthors().add(evans);               // A cross reference
library.getBooks().add(ddd);

assertThat(evans.getBooks()).containsExactly(ddd); // The opposite is maintained
assertThat(ddd.eContainer()).isSameAs(library);

Two lines in that listing are EMF earning its keep. Adding the book to the library’s books made the library its container, and adding the author to the book’s authors added the book to the author’s books, because the two references are declared as opposites.

7.6. Registering the model

A model module tells the runtime about its package with a Java service. The service is the EPackage interface, and the provider is a class with a static provider() method that returns the package singleton. ServiceLoader calls a provider method instead of a constructor when there is one, which is exactly what a singleton needs:

Listing 17. A package provider (library/…​/services/LibraryEPackageProvider.java)
/**
 * Registers the library package with resource sets configured from services. A provider
 * method hands {@link java.util.ServiceLoader} the singleton instead of a new instance.
 */
public final class LibraryEPackageProvider {

	private LibraryEPackageProvider() {
	}

	public static EPackage provider() {
		return LibraryPackage.eINSTANCE;
	}

}
Listing 18. The model module’s declaration (library/src/main/java/module-info.java)
import org.eclipse.emf.ecore.EPackage;
import org.example.library.services.LibraryEPackageProvider;
import org.example.library.services.LibraryResourceSetContributor;
import org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.common.services.ResourceSetContributor;

module org.example.library {

	exports org.example.library;        // Generated interfaces
	exports org.example.library.impl;   // Generated implementations
	exports org.example.library.util;   // Generated switch and adapter factory
	exports org.example.library.services;

	requires transitive org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.models.core;
	requires transitive org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.common;
	requires org.eclipse.emf.ecore.xmi;

	provides EPackage with LibraryEPackageProvider;                          (1)
	provides ResourceSetContributor with LibraryResourceSetContributor;     (2)

}
1 Every resource set configured from services will have the library package in its package registry, so files that mention example.org/library load without any setup.
2 A contributor, shown next, gives the model a file extension of its own.

The module exports the generated impl and util packages as well as the interfaces. EMF’s reflective machinery and the runtime’s serializers work with the implementation classes, and a JPMS module that hides them makes the model unusable outside it.

7.7. Resource sets configured from services

NasdanikaResourceSet.createAndConfigure() is the line that connects EMF to everything on the module path. It creates a resource set and configures it from four kinds of services:

  • URI handlers (URIHandler), added in front of EMF’s own, so a module can teach every resource set a new URI scheme.

  • Adapter factories (AdapterFactory).

  • Packages (EPackage), registered by namespace URI.

  • Contributors (ResourceSetContributor), which may do anything else with the resource set, typically register resource factories.

Configuration runs in a ResourceSetContributor.configure span with a log record per contribution, and then wraps every URI handler, the default one included, in a TelemetryURIHandler, so that every stream a resource set opens is a span with a byte count and progress records. That is why the first program in Chapter 6 was observable without trying.

Three variants of createAndConfigure exist for when the defaults do not fit. One takes a ClassLoader, for code that is not on the module path, such as plugins loaded at run time. One takes an OpenTelemetry instance and attaches it to the resource set, so that work done outside any unit of work, proxy resolution much later for example, still reports somewhere. And one takes both.

NasdanikaResourceSet also supports global objects: registerGlobal(uri, object) makes an object resolvable by a URI that no resource contains, which is how a catalog of shared elements is offered to every model that references it.

7.8. Contributing to resource sets

A ResourceSetContributor is the service for everything that is not a package, a URI handler or an adapter factory. The library module uses one to give libraries their own extension, .library, stored as XMI and instrumented like every resource the runtime creates:

Listing 19. A resource set contributor (library/…​/services/LibraryResourceSetContributor.java)
/**
 * Gives libraries a file extension of their own: {@code catalog.library} is XMI,
 * loaded and saved in spans like every resource the runtime creates.
 */
public class LibraryResourceSetContributor implements ResourceSetContributor {

	public static final String EXTENSION = "library";

	@Override
	public void contribute(ResourceSet resourceSet, Span span, Logger logger) { (1)
		Map<String, Object> factories =
				resourceSet.getResourceFactoryRegistry().getExtensionToFactoryMap();
		factories.put(EXTENSION, new XMIResourceFactoryImpl() {

			@Override
			public Resource createResource(URI uri) {
				return ResourceTelemetry.created(resourceSet, new XMIResourceImpl(uri) { (2)

					@Override
					public void doLoad(InputStream in, Map<?, ?> options) throws IOException {
						ResourceTelemetry.load(this, in, s -> super.doLoad(s, options));
					}

					@Override
					public void doSave(OutputStream out, Map<?, ?> options) throws IOException {
						ResourceTelemetry.save(this, out, s -> super.doSave(s, options));
					}

				});
			}

		});
		span.setAttribute("library.extension", EXTENSION);                          (3)
		Telemetry.log(logger, Severity.DEBUG, null, "Registered ." + EXTENSION, null);
	}

}
1 The interface’s default contribute(ResourceSet) runs this method in a span, with the contributor’s class and module as attributes, and hands it the span and a logger. A contributor that wants no span overrides contribute(ResourceSet) instead.
2 ResourceTelemetry gives a resource the same spans and log records as the runtime’s own: Resource.load and Resource.save with the URI, the byte count and the number of root objects.
3 The span is the contributor’s own, so anything it wants to record about the contribution goes on it.

7.9. Formats

The extension of a resource’s URI selects its factory, and the runtime contributes six:

Extension Format Contributed by

xmi and any unregistered extension

XMI

common

ebin

EMF binary

common

egz

EMF binary, gzipped

common

json

EMF JSON

emf-json

yaml, yml

EMF JSON, written as YAML

emf-json

library

XMI

the library example

The test below saves the sample library in every one of them and loads each back in a fresh resource set:

Listing 20. Every format, round-tripped (library/src/test/java/…​/TestLibrary.java)
ResourceSet resourceSet = NasdanikaResourceSet.createAndConfigure();
Library library = Samples.library();
for (String extension: List.of("xmi", "library", "ebin", "egz", "json", "yml")) {
