	URI uri = URI.createFileURI(directory.resolve("shelf." + extension).toString());
	Resource resource = resourceSet.createResource(uri);   // The extension picks the factory
	resource.getContents().add(EcoreUtil.copy(library));
	resource.save(null);

	Resource loaded = NasdanikaResourceSet.createAndConfigure().getResource(uri, true);
	EObject root = loaded.getContents().getFirst();
	assertThat(EcoreUtil.equals(root, library)).as(extension).isTrue();
}

Which one to use is a question of who reads the file. XMI is the interchange format every EMF tool understands, and it diffs reasonably. YAML is the one people edit and review. JSON is the one a browser or a JavaScript program consumes, and Chapter 23 shows where that leads. The binary formats are for size and speed, such as telemetry from a long run or a snapshot of a large system.

7.10. Loading from modules

Two URI schemes contributed by common load resources from the code itself:

  • classpath://path/to/resource reads through the context class loader.

  • module://module.name/path/to/resource reads from a named module.

The library module ships a small catalog at the root of its jar, and the test loads it by the module’s name:

Listing 21. Loading a resource from a module
ResourceSet resourceSet = NasdanikaResourceSet.createAndConfigure();
URI uri = URI.createURI("module://org.example.library/catalog.library");
Library catalog = (Library) resourceSet.getResource(uri, true).getContents().getFirst();
assertThat(catalog.getBooks()).extracting(Book::getName).contains("Domain-Driven Design");

JPMS encapsulation applies here. A resource in a directory that corresponds to one of the module’s packages is visible to other modules only if that package is open; a resource outside any package, such as at the root of the module or under META-INF, is always visible. Put resources meant to be loaded by URI outside the package directories, or open the package they are in.

7.11. One model, several files

A contained object can be saved in a file of its own and still be contained, which keeps a large model reviewable file by file: each module of a JVM in its own file, for example, so that Git shows which module changed. EMF calls this containment proxies, and it is off by default. The rule for a containment whose objects may be in files of their own:

  • Declare the containment contains resolving, and set containmentProxies="true" in the package’s @GenModel; generated code needs both.

  • Give it a container reference as its opposite, declared container resolving. The opposite makes an object’s file refer back to its container’s file, so that the object loaded alone still knows where it belongs. resolving makes reading the container reference return the container, the same as eContainer(), and not a proxy.

@GenModel(containmentProxies="true")
package org.example.tree

class Node {
	String name
	contains resolving Node[] children opposite parent
	container resolving Node parent opposite children
}

Saving the model then means saving every modified resource, not only the root’s, and walking a model in either direction loads files as it goes. The field note "Cross-Resource Containment in EMF", at Nasdanika Field Notes, shows each of these behaviors with a test.

7.12. Operations

Operations defined in Xcore are ordinary Java methods on the generated classes, and, with operation reflection, also callable by name:

Listing 22. Calling an operation directly and reflectively
Library library = Samples.library();
List<Book> classics = library.publishedBefore(1900);   // An operation implemented in Xcore
assertThat(classics).extracting(Book::getName)
	.containsExactly("On the Origin of Species", "War and Peace");

// The same operation, invoked reflectively: what a tool, a CLI or an agent would do
EOperation operation = LibraryPackage.Literals.LIBRARY___PUBLISHED_BEFORE__INT;
Object result = library.eInvoke(operation, ECollections.asEList(1900));
assertThat(result).isEqualTo(classics);

The reflective call is what a generic tool does. A command line can offer every operation of a model as a command, a viewer can offer it as a button, and an agent can be offered it as a tool, all from the model, with the operation’s documentation as the description.

7.13. What you have now

A model is a text file in a Maven module. The build generates its Java; a service registers it with every resource set; a contributor adds whatever else the model needs; and the model is saved and loaded in the format each reader prefers. No IDE was involved.

The next chapter turns to a problem that shows up the moment you start connecting components by type: Java forgets type arguments at run time, and the runtime needs them.

Chapter 8. Generic types at run time

Components that find each other by type run into a limit of Java almost immediately. ServiceLoader can be asked for a Supplier, and then every supplier in the assembly answers, whatever it supplies. It cannot be asked for a Supplier<Library>, because at run time there is no such thing: type arguments are erased.

The runtime needs them anyway. A command that needs a supplier of libraries should not be offered a supplier of authors, and a requirement for "something that renders a library" should not be answered by something that renders a book. This chapter shows what survives erasure, how the runtime matches generic types with Java’s own rules, and how objects declare what they can be adapted to. The capability framework (Chapter 10) and command wiring (Chapter 17) are both built on it.

8.1. Matching and wiring

Much of software development is matching and wiring: connecting something that needs to something that provides, by a rule, and then checking that the connection is right. The Java compiler does it all the time. A method call is matched to a method by its name and signature. Generics are a check on that match and nothing more: after erasure, get on a List<Book> is a call to List.get returning Object, followed by a cast, and the type argument is there to prove at compile time that the cast will succeed. Overriding is matched by signature too, and @Override validates the match: it changes nothing in the program, it states that the method is meant to override one, and the compiler checks that there is one.

Wiring at run time has usually had less to work with. ServiceLoader and most registries match on a Class, which is the erased type, or on a string. Matching on java.lang.reflect.Type instead brings run-time matching to the level the compiler works at: not "a supplier", but "a supplier of libraries", decided by the compiler’s rules. The runtime’s Zephyr Book Matching and Wiring develops the argument and documents the common module in depth.

8.2. What survives erasure

Objects carry no type arguments. A new ArrayList<String>() and a new ArrayList<Integer>() are the same class at run time, and nothing can recover the difference from the objects.

Declarations are different. The class file keeps the generic signature of every class, field and method, and reflection reads it: Field.getGenericType(), Method.getGenericReturnType(), Class.getGenericInterfaces(). A class declared as implements Supplier<Library> says so at run time, forever. So does a field declared as Supplier<Library>, and a method declared to return one.

That gives the runtime a rule it applies everywhere: what is matched is always a declaration, never an instance. A capability method is matched by its declared generic return type, an adapter field by its declared type, a command’s parent member by its declared type. The compiler checks the declarations, and the runtime trusts them.

8.3. Types

org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.common.Types is the runtime’s small library of generic type operations, built on geantyref and hiding it. The examples in this chapter use a few types of their own: a catalog lists titles, and a shelf is a catalog you can also put books on.

Listing 23. The types the examples adapt to (generics/…​/Catalogs.java)
/**
 * Something that lists book titles.
 */
public interface Catalog {

	List<String> titles();

}

/**
 * A catalog you can also put books on.
 */
public interface Shelf extends Catalog {

	void put(String title);

}

public record ReadingList(List<String> titles) implements Catalog {
}

public static final class OakShelf implements Shelf {

	private final List<String> titles = new ArrayList<>();

	@Override
	public List<String> titles() {
		return titles;
	}

	@Override
	public void put(String title) {
		titles.add(title);
	}

}

A generic type is captured with a type token, an anonymous subclass of TypeToken whose type argument reflection can read back:

Listing 24. Type tokens (generics/src/test/java/…​/TestGenerics.java)
static final Type SHELVES = new TypeToken<Supplier<Shelf>>() {}.getType();
static final Type CATALOGS = new TypeToken<Supplier<Catalog>>() {}.getType();
static final Type ANY_CATALOGS =
		new TypeToken<Supplier<? extends Catalog>>() {}.getType();

Types.isAssignable(target, source) answers the question the compiler answers for an assignment: may a value declared as source be used where target is required?

Listing 25. Assignability, by Java’s rules for generics
// ? extends Catalog accepts Shelf
assertThat(Types.isAssignable(ANY_CATALOGS, SHELVES)).isTrue();
// Supplier<Shelf> is not a Supplier<Catalog>
assertThat(Types.isAssignable(CATALOGS, SHELVES)).isFalse();
// A raw target accepts any parameterization
assertThat(Types.isAssignable(Supplier.class, SHELVES)).isTrue();
// A raw source promises nothing about shelves
assertThat(Types.isAssignable(SHELVES, Supplier.class)).isFalse();

The first three lines are Java’s rules. Supplier<Shelf> can be used where Supplier<? extends Catalog> is required, because a shelf is a catalog and the wildcard allows subtypes. It cannot be used where Supplier<Catalog> is required, because Java generics are invariant: Supplier<Shelf> is not a subtype of Supplier<Catalog>, even though Shelf is a subtype of Catalog. A wildcard is how a requirement says that subtypes are welcome, and it is the requirement’s choice, not the provider’s. And anything parameterized can be used where the raw type is required.

The fourth line is where the runtime is deliberately stricter than Java. Java lets a raw Supplier be used where Supplier<Shelf> is required, with an unchecked warning. For matching that would let something declared as a raw supplier answer a requirement for shelves, about which it has said nothing, so Types refuses. The one exception is a target whose type arguments are all unbounded wildcards, such as Supplier<?>, which Java itself accepts from a raw type without a warning.

Two more operations read type arguments from declarations. getTypeArgument finds the argument a subtype fixes for a type parameter of a supertype, however many classes lie in between:

Listing 26. The type argument a declaration fixes
final class ShelfSupplier implements Supplier<Shelf> {

	@Override
	public Shelf get() {
		return new OakShelf();
	}

}
Type argument = Types.getTypeArgument(
		ShelfSupplier.class,
		Supplier.class.getTypeParameters()[0]);
assertThat(argument).isEqualTo(Shelf.class); // What survives erasure: the declaration

getElementType does the same for containers, replacing a wildcard by its bound: an element of List<? extends Shelf> is a Shelf, an element of List<?> is an Object.

Finally, isGround says whether a type can be required or provided at all. A type variable means something only inside the scope that declares it, so T, or List<T>, cannot be matched against anything. This is the trap of type tokens created inside generic methods: new TypeToken<T>() {} captures the variable T, not what T stands for at the call site, because erasure leaves nothing else to capture. The capability framework refuses such types with an error instead of matching them wrongly.

8.4. Adaptation

Matching declared types answers "is this declaration compatible with that one". Adaptation answers a question objects are asked all the time in a system assembled from parts: "can you give me what I need?"

An object declares what it can be adapted to with @Adapter on fields and methods. The declared generic type of the member is what it provides:

Listing 27. An adaptable object (generics/…​/Branch.java)
/**
 * A library branch. What it can be adapted to is declared by its adapter members,
 * and their generic types say exactly what each one provides.
 */
public class Branch implements Adaptable {

	private final Map<String, String> titles = Map.of(
			"978-0321125217", "Domain-Driven Design",
			"978-0201633610", "Design Patterns");

	@Adapter
	private final Supplier<Shelf> shelves = OakShelf::new;                   (1)

	@Adapter
	private final Supplier<Catalog> catalogs =                               (2)
			() -> new ReadingList(List.copyOf(titles.values()));

	@Adapter
	public String title(String isbn) {                                        (3)
		return titles.get(isbn); // null declines: "not this time"
	}

}
1 A field: the branch can be adapted to Supplier<Shelf>.
2 Another field of the same raw type, told apart by its type argument.
3 A method with a parameter takes context. It answers a request for a String with one String of context, and returns null to decline.

Asking is adaptTo(type, context…​):

Listing 28. Adapting
Branch branch = new Branch();

Supplier<Shelf> shelves = branch.adaptTo(SHELVES);
Supplier<Catalog> catalogs = branch.adaptTo(CATALOGS);
Supplier<? extends Catalog> any = branch.adaptTo(ANY_CATALOGS); // Both members qualify

assertThat(shelves.get()).isInstanceOf(Shelf.class);
assertThat(catalogs.get().titles()).contains("Design Patterns");
assertThat(any.get()).isInstanceOf(Catalog.class);

// Context is matched to the parameters of adapter methods
String title = branch.adaptTo(String.class, "978-0321125217");
assertThat(title).isEqualTo("Domain-Driven Design");
assertThat(branch.<String>adaptTo(String.class, "000")).isNull(); // Declined
Type strings = new TypeToken<Supplier<String>>() {}.getType();
assertThat(branch.<Object>adaptTo(strings)).isNull();

The rules, in order:

  • With no context, the object itself is returned if its own declared type matches, generic supertypes included: a class that implements Supplier<Shelf> adapts to Supplier<Shelf> without any annotation.

  • Otherwise adapter fields and adapter methods without parameters are tried. With context, adapter methods whose parameters accept the context values are tried: as many parameters as values, each value an instance of its parameter’s class, or null for a parameter that is not primitive.

  • Of the candidates whose declared type is assignable to the requested one, the more specific are tried first, fields before methods, then by name. The first non-null value wins; null means "not this time".

"More specific first" is computed by Types.specificity, which counts the supertypes of the erased type. Supplier<Shelf> and Supplier<Catalog> both erase to Supplier, so they tie, and the member name decides. In the example, a request for Supplier<? extends Catalog> gets the catalogs field, not the more specific shelves. The runtime’s TestAdaptable passes its equivalent assertion only because "volumes" sorts before "writables". The same ordering is used by ReflectiveCapabilityFactory and CommandWiring. A fix: break ties between members whose types are both assignable to the request by comparing them with Types.isAssignable, so that a member assignable to the other comes first.

Objects that do not implement Adaptable can still be adapted through their annotations, with Adapters.adapt:

Listing 29. Adapting a plain object (generics/…​/Archive.java and the test)
/**
 * A plain object, not an Adaptable: the annotations are enough for Adapters.adapt().
 */
public class Archive {

	@Adapter
	public Supplier<Catalog> catalog() {
		return () -> new ReadingList(List.of("On the Origin of Species"));
	}

}

Supplier<Catalog> catalog = Adapters.adapt(new Archive(), CATALOGS);
assertThat(catalog.get().titles()).containsExactly("On the Origin of Species");

Implementing Adaptable is needed only to adapt in ways an annotation cannot express: computed, delegated or cached. The override can fall back to the declared adapters:

Listing 30. Adaptation in code, with a fallback to the declarations
/**
 * Adaptation that annotations cannot express goes into an override, which falls back
 * to the declarations.
 */
public class Reserve implements Adaptable {

	@Adapter
	private final Supplier<Shelf> shelves = Catalogs.OakShelf::new;

	@Override
	public <T> T adaptTo(Type type, Object... context) {
		if (type == String.class && context.length == 1
				&& context[0] instanceof Integer floor) {
			@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
			T location = (T) ("Reserve, floor " + floor); // Computed, not declared
			return location;
		}
		return Adaptable.super.adaptTo(type, context);   // The declared adapters
	}

}

Reserve reserve = new Reserve();
assertThat(reserve.<String>adaptTo(String.class, 3)).isEqualTo("Reserve, floor 3");
Supplier<Shelf> shelves = reserve.adaptTo(SHELVES);
assertThat(shelves.get().titles()).isEqualTo(List.of());

8.5. Asking before there is an instance

Sometimes the question comes before the object exists. The command line builds its tree of commands before any command has parsed an option, and it needs to know whether a command could work under a given parent without creating either. Adapters.isAdaptable(class, type, contextTypes…​) answers from declarations only:

Listing 31. Asking a class instead of an object
// Before there is an instance: can a Branch be asked for these?
assertThat(Adapters.isAdaptable(Branch.class, SHELVES)).isTrue();
assertThat(Adapters.isAdaptable(Branch.class, String.class, String.class)).isTrue();
assertThat(Adapters.isAdaptable(Branch.class, String.class, Integer.class)).isFalse();

True means an instance can be asked and has a declared way to answer, not that it will: an adapter may still decline at run time. A class whose adaptation lives only in an adaptTo override is not adaptable by this check; an @Adapter method that delegates to the override makes it so.

8.6. Access

Adapters are read and invoked reflectively by common, so JPMS has to let it. Public members of an exported package are accessible; private members, like the fields of Branch, need their package to be open to common:

Listing 32. Opening a package to the runtime (generics/src/main/java/module-info.java)
module org.example.generics {

	requires transitive org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.common;

	exports org.example.generics;

	// Adapter fields and methods are read reflectively by common
	opens org.example.generics to org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.common;

}

A qualified opens …​ to keeps the package closed to everybody else. Command modules usually open their packages without qualification anyway, because picocli needs the same access (Chapter 16).

8.7. Where this is used

Three parts of the runtime are built on these few operations:

  • The capability framework matches a requirement’s type against each capability method’s declared return type with isAssignable, so Function<Library, String> and Function<Book, String> are different requirements (Chapter 10).

  • Command wiring matches a command’s @Parent and @SubCommand members against what other commands can be adapted to, first by declarations with isAdaptable, then by instances with adapt (Chapter 17).

  • Adaptation itself is how a command group offers its sub-commands what they need without knowing them.

In all three, no string names a type, and the compiler checks every declaration that takes part.

8.8. A trained eye

There is a hypothesis in evolutionary biology that describes how this design works on the people who use it. The sensory bias hypothesis holds that a receiver’s preferences can evolve first in a context unrelated to mating, such as finding food, and be exploited later by senders signaling to mates: a butterfly whose eyes were tuned to the colors of flowers, and mates that evolve wings of those colors.

Java developers have a trained eye for generic types. It was trained by collections, from Java 5 on, to read List<Book>, to know why a List<Novel> is not a List<Book>, and to reach for ? extends when only reading. That skill evolved for type-safe collections, not for wiring, and the runtime piggybacks on it: a requirement for Supplier<? extends Catalog> asks for exactly what a Java developer reads in it, so there is no new notation to learn, no qualifiers, no string identifiers and no wiring files.

8.9. The JVM, not Java

What the runtime matches on is in the class file: the Signature attribute, part of the JVM specification. Kotlin, Scala and Groovy write it for the types their programs declare, so their classes are matched like Java’s. This is a property of the JVM, not of the Java language.

With all due respect to two excellent platforms, TypeScript and Python do not have it. TypeScript’s type system is in many ways richer than Java’s, but it is checked at compile time and erased completely; the decorator metadata it can emit records constructors, Array for a Book[], not type arguments. Python keeps annotations at run time, generic arguments included, and FastAPI and Pydantic match on them well, but the language does not check them; a type checker does, if somebody runs it, so a match on an annotation is a match on an unchecked claim. .NET, to be fair, goes further than the JVM: its generics are reified, and even instances know their type arguments.

The butterfly is an illustration of the hypothesis, not a documented case. Documented cases include platyfish and swordtails (Basolo, 1990) and guppies, whose females' attraction to orange fruit may explain the males' orange spots (Rodd and colleagues, Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 2002). Verify the citations, or keep the wording that says the butterfly is an illustration.

Chapter 9. Flows, pumps and transformations

Most code in the runtime is plain blocking Java on virtual threads, and should be. Some of it is genuinely asynchronous: resolving capabilities that depend on each other, wiring a graph of objects that reference each other, delivering telemetry events to subscribers while the work they describe continues. For that code the runtime uses java.util.concurrent.Flow, a handful of operators, and one engine, the pump, that makes asynchronous resolution deterministic and able to say what went wrong.

This chapter is the most technical in the foundations. Architects can read the first section of each topic and skip the rest; the capability framework in the next chapter is built on what is here, and makes more sense with it.

9.1. Flow, not Reactor

The JDK has had the reactive streams interfaces since Java 9: Flow.Publisher, Flow.Subscriber, Flow.Subscription and Flow.Processor, plus one implementation, SubmissionPublisher. It does not have operators: no map, no filter, no retry. Reactive libraries such as Reactor fill that gap, and bring a large API, their own threading model and their own dependencies with them.

The runtime does not use them, for the reasons in Chapter 2, and takes a narrower position: write the few operators that are needed, and do not write a Reactor. On virtual threads, blocking is cheap, so most processing is better done on the pull side, with java.util.stream. The push-side operators exist for results that must stay a publisher: fed to another subscriber, subscribed to by several consumers, or delivered as soon as each item is ready.

9.2. Flows

org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.common.flow.Flows holds sources, operators and terminals, named in the style of Collectors and Executors.

Kind Members

Sources

of, fromIterable, fromStream, fromFuture, empty, error

Operators

map, mapNotNull, filter, peek, onTerminate, take, concat, concatMap

Terminals

toList and first, which return a CompletableFuture; forEach; toStream, the bridge to the pull side

Every operator follows three rules. It is lazy: it subscribes upstream once per downstream subscriber, at subscription time. Demand is accounted: filter requests one more item for every item it drops, and take cancels upstream after the last one. And an exception in a function you pass cancels upstream and signals onError downstream, so a failure never escapes as a thrown exception from somewhere unexpected.

Listing 33. Operators and a terminal (flow/src/test/java/…​/TestFlow.java)
Flow.Publisher<String> titles =
		Flows.of("Design Patterns", "Domain-Driven Design", "War and Peace");
Flow.Publisher<String> d = Flows.filter(titles, title -> title.startsWith("D"));
Flow.Publisher<Integer> lengths = Flows.map(d, String::length);
CompletableFuture<List<Integer>> result = Flows.toList(lengths); // Nothing ran until toList
assertThat(result.join()).containsExactly(15, 20);
Listing 34. The pull side
// On a virtual thread blocking is cheap, so the pull side is java.util.stream
try (Stream<String> stream = Flows.toStream(Flows.of("a", "bb", "ccc"))) {
	assertThat(stream.mapToInt(String::length).sum()).isEqualTo(6);
}

Absent on purpose: flatMap, merge, zip, schedulers and time operators. They are where reactive libraries get large and hard to reason about, and on virtual threads they are ordinary blocking code. concatMap is present because sequential composition is deterministic, and the capability framework needs it.

9.3. The pump

Asynchronous resolution has two classic failure modes. Work that depends on other work deadlocks when the dependency graph has a cycle, and the program hangs with no explanation. Or a pass counter gives up after some number of iterations, finds the same condition late, and says nothing about what was stuck.

org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.common.flow.Pump replaces both with one idea: block by pumping. A pump is a serial work queue drained by one thread at a time. Its blocking operations, join and settle, do not sleep: the waiting thread runs queued work itself until what it waits for is done. ForkJoinTask.join works this way, as do SWT’s readAndDispatch loop and Kotlin’s runBlocking.

Listing 35. Blocking by pumping
Pump pump = new Pump();                    // No executor: nothing runs until somebody pumps
CompletableFuture<String> answer = new CompletableFuture<>();
pump.execute("ask", () -> pump.execute("answer", () -> answer.complete("42")));
assertThat(pump.join(answer)).isEqualTo("42"); // The calling thread drains the queue

A pump created without an executor runs nothing until somebody pumps, which makes it deterministic: the same work runs in the same order every time, on the calling thread. That is the mode for tests and for resolutions that settle before returning. A pump created with an executor, such as Pump.Options.VIRTUAL_THREADS, drains work enqueued while nobody pumps, so publishers on it make progress without a blocking caller.

Idle and stalls

The pump knows when it is idle: no task can run, and no work it is tracking is in flight. What happens then while something is still waiting is a policy, not a guess:

Policy Meaning

COMPLETE

A closed world: every source feeds this pump, so nothing more can arrive. Waiters are released, a pumped publisher completes, and whatever is still unsatisfied is reported as a stall. This is the default, and what capability resolution uses.

WAIT

An open world: change reports, the network, webhooks. The pump waits for new work for a quiet period, then behaves as COMPLETE.

FAIL

A closed world where going idle early is a bug, for tests: the pump fails at once with a stall report.

A stall is reported as a StallException that lists everything that was waiting and what it was waiting for:

Listing 36. A stall, reported
Pump pump = new Pump();
CompletableFuture<String> nobodyCompletesThis = new CompletableFuture<>();
pump.when(nobodyCompletesThis, "waiting for a reply that never comes", (value, error) -> {});
assertThatThrownBy(pump::settle)
	.isInstanceOf(StallException.class)
	.hasMessageContaining("waiting for a reply that never comes");

Work that leaves the pump

The pump can only reason about work it knows of. Work that leaves it, an HTTP call or a model turn on another thread, must be tracked, or the pump would consider itself idle while the work is still out:

Listing 37. Tracking work done elsewhere
Pump pump = new Pump();
try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
	// Work that leaves the pump, like a remote call
	CompletableFuture<String> call = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "response", executor);
	CompletableFuture<String> tracked = pump.track(call, "remote call"); // In flight
	assertThat(pump.join(tracked)).isEqualTo("response");
}

track counts the stage as in flight until it completes, and returns a stage that completes on the pump, so whatever is composed on it runs in order with everything else. Code running inside a pump task can find its pump with Pump.current(), which is how a capability factory tracks the calls it makes.

Items that cannot proceed yet can yield. when(stage, description, action) parks an action until a stage completes, with a reason that appears in stall reports. submit(description, step) is a blind yield for a step that returns false while it cannot proceed; it is retried at a lower priority, and priorities age so that nothing starves.

Context and rules

A task runs in the OpenTelemetry context that was current when it was enqueued. Spans started by tasks are children of the span that enqueued them, whichever thread happens to drain the queue, and the unit of work’s OpenTelemetry instance travels with them (Chapter 11).

Two rules keep the pump honest. A blocking terminal on the pump’s own draining thread is refused, because a nested pump is re-entrancy, the classic event-loop bug. And an exception escaping a task fails the pump: new work is dropped and terminals rethrow it. Operators route exceptions to onError, so tasks rarely throw.

9.4. The transformer

A transformation turns sources into targets, and the interesting ones have dependencies: the target of one source references the targets of others. A model loaded from a diagram, a graph of modules that read each other, and a set of capabilities that depend on each other all have this shape, and the references can be cyclic.

Transformer maps each source to a publisher of its targets. A factory receives the source and a context, and the context’s get(otherSource) returns the targets of another source in the same transformation. Within one transformation each source is created once, its targets are replayed to everyone who asks, and all work runs through one pump, so it is deterministic and never recursive: requesting a source enqueues its creation instead of running it inline.

The example turns module descriptions, which name the modules they read, into nodes that reference each other:

Listing 38. Module descriptions and nodes (flow/…​/ModuleGraph.java)
/**
 * What a module says about itself: its name and the names of the modules it reads.
 */
public record Description(String name, List<String> reads) {
}

/**
 * A node of the graph, with references to the nodes it reads.
 */
public static final class Node {

	private final String name;
	private final List<Node> reads = new ArrayList<>();

	Node(String name) {
		this.name = name;
	}

	public String name() {
		return name;
	}

	public List<Node> reads() {
		return reads;
	}

	@Override
	public String toString() {
		return name + " -> " + reads.stream().map(Node::name).toList();
	}

}
Listing 39. Wiring a graph by subscription
public static Map<String, List<Node>> build(Map<String, Description> modules, String root) {
	Transformer<String, Node> transformer = new Transformer<>((name, context) -> { (1)
		Node node = new Node(name);
		for (String read: modules.get(name).reads()) {
			Flows.forEach(context.get(read), node.reads()::add);                    (2)
		}
		return Flows.of(node);                                                      (3)
	});
	return transformer.transform(List.of(root));                                   (4)
}
1 The factory: a source, here a module name, and the transformation’s context.
2 Wiring is subscription. The node subscribes to the targets of each module it reads and adds them as they arrive.
3 The node is emitted at once, without waiting for its references. That is what lets cyclic graphs wire without deadlock.
4 transform runs the transformation on a new pump and settles it. The result holds the targets of every source resolved, including those requested by factories, in the order they were requested.
Listing 40. A cycle, wired
Map<String, Description> descriptions = Map.of(
		"app", new Description("app", List.of("model", "common")),
		"model", new Description("model", List.of("common", "app")),   // A cycle back to app
		"common", new Description("common", List.of()));

Map<String, List<Node>> graph = ModuleGraph.build(descriptions, "app");

assertThat(graph.keySet()).containsExactly("app", "model", "common"); // In request order
Node app = graph.get("app").getFirst();
Node model = graph.get("model").getFirst();
Node common = graph.get("common").getFirst();
assertThat(app.reads()).containsExactlyInAnyOrder(model, common);
assertThat(model.reads()).containsExactlyInAnyOrder(common, app);     // The cycle, wired

app reads model and model reads app, and both nodes are created exactly once and reference each other. Note what the test does not assert: the order of a node’s references. References arrive in the order their targets are produced, not the order they were requested; when model subscribes, the node for app already exists and arrives at once, while the node for common is still queued. If order matters, keep the position with each reference, or wait for all of them.

Waiting is allowed. A factory that needs another source’s targets before it can emit its own collects them, for example with Flows.toList(context.get(other)), and emits when they are there. If two sources wait on each other, the pump goes idle with both waiting, and the transformation fails with the cycle named:

Listing 41. A waiting cycle, reported with its path
// Each source needs the other's targets before it can emit its own
Transformer<String, String> transformer = new Transformer<>((name, context) -> {
	String other = name.equals("chicken") ? "egg" : "chicken";
	CompletableFuture<List<String>> others = Flows.toList(context.get(other));
	return Flows.fromFuture(others.thenApply(targets -> name + targets));
});
assertThatThrownBy(() -> transformer.transform(List.of("chicken")))
	.isInstanceOf(StallException.class)
	.hasMessageContaining("cycle: chicken -> egg -> chicken");

Every transformation reports itself: transform runs in a Transformer.transform span, and each source is created in a Transformer.create span, from the factory call to the completion of its publisher. A source requested by a factory is created in a child span of the requesting source’s span, so the span tree shows the dependency graph.

9.5. Mapping methods

Writing one factory per kind of source gets repetitive. ReflectiveFactory assembles a factory from methods annotated with @Mapping, so one class contributes many mappings. A mapping method takes the source, and optionally the context, and returns a publisher of targets, a completion stage of one target, a target, or null for none. The method matches sources that are instances of its first parameter’s type, or of the type the annotation names.

The example renders a small document tree as outline lines, one method per kind of node:

Listing 42. Nodes (flow/…​/Outline.java)
public sealed interface Part permits Chapter, Section, Paragraph, Note {
}

public record Chapter(String title, List<Part> parts) implements Part {
}

public record Section(String title, List<Part> parts) implements Part {
}

public record Paragraph(String text) implements Part {
}

public record Note(String text) implements Part {
}
Listing 43. Mapping methods
public static class Mappings {

	@Mapping
	public Flow.Publisher<String> chapter(Chapter chapter, Context<Object, String> context) {
		return Flows.concat(
				Flows.of("# " + chapter.title()),
				Flows.concatMap(Flows.fromIterable(chapter.parts()), context::get)); (1)
	}

	@Mapping
	public Flow.Publisher<String> section(Section section, Context<Object, String> context) {
		return Flows.concat(
				Flows.of("## " + section.title()),
				Flows.concatMap(Flows.fromIterable(section.parts()), context::get));
	}

	@Mapping
	public String paragraph(Paragraph paragraph) {                                      (2)
		return paragraph.text();
	}

	@Mapping
	public String note(Note note) {                                                     (3)
		return "> Note: " + note.text();
	}

}

public static List<String> render(Chapter chapter) {
	ReflectiveFactory<Object, String> factory =
			ReflectiveFactory.first(MethodHandles.lookup(), new Mappings());
	return new Transformer<>(factory).transform(List.of(chapter)).get(chapter);
}
1 A chapter maps to its heading followed by the targets of its parts, each obtained from the context, in order.
2 A paragraph maps to its text.
3 A note is a different type, so it gets its own method rather than a condition inside the paragraph method.
Listing 44. The rendered outline
Chapter chapter = new Chapter("Flows", List.of(
		new Paragraph("Publishers, subscribers and pumps."),
		new Section("The pump", List.of(
				new Paragraph("Block by pumping."),
				new Note("Never join on the pumping thread.")))));
assertThat(Outline.render(chapter)).containsExactly(
		"# Flows",
		"Publishers, subscribers and pumps.",
		"## The pump",
		"Block by pumping.",
		"> Note: Never join on the pumping thread.");

Matching methods are ordered by priority (higher first), then by how specific the matched type is, then by how specific the declaring class is, then by name. ReflectiveFactory.first uses only the best match, which is polymorphic dispatch; ReflectiveFactory.all uses every match, in that order.

With first, the best match is chosen by type and priority before the method runs, and a method that returns null produces no target; it does not pass the source on to the next method. A high-priority method that matches every paragraph and returns null for most of them makes most paragraphs disappear. Distinguish cases by type, as the note does, or use all and let several methods contribute.

9.6. One engine

The pump, the transformer and the capability loader were written as separate pieces of code in older Nasdanika versions, and each hand-built the same four things: a memoizing registry, a queue drained on the caller’s thread, a loop guard, and a collector of results. In the runtime they are one engine. The transformer runs on the pump, and the capability loader, the subject of the next chapter, is a transformer whose sources are requirements and whose targets are providers of capabilities. Everything in this chapter about memoization, cycles, stall reports, context propagation and spans applies to capability resolution unchanged.

Chapter 10. The capability framework

ServiceLoader answers one question: give me every implementation of this interface. That is enough surprisingly often, and the runtime uses it whenever it is (Chapter 2). It is not enough when the question carries more than a type.

"A renderer for libraries, in Markdown." "A contents handler for a file named shelf.csv." "The sub-commands that can work under this command." Each of these is a requirement that the providers have to interpret, some providers will decline it, several may answer, and answering may require resolving other requirements first. That is what the capability framework is for.

10.1. Concepts

Five words carry the whole framework, and the rest of the book uses them in exactly these senses.

Requirement

What is asked for: an object that capability factories interpret. Usually a Requirement, a type with optional payloads, but any object can be one.

Capability factory

A service that says whether it can handle a requirement, and if so creates providers for it. It may raise requirements of its own while doing so.

Capability provider

A publisher of the capabilities that satisfy a requirement. A provider is subscribed lazily, and may carry information about what it provides, so that a caller can choose between providers without subscribing.

Capability

What a provider publishes: the object the requirement asked for.

Capability loader

Resolves a requirement against a set of factories: asks each whether it can handle it, collects their providers, and resolves the requirements the factories raise, once each, on a pump.

Figure 6. Resolution of a requirement that depends on another

The loader’s load returns a Flow.Publisher of providers, and blocking conveniences, loadAll and loadOne, flatten them into capabilities. Resolution runs on a pump (Chapter 9): every requirement is resolved once per resolution however many factories ask for it, a cycle is reported with its path instead of hanging, and each step is a span.

10.2. Requirements

A Requirement is a record of a type and a list of payloads. The type says what is wanted and may be generic; the payloads select and parameterize.

// Anything that is a Library
Requirement.of(Library.class)

// A supplier of libraries, not of books
Requirement.of(new TypeToken<Supplier<Library>>() {})

// A renderer of libraries to text, for the markdown format
Requirement.of(new TypeToken<Function<Library, String>>() {}, new Format("markdown"))

With no payloads, a requirement is a plain lookup by type, which is what ServiceLoader does, but generic, lazy and asynchronous. The type must be ground: a class, or a parameterized type whose arguments are classes or wildcards, never a type variable (Chapter 8).

Because a requirement is a cache key within a resolution, payloads should have value equality. Records do; the examples use them for formats and ISBNs. A type obtained from reflection, from a TypeToken or built some other way is equal to another describing the same type, so it does not matter where a type came from.

The example keeps its generic requirement types in one place:

Listing 45. Generic types used in requirements (capability/…​/Requirements.java)
/**
 * Generic types used in requirements. A class literal cannot say
 * Function<Library, String>; a type token can.
 */
public final class Requirements {

	public static final Type LIBRARY_SUPPLIER =
			new TypeToken<Supplier<Library>>() {}.getType();

	public static final Type LIBRARY_RENDERER =
			new TypeToken<Function<Library, String>>() {}.getType();

	public static final Type BOOK_RENDERER =
			new TypeToken<Function<Book, String>>() {}.getType();

	private Requirements() {
	}

}

Any other object can be a requirement too, and is handed to factories as it is. IsbnLookup, below, handles requirements that are Isbn records.

10.3. Factories with capability methods

Most factories are written as methods. A class extending ReflectiveCapabilityFactory contributes one capability per method annotated with @Capability, behind a single entry in module-info.java:

Listing 46. Four capabilities in one class (capability/…​/Renderers.java)
/**
 * One class, one entry in module-info, four capabilities. What each method provides
 * is its generic return type; what it needs are its parameters.
 */
public class Renderers extends ReflectiveCapabilityFactory {

	public Renderers() {
		super(MethodHandles.lookup());                                  (1)
	}

	@Capability
	public Supplier<Library> sample() {                                 (2)
		return Samples::library;
	}

	@Capability
	public Function<Book, String> markdownLine(Format format) {        (3)
		if (!"markdown".equals(format.name())) {
			return null;                                                (4)
		}
		return book -> "* _" + book.getName() + "_ (" + book.getYear() + ")";
	}

	@Capability
	public CompletionStage<Function<Library, String>> markdown(
			Format format,
			Loader loader,                                              (5)
			Span span) {
		if (!"markdown".equals(format.name())) {
			return null;
		}
		span.setAttribute("format", format.name());
		CompletableFuture<List<Function<Book, String>>> lines =
				loader.loadAll(Requirement.of(BOOK_RENDERER, format));      (6)
		return lines.thenApply(renderers -> library -> "# " + library.getName() + "\n\n"
				+ library.getBooks().stream().map(renderers.getFirst()).collect(joining("\n")));
	}

	@Capability
	public Function<Library, String> csv(Format format) {
		if (!"csv".equals(format.name())) {
			return null;
		}
		return library -> new CsvLibraryHandler().write(library);
	}

}
1 A method handle lookup from the declaring module, so the methods are invoked through method handles and need not be in an exported package.
2 No parameters: answers Requirement.of(new TypeToken<Supplier<Library>>() {}), and nothing else, because the generic return type is what is matched.
3 One parameter that is not injected takes a payload: this method is offered requirements of a compatible type with exactly one payload that is a Format.
4 Returning null declines. The method saw the requirement and it was not for markdown.
5 Loader and Span are injected by type. The method’s own span is a child of the resolution’s.
6 A dependency, resolved within the same resolution. The method does not block: it returns a stage that completes when the dependency is resolved.

What a method provides is its generic return type, matched with Types.isAssignable, so type arguments count. A method may return its capability directly, or wrapped in a way that says how it is delivered:

Return type Meaning

X

One capability, now

CompletionStage<X>

One capability, later

Flow.Publisher<X>

Any number of capabilities, as they are produced

CapabilityProvider<X>, Flow.Publisher<CapabilityProvider<X>>

Providers, for methods that want to control them

X[], List<X> and other iterables

The container is matched first; if it does not satisfy the requirement, its elements are offered as separate capabilities

Delivery wrappers are always unwrapped: a requirement for Object gets the values, not the publisher. Containers are values that hold others, so a requirement for List<Book> gets the list from a method returning one, while a requirement for Book gets its elements.

What a method takes is its parameters. Loader, Span, Logger, Meter, OpenTelemetry and Type (the required type, for a method that serves a range of them) are injected by their exact type, in any position. Every other parameter takes a payload, in order: a method matches when it has as many payload parameters as the requirement has payloads, and each payload is an instance of its parameter’s class. A requirement that is neither a Requirement nor a type is read as one payload with Object as the type, so a method taking an Isbn answers loadAll(new Isbn(…​)).

When several methods match, all of them contribute, the most specific provided type first. Choosing between the capabilities is the caller’s business, as with any requirement several factories answer.

10.4. Factories against the interface

A factory can also implement CapabilityFactory directly. That is the right choice when the factory interprets its requirements in a way no method signature can express, or simply for small factories with one job:

Listing 47. A factory written against the interface (capability/…​/IsbnLookup.java)
/**
 * A factory written against the interface: it interprets requirements of its own type
 * and depends on another capability, the libraries, which it requests through the loader.
 */
public class IsbnLookup implements CapabilityFactory<Isbn, Book> {

	@Override
	public boolean canHandle(Object requirement) {                       (1)
		return requirement instanceof Isbn;
	}

	@Override
	public Flow.Publisher<CapabilityProvider<Book>> create(
			Isbn isbn,
			Loader loader,
			Span span,
			Logger logger,
			Meter meter) {                                                 (2)
		span.setAttribute("isbn", isbn.value());
		CompletableFuture<List<Supplier<Library>>> libraries =
				loader.loadAll(Requirement.of(LIBRARY_SUPPLIER));           (3)
		return Flows.fromFuture(libraries.thenApply(suppliers -> CapabilityProvider.of(
				suppliers.stream()
					.map(Supplier::get)
					.flatMap(library -> library.getBooks().stream())
					.filter(book -> isbn.value().equals(book.getIsbn()))
					.toArray(Book[]::new))));                            (4)
	}

	@Override
	public String toString() {
		return "IsbnLookup";
	}

}
1 canHandle is called for every requirement in a resolution, so it must be cheap.
2 create is called once per requirement per resolution, on the resolution’s pump, in a span. The interface’s default create(requirement, loader) creates that span and calls this method with it, a logger, and a meter for measuring what providing the capability costs.
3 Factories raise dependencies through the loader they are given, never through a loader of their own, so that the dependency is resolved within the same resolution, memoized, and checked for cycles.
4 The providers are published when the dependency completes.

10.5. Registering and loading

A factory is a Java service. The example’s module declares all three of its factories, and the ResourceSetContributor discussed below:

Listing 48. Registering capability factories (capability/src/main/java/module-info.java)
import org.example.capability.CsvContributor;
import org.example.capability.CsvHandlers;
import org.example.capability.IsbnLookup;
import org.example.capability.Renderers;
import org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.common.capability.CapabilityFactory;
import org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.common.services.ResourceSetContributor;

module org.example.capability {

	requires transitive org.example.library;

	exports org.example.capability;

	// One entry per class, however many capabilities it has
	provides CapabilityFactory with
		Renderers,
		IsbnLookup,
		CsvHandlers;

	provides ResourceSetContributor with CsvContributor;

}

CapabilityLoader.getInstance() is the shared loader over every factory the service loader finds. It is created on first use, and it is stateless: memoization lives in a resolution, not in the loader, so sharing it is safe.

Listing 49. Loading by generic type (capability/src/test/java/…​/TestCapabilities.java)
CapabilityLoader loader = CapabilityLoader.getInstance(); // Factories registered as services
Supplier<Library> sample = loader.loadOne(Requirement.of(LIBRARY_SUPPLIER));
assertThat(sample.get().getName()).isEqualTo("A Modeler's Shelf");
Listing 50. Loading by type and payload
Function<Library, String> markdown = CapabilityLoader.getInstance()
		.loadOne(Requirement.of(LIBRARY_RENDERER, new Format("markdown")));
String text = markdown.apply(Samples.library());
assertThat(text)
	.startsWith("# A Modeler's Shelf")
	.contains("* _Domain-Driven Design_ (2003)");
Listing 51. A plain object as the requirement
List<Book> books = CapabilityLoader.getInstance().loadAll(new Isbn("978-0321125217"));
assertThat(books).extracting(Book::getName).containsExactly("Domain-Driven Design");

loadAll and loadOne are the blocking conveniences, for the edge of a program. Each creates a pump and pumps it on the calling thread until the result is complete; loadOne stops at the first capability and abandons work still queued. Inside a larger asynchronous computation, call load(requirement, pump) with the computation’s pump instead, so that resolution is ordered and settled with the rest of the work. load(requirement) without a pump resolves on virtual threads, for subscribers that do not pump.

10.6. Composing sources and loaders

A loader resolves against a source of factories, and the two can be composed separately, with different effects.

Composing sources puts factories into one resolution. A factory from one source can then satisfy a dependency raised by a factory from another. That is the way to put a local, task-specific factory in front of everything registered globally, for a test double or a one-off override:

Listing 52. A local source in front of the registered factories
/**
 * A test double, in front of everything registered: its sample wins with loadOne.
 */
public static class EmptyLibrary {

	@Capability
	public Supplier<Library> empty() {
		return () -> {
			Library library = LibraryFactory.eINSTANCE.createLibrary();
			library.setName("Empty");
			return library;
		};
	}

}

@Test
void localInFrontOfGlobal() {
	var factory = new ReflectiveCapabilityFactory(MethodHandles.lookup(), new EmptyLibrary());
	CapabilityFactorySource local = CapabilityFactorySource.of(factory);
	CapabilityFactorySource global = CapabilityFactorySource.serviceLoader();
	CapabilityFactorySource both = CapabilityFactorySource.concat(local, global);
	CapabilityLoader loader = CapabilityLoader.of(both);
	Supplier<Library> first = loader.loadOne(Requirement.of(LIBRARY_SUPPLIER));
	assertThat(first.get().getName()).isEqualTo("Empty");
	List<Supplier<Library>> all = loader.loadAll(Requirement.of(LIBRARY_SUPPLIER));
	assertThat(all).hasSize(2); // The registered sample is still there
}

Filtering a source is stronger than filtering results. A factory that is not in the filtered set cannot satisfy a dependency raised by another factory either, so a filtered source is a closure, not a check on the surface. That is how a trust level is enforced structurally:

Listing 53. Only factories from trusted modules
// Only factories from our own modules: a factory outside the set cannot satisfy
// a dependency raised inside it either
CapabilityFactorySource trusted = CapabilityFactorySource.serviceLoader()
		.filtered(f -> f.getClass().getModule().getName().startsWith("org.example."));
CapabilityLoader loader = CapabilityLoader.of(trusted);
assertThat(loader.<Book>loadAll(new Isbn("978-0201633610"))).hasSize(1);

Composing loaders keeps resolutions separate. CapabilityLoader.concat lets every loader contribute, in order; fallback consults the next loader only if the previous one produced nothing; cached memoizes across calls, which a loader deliberately does not do on its own, and should be used only where the same requirements recur and the answers are stable.

Sources are closeable. Closing one closes the factories in it that are AutoCloseable, which is how a factory that holds resources, a connection pool for example, is disposed of. A source owns its factories; a loader borrowing a shared source does not, which is why close is on the source.

10.7. When nothing comes back

A resolution that produces nothing has two very different causes: no factory claimed the requirement, or a factory claimed it and produced nothing. They have different fixes, and the explaining listener tells them apart:

Listing 54. Explaining a resolution
List<String> lines = new ArrayList<>();
CapabilityLoader loader = CapabilityLoader
		.of(new Renderers(), new IsbnLookup())
		.withListener(ResolutionListener.explaining(lines::add));
loader.loadAll(Requirement.of(LIBRARY_RENDERER, new Format("markdown")));
lines.forEach(System.out::println);

For the markdown renderer it prints the following, shortened here: package names are removed, the factory’s list of methods is elided, and F<A> stands for Function<A, String> with the markdown format as its payload.

requested F<Library>
  Renderers[...] handles F<Library>
  IsbnLookup declines F<Library>
  Renderers[...] needs F<Book> for F<Library>
requested F<Book> by F<Library>
  Renderers[...] produced 1 provider(s) for F<Library>
completed F<Library> with 1 provider(s) in 1389 us
  Renderers[...] handles F<Book>
  IsbnLookup declines F<Book>
  Renderers[...] produced 1 provider(s) for F<Book>
completed F<Book> with 1 provider(s) in 649 us

The order of the lines is worth a second look. The library renderer’s provider was produced before the book renderer it depends on was resolved, because the method returned a stage at once; the provider delivers its capability when the stage completes.

Listeners receive a sealed hierarchy of ResolutionEvent records (Requested, CacheHit, FactoryConsidered, DependencyRequested, Resolved, Failed, Completed), so a listener of your own pattern-matches on them. FactoryNodeCollector is one that rebuilds the dependency graph of a resolution, for troubleshooting or for drawing:

Listing 55. Collecting the dependency graph
FactoryNodeCollector collector = FactoryNodeCollector.create();
CapabilityLoader.of(new Renderers())
	.withListener(collector)
	.loadAll(Requirement.of(LIBRARY_RENDERER, new Format("markdown")));
// The markdown renderer needed a book renderer
assertThat(collector.getFactoryNodes())
	.anySatisfy(node -> assertThat(node.dependencies()).hasSize(1));

A requirement cycle fails the resolution with a StallException naming the path, for example cycle: chicken -> egg -> chicken, exactly as in a transformation. And every resolution is visible in telemetry: CapabilityLoader.loadAll or loadOne, a Transformer.create span per requirement, a CapabilityFactory.create span per factory that handles it, and a CapabilityFactory.method span per capability method invoked, with the requirement, the factory and the number of providers as attributes.

10.8. A case study: file names as pipelines

The runtime uses capabilities for one job that shows the framework at its best: deciding how to load a resource from its name.

A ContentsHandlingResource splits the last segment of its URI on dots and reads the parts as qualifiers, right to left. reading-group.library.groovy has the qualifiers groovy and library. The resource asks the capability loader for a ResourceContentsHandler with a requirement that carries the resource, the expected contents type and the qualifiers, starting with the leftmost qualifier, so that the most specific handler wins. The handler for library needs a compiled script, so it asks for a handler of the groovy qualifier to its right, and the two together turn a Groovy script into library objects (Chapter 19).

Adding a file format is therefore three small pieces. The example adds CSV for libraries. First the handler, which reads and writes the format:

Listing 56. A resource contents handler (capability/…​/CsvLibraryHandler.java)
/**
 * Libraries as CSV: an optional "# name" line, a header, then one book per line with
 * its authors separated by semicolons. Loading builds the model; saving writes it back.
 */
public class CsvLibraryHandler implements ResourceContentsHandler<EObject[]> {

	static final String HEADER = "title,year,genre,isbn,authors";

	@Override
	public Order getOrder() {
		return Order.of(0);
	}

	@Override
	public EObject[] load(InputStream in, Map<?, ?> options) throws IOException {
		LibraryFactory factory = LibraryFactory.eINSTANCE;
		Library library = factory.createLibrary();
		Map<String, Author> authors = new LinkedHashMap<>();
		var reader = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(in, StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
		for (String line = reader.readLine(); line != null; line = reader.readLine()) {
			if (line.startsWith("# ")) {
				library.setName(line.substring(2).trim());
			} else if (!line.isBlank() && !line.equals(HEADER)) {
				List<String> cells = split(line);
				Book book = factory.createBook();
				book.setName(cells.get(0));
				book.setYear(Integer.parseInt(cells.get(1)));
				book.setGenre(Genre.get(cells.get(2)));
				book.setIsbn(cells.get(3).isEmpty() ? null : cells.get(3));
				for (String name: cells.get(4).split(";")) {
					book.getAuthors().add(authors.computeIfAbsent(name.trim(), n -> {
						Author author = factory.createAuthor();
						author.setName(n);
						return author;
					}));
				}
				library.getBooks().add(book);
			}
		}
		library.getAuthors().addAll(authors.values());
		return new EObject[] { library };
	}

	@Override
	public void save(EObject[] roots, OutputStream out, Map<?, ?> options) throws IOException {
		out.write(write((Library) roots[0]).getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
	}

Then a capability method that offers the handler for the csv qualifier and declines everything else:

Listing 57. Offering the handler as a capability (capability/…​/CsvHandlers.java)
/**
 * Offers the CSV handler for resources whose name has a {@code csv} qualifier at the
 * position being resolved, such as {@code shelf.csv}. It reads the bytes of the resource
 * itself, so it does not chain to a handler on its right.
 */
public class CsvHandlers extends ReflectiveCapabilityFactory {

	public CsvHandlers() {
		super(MethodHandles.lookup());
	}

	@Capability
	public ResourceContentsHandler<EObject[]> csv(ResourceContentsHandler.Requirement r) {
		String qualifier = r.getQualifiers()[r.getQualifierIndex()];
		boolean mine = r.getContentsType() == EObject[].class
				&& "csv".equalsIgnoreCase(qualifier);
		return mine ? new CsvLibraryHandler() : null;
	}

}

And a resource set contributor that registers a factory of contents-handling resources for the csv extension:

Listing 58. Registering the extension (capability/…​/CsvContributor.java)
/**
 * Registers a factory for the csv extension whose resources find their contents handler
 * as a capability. The registration is a plain service (a lookup by extension); the
 * handler is a capability (a requirement the providers interpret).
 */
public class CsvContributor implements ResourceSetContributor {

	@Override
	public void contribute(ResourceSet resourceSet, Span span, Logger logger) {
		CapabilityLoader loader = CapabilityLoader.getInstance();
		var factory = new ContentsHandlingResourceFactory(loader, resourceSet);
		resourceSet.getResourceFactoryRegistry().getExtensionToFactoryMap().put("csv", factory);
	}

}

The split follows the principle of services before capabilities. Registering a factory for an extension is a lookup by type: every contributor, applied to every resource set, so it is a service. Choosing a handler is a requirement that providers interpret, a resource with a name and a contents type, so it is a capability.

With the three pieces on the module path, a CSV file is a model:

Listing 59. A CSV file, loaded, edited and saved as a model
Path file = directory.resolve("shelf.csv");
Files.writeString(file, """
		# Two classics
		title,year,genre,isbn,authors
		Domain-Driven Design,2003,TECHNOLOGY,978-0321125217,Eric Evans
		"Design Patterns, Elements",1994,TECHNOLOGY,,Erich Gamma; Richard Helm
		""");

URI uri = URI.createFileURI(file.toString());
Resource resource = NasdanikaResourceSet.createAndConfigure().getResource(uri, true);
Library library = (Library) resource.getContents().getFirst();
assertThat(library.getName()).isEqualTo("Two classics");
assertThat(library.getAuthors()).hasSize(3);
assertThat(library.getBooks().get(1).getName()).isEqualTo("Design Patterns, Elements");

library.getBooks().getFirst().setYear(2004);   // Edit the model, save the CSV
resource.save(null);
assertThat(Files.readString(file)).contains("Domain-Driven Design,2004,TECHNOLOGY");

The mechanism chains. A handler for one qualifier can ask for the handler of the qualifier to its right and transform what that one produces, which is how library builds on groovy. Each qualifier is a step, and the file name declares the pipeline.

10.9. When to use which

Use When

A Java service

The lookup is by type alone, such as every contributor or every EPackage.

A capability

There is a requirement for providers to interpret, providers may decline, or resolving it requires resolving something else.

Adaptation

You already have an object and need it in another shape (Chapter 8).

The capability framework is how the command line is assembled, which is where the next part of the book is heading after a detour through telemetry. Every resolution above was a span, and the next chapter explains why that was free.

Part III: Observability

Telemetry as part of the code: how the runtime instruments itself, how to watch a unit of work while it runs, and how telemetry and recorded changes become models kept next to the models they describe.

Chapter 11. Telemetry in the runtime

Telemetry usually arrives late in a project. The code works, it goes to production, something misbehaves, and somebody adds logging, then tracing, then a vendor’s agent that instruments what it can guess at. By then the code was written without the question "how will anyone know what this did?", and it shows.

In the runtime, telemetry is part of the code from the first line, and the first program in Chapter 6 showed what that buys: a program with no telemetry code of its own was observable, because everything it called reported what it did. This chapter explains the conventions behind that, how to instrument your own code the same way, and where the telemetry goes.

11.1. Two kinds of telemetry

Mainstream observability is built for the firehose. It collects everything cheaply, samples, keeps it for days or weeks, and answers "is it healthy right now?". That is the right tool for operations, and the runtime does not compete with it.

There is another kind, which most organizations do not have at all: telemetry that is collected deliberately, kept indefinitely, and resolved against models of the systems and the work, so that years later it can answer "who changed what, in the course of what work?". I call it strategic telemetry, and its rule is that every signal is precious. It is cheap at the scale it operates on, and what is expensive is not being able to answer.

Both kinds start from the same instrumentation. Code reports through the OpenTelemetry API, and whoever runs the code decides whether the signals go to an operational backend, to a console, into a model that is kept forever, or to all three.

11.2. The conventions

Four conventions make the runtime’s telemetry consistent. They were stated in Chapter 2; here is what each means in code.

Spans for operations, log records for what happens in them. An operation that has a duration is a span: loading a resource, resolving a requirement, executing a command. Everything that happens within an operation is a log record emitted through the OpenTelemetry Logs API and correlated with the current span: a message, a warning, a measurement, progress. Span events, Span.addEvent, are not used, because OpenTelemetry is moving events onto the Logs API, where an event is a log record with an event name.

One OpenTelemetry per unit of work. A command, a request and a test are units of work. Each builds or is handed its own OpenTelemetry instance and makes it current, the way it would make a span current. Instrumented code gets the instance from the context, never from GlobalOpenTelemetry, which the runtime does not use. Two commands running in one JVM can therefore send their telemetry to different places, and a test can capture exactly the telemetry of the code it tests.

The context carries everything. The current instance travels in the OpenTelemetry Context next to the current span, so it crosses threads wherever the context does: the pump propagates it to its tasks, and content written on another thread runs in the context of the code that asked for it.

Watching is subscribing. A console, a progress bar, a test or a browser watching a unit of work subscribes to the same spans and log records an exporter receives, through a publishing wrapper (Chapter 12).

11.3. The Telemetry class

org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.common.telemetry.Telemetry is where instrumented code gets its instance, and where the runtime’s attribute keys and event names are defined.

Member Purpose

current()

The instance in the current context, or the no-op instance

makeCurrent(openTelemetry), with(context, openTelemetry)

Make an instance current, as a scope to close

of(notifier)

The current instance, or the one attached to a resource set, for EMF code that runs outside a unit of work

attach(resourceSet, openTelemetry)

Attach an instance to a resource set

tracer, logger, meter

The runtime’s tracer, logger and meter of an instance

inSpan(tracer, name, attributes, body)

Run a body in a new current span; a failure is recorded on the span and rethrown

log(logger, severity, eventName, body, attributes)

Emit a log record in the current context, if the logger is enabled for the severity

recordFailure(span, failure)

Record an exception and set the error status

w3cPropagators(), extract, extractFromEnvironment

Continue a trace started by another process

The keys and event names are listed in Appendix B.

11.4. Instrumenting your code

The telemetry example catalogs books, one at a time, and reports what it does. It starts with a few constants:

Listing 60. Instrumentation scope and attribute keys (telemetry/…​/Cataloging.java)
/**
 * The instrumentation scope is the module name, by the runtime's identity rule.
 */
static final String SCOPE = Cataloging.class.getModule().getName();

static final AttributeKey<String> TITLE = AttributeKey.stringKey("library.book.title");
static final AttributeKey<Long> BOOKS = AttributeKey.longKey("library.books");

The instrumentation scope identifies who produced a span or a log record. By the runtime’s identity rule it is the JPMS module name, which the code reads from its own class rather than repeating it in a string. Attribute keys are typed, AttributeKey<String> and AttributeKey<Long>, and named in the dotted lowercase style of OpenTelemetry’s semantic conventions, with a prefix that says whose they are.

The operation itself:

Listing 61. Work in a span, with log records, progress and a metric
public static int catalog(List<String> titles) {
	OpenTelemetry openTelemetry = Telemetry.current();                   (1)
	Tracer tracer = openTelemetry.getTracer(SCOPE);
	Logger logger = openTelemetry.getLogsBridge().get(SCOPE);
	LongCounter cataloged = openTelemetry.getMeter(SCOPE)
			.counterBuilder("library.books.cataloged")
			.build();
	long total = titles.size();
	Attributes attributes = Attributes.of(BOOKS, total);

	return Telemetry.inSpan(tracer, "Catalog books", attributes, span -> { (2)
		int done = 0;
		for (String title: titles) {
			try {
				catalogOne(tracer, title);
				cataloged.add(1);                                           (3)
			} catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
				String message = "Skipped: " + e.getMessage();
				Telemetry.log(logger, Severity.WARN, null, message, null);    (4)
			}
			++done;
			Telemetry.log(                                                  (5)
					logger,
					Severity.INFO,
					PROGRESS_EVENT,
					"Processed " + done + " of " + total,
					Attributes.of(PROGRESS_WORKED, (long) done, PROGRESS_TOTAL, total));
		}
		return done;
	});
}
1 The instance of the current unit of work. The code does not know or care whether it is an SDK exporting to a backend, a publishing wrapper feeding a console, or the no-op instance.
2 Telemetry.inSpan starts a span, makes it current, runs the body with the span, records a failure if the body throws, and ends the span. It returns what the body returns.
3 A counter from the instance’s meter. Metrics are aggregated by the SDK and exported periodically.
4 A warning is a log record in the current span. The span does not fail: skipping one book is part of the operation, not a failure of it.
5 Progress is a log record with the event name nasdanika.progress and two attributes, the work done and the total. Anything watching the operation can draw a progress bar from it.

When the work is not a lexical block, or when you want control over the span, start one yourself:

Listing 62. A span started and ended by hand
static void catalogOne(Tracer tracer, String title) {
	Span span = tracer.spanBuilder("Catalog a book")
			.setAttribute(TITLE, title)                                   (1)
			.startSpan();
	try (Scope scope = span.makeCurrent()) {                            (2)
		if (title.isBlank()) {
			throw new IllegalArgumentException("a book needs a title");
		}
		span.setStatus(StatusCode.OK);
	} catch (RuntimeException e) {
		Telemetry.recordFailure(span, e);                               (3)
		throw e;
	} finally {
		span.end();                                                     (4)
	}
}
1 Attributes known up front go on the builder.
2 Making the span current is what makes spans and log records created inside it its children.
3 A failure is recorded on the span with its exception, and the span gets the error status.
4 A span must end, whatever happens, or it is never exported.

11.5. Units of work

Instrumented code only reports. The unit of work decides where the reports go, by making an instance current:

Listing 63. A unit of work, watched live (telemetry/…​/UnitOfWork.java)
public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
	SpanTree tree = new SpanTree(System.out);
	try (var openTelemetry = new PublishingOpenTelemetry(OpenTelemetry.noop())) { (1)
		openTelemetry.subscribe(tree);                                        (2)
		try (Scope scope = Telemetry.makeCurrent(openTelemetry)) {            (3)
			Cataloging.catalog(List.of("Domain-Driven Design", " ", "Design Patterns"));
		}
	}                                                                       (4)
	tree.await();                                                           (5)
}
1 A publishing wrapper around the no-op instance: no SDK, and everything is published to subscribers.
2 A subscriber that prints the spans as a tree, shown in Chapter 12.
3 The instance is current for the unit of work, and only for it.
4 Closing the wrapper completes the subscribers.
5 Delivery is asynchronous by default, so the program waits for the subscriber to finish.

It prints:

+ Catalog books {library.books=3}
  + Catalog a book {library.book.title=Domain-Driven Design}
  - Catalog a book (0 ms)
  [1/3] Processed 1 of 3
  + Catalog a book {library.book.title= }
    ! a book needs a title
  - Catalog a book (0 ms)
  WARN Skipped: a book needs a title
  [2/3] Processed 2 of 3
  + Catalog a book {library.book.title=Design Patterns}
  - Catalog a book (0 ms)
  [3/3] Processed 3 of 3
- Catalog books (5 ms)

In a real assembly the unit of work is created once, in one place. The launcher creates one per command, with an OpenTelemetry SDK whose exporters save the telemetry as models (Chapter 18). The HTTP handler creates one per request (Chapter 15). A test creates one per test, usually a publishing wrapper with deterministic delivery, so that it can assert on what the code reported.

11.6. What the runtime instruments

Most of the telemetry of a typical program comes from the runtime itself.

Spans Produced by

ResourceSetContributor.configure, with a log record per contribution

Configuring a resource set from services

Contribute To Resource Set

Each contributor that uses the interface’s default

Resource.load, Resource.save, Resource.unload, with URI, bytes and root objects

Every resource the runtime’s factories create, and yours if you use ResourceTelemetry

URIHandler.read, URIHandler.write, URIHandler.delete, with progress every second

Every stream a configured resource set opens

Content.writeTo, Content.pipe, and client spans named after the HTTP method

Transfers of volume content (Chapter 14)

Server spans named <method> <route>

Requests through the volume HTTP handlers (Chapter 15)

Transformer.transform, Transformer.create

Transformations (Chapter 9)

CapabilityLoader.loadAll, CapabilityLoader.loadOne, CapabilityFactory.create, CapabilityFactory.method, Create Capability

Capability resolution (Chapter 10)

One span per executed command, named after the command

The command line (Chapter 16)

Evaluating script, Loading <Type>, Setting <feature>, with script line numbers

The Groovy DSL (Chapter 19)

Two span names are phrases, Contribute To Resource Set and Create Capability, while the rest follow Type.operation. Renaming them to ResourceSetContributor.contribute and CapabilityFactory.create would make the names predictable, but CapabilityFactory.create is already the name of the loader’s span around the same call, so the factory’s own span would need another name, or could be dropped.

11.7. Crossing threads and processes

Within a JVM, the OpenTelemetry context lives in a thread local, and the runtime carries it wherever work moves. A pump task runs in the context that was current when it was enqueued. A stage tracked or awaited on a pump completes in the caller’s context. Content produced by a writer on a virtual thread runs the writer in the context of the reader that started it. Spans therefore nest the way the work nests, whichever thread does it, and the unit of work’s instance travels along.

Across processes, context travels in W3C trace context headers. Telemetry.w3cPropagators() returns the propagators for W3C trace context and baggage; an instance built with them injects traceparent into the requests the volume HTTP client makes, and the volume HTTP handler extracts it, so one trace spans both sides (Chapter 15).

A process can also be invoked by something that has a trace of its own: a build step, a function call, a workflow engine. The runtime continues it from a map of carrier values, such as request parameters, or from the environment variables TRACEPARENT, TRACESTATE and BAGGAGE:

Listing 64. Continuing a trace started elsewhere (telemetry/…​/Propagation.java)
/**
 * Runs the work as part of the trace whose context the carrier holds, for example
 * traceparent from request parameters or TRACEPARENT from the environment.
 */
public static <T> T continueTrace(
		OpenTelemetry openTelemetry,
		Map<String, String> carrier,
		Supplier<T> work) {
	Context remote = Telemetry.extract(openTelemetry, Context.current(), carrier); (1)
	try (Scope scope = Telemetry.with(remote, openTelemetry).makeCurrent()) {     (2)
		return work.get();
	}
}

/**
 * The launcher's way: TRACEPARENT, TRACESTATE and BAGGAGE environment variables.
 */
public static <T> T continueFromEnvironment(OpenTelemetry openTelemetry, Supplier<T> work) {
	Context remote = Telemetry.extractFromEnvironment(openTelemetry, Context.current());
	try (Scope scope = Telemetry.with(remote, openTelemetry).makeCurrent()) {
		return work.get();
	}
}
1 Extraction reads traceparent, or TRACEPARENT as environment variables are named, with the instance’s propagators. If the carrier holds nothing valid, the context is returned unchanged.
2 The extracted context and the instance become current together, so spans started inside continue the remote trace.
Listing 65. A span in the continued trace
var propagating = OpenTelemetry.propagating(Telemetry.w3cPropagators());   (1)
var carrier = Map.of("traceparent", "00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01");
String traceId = Propagation.continueTrace(propagating, carrier, () -> {
	Tracer tracer = Telemetry.tracer(Telemetry.current());
	Span span = tracer.spanBuilder("Handle request").startSpan();
	try {
		return span.getSpanContext().getTraceId();
	} finally {
		span.end();
	}
});
assertThat(traceId).isEqualTo("4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736");          (2)
1 The no-op instance with propagators: enough to extract a context, with no SDK.
2 The span started inside belongs to the trace from the carrier.

The launcher does this for every command it runs, so nsdk started by a CI job with TRACEPARENT set adds its spans to the job’s trace.

11.8. Where telemetry goes

Instrumented code never decides, which is the point. The options are the unit of work’s:

  • Nowhere. With no instance current, Telemetry.current() is the no-op instance, and instrumentation costs almost nothing.

  • To subscribers. A PublishingOpenTelemetry wrapper publishes spans and log records as they happen, with or without an SDK behind it (Chapter 12).

  • To an operational backend. An OpenTelemetry SDK with an OTLP exporter sends everything to a collector, as any OpenTelemetry application would.
