  • Into models. An SDK with the runtime’s model exporters saves traces, logs and metrics as EMF resources, next to the models they describe (Chapter 13).

These combine. A launcher can export to a backend and to models at once, and still publish to a console.

Chapter 12. Watching work live

Exported span data arrives when a span ends, often in a batch some seconds later. That is fine for looking at what happened, and useless for a person watching a long operation, who wants to know what is happening now and how far along it is. It is also awkward for tests, which want to see what the code under test reported, in order, without an exporter and a collector in between.

The runtime publishes telemetry as it happens. This chapter shows how, and how to subscribe.

12.1. Publishing OpenTelemetry

PublishingOpenTelemetry wraps any OpenTelemetry instance, the no-op instance included, and is a Flow.Publisher<SpanEvent>. Its tracers publish an event for every change to the spans they start: started, attribute set, status set, exception recorded, renamed, ended. Its loggers publish every log record they emit, together with the span that was current. Meters and propagators are the delegate’s.

Delivery has three properties that make it safe to leave on:

  • It never blocks the instrumented code. Events are offered to a bounded buffer per subscriber; a subscriber that cannot keep up loses events, and the losses are counted in getDroppedCount().

  • It costs nothing when nobody listens. With no subscribers, events are not even created.

  • It does not need an SDK. Over the no-op instance, spans record nothing, and events are still published. Tracers and loggers report themselves as enabled while anybody is subscribed, so instrumentation that checks before doing work does not go quiet on a progress bar because no SDK is installed.

Events are delivered asynchronously, in order per subscriber, on virtual threads by default. For tests and consoles, a tracer provider created with Runnable::run delivers each event on the thread that produced it:

Listing 66. Deterministic delivery for tests (telemetry/src/test/java/…​/TestTelemetry.java)
/**
 * Delivers events on the instrumented thread, in order: deterministic, as tests want.
 */
static PublishingOpenTelemetry deterministic(OpenTelemetry delegate) {
	var provider = new PublishingTracerProvider(TracerProvider.noop(), Runnable::run, 1024);
	return new PublishingOpenTelemetry(delegate, provider);
}

12.2. Span events

SpanEvent is a sealed interface with one record per kind of event:

Event When

Started

A span started, with its name, kind and initial attributes

AttributeSet

An attribute was set on a live span

StatusSet

The status was set

ExceptionRecorded

An exception was recorded

Renamed

The span was renamed

Ended

The span ended

EventAdded

Span.addEvent was called. The runtime itself does not do this; it emits log records instead

LogEmitted

A log record was emitted, with the publishing span that was current, if any

A subscriber pattern-matches on them, and its switch decides what a new kind of event does to it. With a default case, as in the tree below, it ignores the new kind. With a case for every kind and no default, it stops compiling when a kind is added, so the compiler shows what needs handling; compiled earlier and run against a newer runtime, it throws MatchException when the new kind arrives.

Every event has the span it concerns and a timestamp. A PublishingSpan knows its publishing parent, so a subscriber can compute nesting, and isWithin(span) tells whether a span is a descendant of another.

12.3. A live tree

The subscriber the previous chapter used prints spans as an indented tree, with errors, log records and progress:

Listing 67. Printing spans as they run (telemetry/…​/SpanTree.java)
/**
 * Prints spans as an indented tree while they run: starts, errors, log records with
 * progress, and ends with durations. A console is one subscriber; a browser, a test or
 * a file is another.
 */
public class SpanTree implements Flow.Subscriber<SpanEvent> {

	private final PrintStream out;
	private final Map<PublishingSpan, Instant> started = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
	private final CountDownLatch completed = new CountDownLatch(1);

	public SpanTree(PrintStream out) {
		this.out = out;
	}

	@Override
	public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription subscription) {
		subscription.request(Long.MAX_VALUE);
	}

	@Override
	public void onNext(SpanEvent event) {
		switch (event) {                                                    (1)
			case SpanEvent.Started s -> {
				started.put(s.span(), s.timestamp());
				out.println(indent(s.span()) + "+ " + s.name() + format(s.attributes()));
			}
			case SpanEvent.StatusSet s when s.code() == StatusCode.ERROR ->
				out.println(indent(s.span()) + "  ! " + s.description());
			case SpanEvent.LogEmitted l ->
				out.println(indent(l.span()) + "  " + describe(l.record()));
			case SpanEvent.Ended e -> {
				Duration duration = Duration.between(started.remove(e.span()), e.timestamp());
				String name = e.span().getName() + " (" + duration.toMillis() + " ms)";
				out.println(indent(e.span()) + "- " + name);
			}
			default -> {
				// Attributes set later, exceptions and renames are not printed
			}
		}
	}

	private static String describe(LogRecord record) {
		if (Telemetry.PROGRESS_EVENT.equals(record.eventName())) {         (2)
			Long worked = record.attributes().get(Telemetry.PROGRESS_WORKED);
			Long total = record.attributes().get(Telemetry.PROGRESS_TOTAL);
			return "[" + worked + "/" + total + "] " + record.bodyAsString();
		}
		return record.severity() + " " + record.bodyAsString();
	}
1 One case per kind of event, with a guard for error statuses. Kinds the tree does not show fall through to default.
2 Progress is recognized by its event name and drawn from its two attributes.

The same twenty lines could update a progress bar, write lines to a file, or push events to a browser. A console is one subscriber among others, not a second logging API.

12.4. Following one operation

A busy unit of work has many concurrent operations. within(span) filters the events to one span and the publishing spans started under it, which is what a progress view for one operation needs:

Listing 68. Subscribing to one operation
try (PublishingOpenTelemetry openTelemetry = deterministic(OpenTelemetry.noop());
		Scope scope = Telemetry.makeCurrent(openTelemetry)) {
	Tracer tracer = openTelemetry.getTracer("org.example.telemetry");
	Span unrelated = tracer.spanBuilder("Unrelated").startSpan();
	Span operation = tracer.spanBuilder("Operation").startSpan();

	Started started = new Started();
	openTelemetry.within((PublishingSpan) operation).subscribe(started);   (1)

	try (Scope operationScope = operation.makeCurrent()) {
		tracer.spanBuilder("Step").startSpan().end();                       // Seen
	}
	Context elsewhere = Context.current().with(unrelated);
	tracer.spanBuilder("Elsewhere").setParent(elsewhere).startSpan().end(); // Not seen
	operation.end();
	unrelated.end();
	assertThat(started.names).containsExactly("Step");
}
1 Only events of operation and its descendants are delivered. Unrelated and the span started under it are filtered out.

Nesting follows the context, not the tracer: a span started by any tracer of the same provider while operation is current is its child, and is seen.

12.5. Testing with telemetry

Because telemetry is published without an SDK, a test can assert on what the code reported as easily as on what it returned:

Listing 69. Asserting on reported telemetry
var bytes = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
try (PublishingOpenTelemetry openTelemetry = deterministic(OpenTelemetry.noop())) {
	openTelemetry.subscribe(new SpanTree(new PrintStream(bytes, true, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)));
	try (Scope scope = Telemetry.makeCurrent(openTelemetry)) {
		List<String> titles = List.of("Domain-Driven Design", " ", "Design Patterns");
		assertThat(Cataloging.catalog(titles)).isEqualTo(3);
	}
}
String tree = bytes.toString(StandardCharsets.UTF_8).replaceAll("\\(\\d+ ms\\)", "(n ms)");
assertThat(tree)
	.contains("+ Catalog books {library.books=3}")
	.contains("  ! a book needs a title")
	.contains("  [2/3] Processed 2 of 3")
	.contains("- Catalog books (n ms)");

This changes what is worth testing. "The import reports progress for every book" and "a book without a title is a warning, not a failure" are now properties a test can check, and keep checking.

12.6. What comes next

The runtime’s direction for live observation is a browser. A command, or a test, starts the JDK HTTP server on a random port, subscribes to its unit of work, and streams span events to a React UI with server-sent events, so that a long operation is watched as a tree of spans with progress bars, live, and the same UI opens recorded telemetry afterwards (PLANNED, Chapter 26). Everything it needs on the Java side exists today: publishing, within, and the model the next chapter describes.

Chapter 13. Telemetry as a model

Telemetry sent to a backend becomes the backend’s: it is stored in its format, queried with its language, and forgotten on its schedule. The runtime can also keep telemetry as models, in files next to the models it describes, in the same formats, versioned in the same repositories. Then a trace is something you load, navigate, query, diff and commit, and a change to a model can be recorded in the span that made it.

This chapter covers the telemetry model, the exporters that fill it from the OpenTelemetry SDK, and change recording.

13.1. Why keep telemetry as a model

"Somebody changed the year of a book" is a log line. "In the course of the work named 'Correct the year', the attribute year of the book 'Domain-Driven Design' changed to 2004" is structure: the work, the object and the attribute are elements you can navigate to, and the statement can be checked years later.

That is the difference between operational and strategic telemetry made concrete. Its uses are the ones where an answer has to survive the people who knew it:

  • Audit and compliance. Every change to an element during an audit period, who made it, and in the course of what work, is a query instead of an archaeology project.

  • Agents. An agent’s run is a trace whose spans are its tool calls, and the changes it made to models are in the spans that made them. Reviewing an agent’s work means reading that trace, and reverting it means applying the changes in reverse.

  • Evidence. Telemetry kept with the build or the release it describes is evidence of what ran, the right end of the line in Chapter 2.

  • Replay. Spans carry timing and nesting, so an execution can be played back over a diagram of the system that ran it, which is planned for the polymorphic UI in React (Chapter 26).

13.2. The telemetry model

The model lives in models/telemetry, in four parts, following OpenTelemetry’s own data model (OTLP) so that nothing is lost on the way in:

Package Contents

telemetry

Resource (the entity that produced the signals), InstrumentationScope, and typed attribute values, KeyValue and AnyValue

traces

TracesData, ResourceSpans, ScopeSpans, Span, SpanEvent, SpanLink, SpanStatus, and the change recording classes

logs

LogsData, ResourceLogs, ScopeLogs, LogRecord

metrics

MetricsData, ResourceMetrics, ScopeMetrics, Gauge, Sum, Histogram, ExponentialHistogram, Summary, their data points, and Exemplar

On top of OTLP, the model adds what makes telemetry navigable as a graph:

  • Spans nest. A span’s children are contained by it, within an instrumentation scope, so a trace reads as a tree. Across scopes, spans reference their parent by id.

  • Log records live in their spans. A log record emitted in a span is contained by that span, not stored in a separate stream to be joined later.

  • Changes live in their spans. A span contains the description of the model changes recorded while it was current.

  • References resolve. Span links and the change classes reference spans as objects, not only by id, and an exemplar references the span that produced a measurement.

13.3. Exporting to the model

The model exporters are OpenTelemetry SDK exporters: ModelSpanExporter, ModelLogRecordExporter and ModelMetricExporter, in the module org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.models.telemetry:exporters. Each writes into an EMF resource and saves it when the SDK flushes or shuts down.

Only the assembly that runs the unit of work needs the SDK. Instrumented code, the runtime’s included, needs only the API:

Listing 70. Dependencies of an assembly that records telemetry (recording/pom.xml)
<dependencies>
	<dependency>
		<groupId>${project.groupId}</groupId>
		<artifactId>library</artifactId>
		<version>${project.version}</version>
	</dependency>
	<!-- Exporters to the telemetry model, and the model itself -->
	<dependency>
		<groupId>org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.models.telemetry</groupId>
		<artifactId>exporters</artifactId>
	</dependency>
	<!-- The SDK: only the assembly that runs the unit of work needs it -->
	<dependency>
		<groupId>io.opentelemetry</groupId>
		<artifactId>opentelemetry-sdk</artifactId>
	</dependency>
	<!-- YAML for the telemetry files -->
	<dependency>
		<groupId>org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime</groupId>
		<artifactId>emf-json</artifactId>
	</dependency>
</dependencies>

The SDK is built as usual, with the model exporters plugged in:

Listing 71. An SDK that exports to models (recording/…​/Recorder.java)
/**
 * The SDK owns the exporters, and the exporters own the telemetry resources: shutting
 * the SDK down exports what is pending and saves them. Log records emitted in a span go
 * into that span.
 */
static OpenTelemetrySdk openTelemetry(
		ModelSpanExporter spans,
		Resource logs,
		Resource metrics) {

	var service = io.opentelemetry.sdk.resources.Resource.create(
			Attributes.of(AttributeKey.stringKey("service.name"), "librarian"));
	var resource = io.opentelemetry.sdk.resources.Resource.getDefault().merge(service);

	var logRecords = new ModelLogRecordExporter(logs, spans);
	var measurements = new ModelMetricExporter(metrics);
	return OpenTelemetrySdk.builder()
			.setPropagators(Telemetry.w3cPropagators())
			.setTracerProvider(SdkTracerProvider.builder()
					.setResource(resource)
					.addSpanProcessor(BatchSpanProcessor.builder(spans).build())
					.build())
			.setLoggerProvider(SdkLoggerProvider.builder()
					.setResource(resource)
					.addLogRecordProcessor(BatchLogRecordProcessor.builder(logRecords).build())
					.build())
			.setMeterProvider(SdkMeterProvider.builder()
					.setResource(resource)
					.registerMetricReader(PeriodicMetricReader.builder(measurements).build())
					.build())
			.build();
}

The log record exporter is given the span exporter, so that log records emitted in exported spans are added to those spans; log records emitted outside any span go to the logs resource. The W3C propagators let the unit of work continue a trace started elsewhere (Chapter 11).

13.4. Recording changes

Change recording is EMF’s, extended so that recorded changes know their spans. Changes.record(target, body) records the changes the body makes to a resource set, a resource or an object, and hands the description to the sink that is current in the OpenTelemetry context. The span exporter is such a sink: it puts each description into the span it was recorded in.

Listing 72. A unit of work whose telemetry and changes are saved as models
public static void curate(Path directory) throws IOException {
	NasdanikaResourceSet telemetry = NasdanikaResourceSet.createAndConfigure(); (1)
	Resource traces = telemetry.createResource(uri(directory, "traces.yml"));
	Resource logs = telemetry.createResource(uri(directory, "logs.yml"));
	Resource metrics = telemetry.createResource(uri(directory, "metrics.yml"));
	ModelSpanExporter spans = new ModelSpanExporter(traces);

	try (OpenTelemetrySdk openTelemetry = openTelemetry(spans, logs, metrics);
			Scope telemetryScope = Telemetry.makeCurrent(openTelemetry);        (2)
			Scope changesScope = Changes.makeCurrent(spans)) {                  (3)

		Tracer tracer = openTelemetry.getTracer(Recorder.class.getModule().getName());
		Telemetry.inSpan(tracer, "Curate the shelf", null, span -> {
			NasdanikaResourceSet models = NasdanikaResourceSet.createAndConfigure();
			Resource shelf = models.createResource(uri(directory, "shelf.library"));
			Changes.record(models, () -> {                                      (4)
				shelf.getContents().add(Samples.library());
				shelf.save(null);
				return null;
			});

			Book ddd = book((Library) shelf.getContents().getFirst(), "Domain-Driven Design");
			return Telemetry.inSpan(tracer, "Correct the year", null, edit -> {
				return Changes.record(models, () -> {                           (5)
					ddd.setYear(2004);
					shelf.save(null);
					return null;
				});
			});
		});
	}                                                                           (6)
}
1 The telemetry resources live in a resource set of their own, created before the instance is made current, so that saving them at shutdown is not itself traced.
2 The SDK is the unit of work’s instance. Everything below reports to it.
3 The span exporter becomes the sink of recorded changes for the unit of work.
4 Creating the library and saving it is recorded in the current span, "Curate the shelf".
5 Correcting the year is recorded in its own span, so the change lands there.
6 Closing the SDK exports what is pending and saves traces.yml, logs.yml and metrics.yml.

The recorded description is turned around before it is stored. EMF’s change recorder produces a description that undoes the changes; the runtime stores one that describes them forward, detached from the model:

  • Objects added in the body are copied into the description, as objects to attach.

  • Objects removed in the body are moved into the description, so their state when they were removed is kept for audit.

  • Other objects are referenced by proxies with their URIs, so the description can be saved in a different resource set and resolves to the model wherever the model is saved.

Nothing is recorded without a current sink or outside a sampled span, so the same code runs unchanged in a unit of work that does not record.

13.5. Reading telemetry back

Recorded telemetry is a model, so reading it is ordinary EMF:

Listing 73. Reading traces and their changes (recording/…​/TraceReader.java)
public static List<String> read(Path directory) {
	TracesData traces = (TracesData) NasdanikaResourceSet.createAndConfigure()
			.getResource(Recorder.uri(directory, "traces.yml"), true)
			.getContents()
			.getFirst();

	// Spans nest within an instrumentation scope; across scopes they have parent ids
	Map<String, Span> spans = new LinkedHashMap<>();
	traces.getResourceSpans().stream()
		.flatMap(resourceSpans -> resourceSpans.getScopeSpans().stream())
		.flatMap(scopeSpans -> scopeSpans.getSpans().stream())
		.forEach(span -> collect(span, spans));
	Map<String, List<Span>> children = new LinkedHashMap<>();
	List<Span> roots = new ArrayList<>();
	for (Span span: spans.values()) {
		if (span.getParentSpanId() == null) {
			roots.add(span);
		} else {
			children.computeIfAbsent(span.getParentSpanId(), id -> new ArrayList<>()).add(span);
		}
	}

	List<String> lines = new ArrayList<>();
	roots.forEach(root -> print(root, children, "", lines));
	return lines;
}

static void print(
		Span span,
		Map<String, List<Span>> children,
		String indent,
		List<String> out) {

	out.add(indent + span.getName() + bytes(span));
	ChangeDescription changes = span.getChangeDescription();                      (1)
	if (changes != null) {
		for (EObject created: changes.getObjectsToAttach()) {
			out.add(indent + "  * created " + label(created));
		}
		changes.getObjectChanges().forEach(entry -> {
			for (FeatureChange change: entry.getValue()) {
				String feature = label(entry.getKey()) + "." + change.getFeatureName();
				out.add(indent + "  * " + feature + " = " + change.getValue());
			}
		});
	}
	children.getOrDefault(span.getSpanId(), List.of()).stream()
		.sorted(Comparator.comparingLong(Span::getStartTimeUnixNano))
		.forEach(child -> print(child, children, indent + "  ", out));
}
1 The change description is a feature of the span. Its object changes are keyed by the changed objects, which resolve through their proxies to the saved model.

For the unit of work above, it prints:

Curate the shelf
  * created Library 'A Modeler's Shelf'
  ResourceSetContributor.configure
    Contribute To Resource Set
    Contribute To Resource Set
    Contribute To Resource Set
    Contribute To Resource Set
  URIHandler.write (2059 bytes)
  Resource.save (2059 bytes)
  Correct the year
    * Book 'Domain-Driven Design'.year = 2004
    URIHandler.write (2059 bytes)
    Resource.save (2059 bytes)

The runtime’s spans, from another instrumentation scope, appear in the tree by their parent ids: the resource set configuration and the saves happened inside "Curate the shelf" and "Correct the year", and the tree says so. Because the trace is a model, the same questions can be asked by a query language instead of a loop, which is on the roadmap (Chapter 26).

13.6. Recording a unit of work

Recording, in the exporters module, packages what this chapter has shown into one object: an OpenTelemetry SDK with the three model exporters, the log record exporter linked to the span exporter, and W3C propagators, recording to a traces, a logs and a metrics resource that are saved when it is closed. Recording.builder().serviceName("import").directory(dir, "yml").build() records to traces.yml, logs.yml and metrics.yml in a directory; makeCurrent() makes its instance the unit of work’s; after close(), getTraces() returns the model. The launcher records every command with it, and tests record with it what they and the servers they start did (Chapter 15).

13.7. Formats and where files go

Telemetry resources use the formats every model uses, selected by extension: yml or json to read, xmi to interchange, ebin and egz for size. The launcher saves the telemetry of every command it runs in a directory per launch:

<home>/telemetry/2026/10/16-14-03-12-345/
  traces.yml
  logs.yml
  metrics.yml

The format is chosen with the system property nsdk.telemetry.format or the environment variable NSDK_TELEMETRY_FORMAT, with the values yml (the default), json, xml, binary and compressed (Chapter 18).

13.8. Every signal is precious

Keeping telemetry forever sounds expensive until you count. A command line run, an agent session or a build step produces hundreds to thousands of spans, which compress to kilobytes. Strategic telemetry is not the firehose; it is the record of work that mattered, and it costs less than the meeting held to reconstruct it.

The discipline that keeps it that way is deciding what is a unit of work worth keeping. A command that changes models, a release, an agent run, a migration: yes. Every request a server handles: no, that is operational telemetry, and it belongs in an operational backend, from the same instrumentation.

Part IV: Files and Serving

Volumes, the runtime’s small file abstraction, and what they make possible: models loaded from anywhere, content written on demand, and anything presented as files over HTTP and WebDAV.

Chapter 14. Volumes and content

Models live in files, and files live in more places than a disk: a zip, a Git repository reached over a REST API, an in-memory sandbox, a remote system with a file-shaped API. The opposite direction is just as useful: a model, a running JVM or an issue tracker presented as files, so that a browser, a mounted drive or an agent with file tools can read it.

The runtime has one small abstraction for both directions, the volume, and one for the bytes of a file, the content. This chapter covers both, and how models are loaded from volumes and saved to them. Chapter 15 serves volumes over HTTP and WebDAV.

14.1. Why not NIO

The JDK has a file system abstraction, java.nio.file, and it is a pleasure to consume. It is expensive to implement. A FileSystemProvider needs a Path class with resolve, relativize, normalize and toUri, channels, attribute views, a provider registry keyed by URI scheme, and care wherever paths of two file systems meet.

The runtime implements file systems often: over models, over Git, over REST APIs, as overlays. So it owns a small interface for implementing them, and uses NIO for consuming: any NIO file system, the default one, a zip or an in-memory one, becomes a volume through one adapter.

This is where prior art converged. Go’s io/fs is almost the same design, Python’s fsspec has string paths and dozens of backends, and Hadoop’s FileSystem, Apache Commons VFS and Eclipse EFS made the same decision in Java. Commons VFS is also the reminder to keep the core small.

14.2. The volume SPI

A volume has five methods:

Method Contract

stat(path)

The entry at a path, or empty when nothing is there

list(directory)

The children of a directory, in a stable order. Blocking, which is fine on virtual threads

content(path)

The content at a path, lazily: no I/O happens until it is opened

caseSensitive()

Declared, because some clients ignore case: Windows Explorer over WebDAV, macOS by default

capability(type)

An optional capability, or empty

Paths follow Go’s rules and are validated once, at the boundary: slash-separated, relative to the root, with no leading or trailing slash and no empty, . or .. segments. The root is .. There is no Path class: a path is a string, and URIs appear only at the edges.

An entry is a record of a path, a kind (FILE, DIRECTORY or LINK), a size, a hash and a modification time. The hash matters most. A content hash, or a Git blob id, gives HTTP ETags and conditional requests, suppression of writes that change nothing, incremental copies and blob caching. A volume that knows its hashes cheaply should report them.

Here is a complete read-only volume: a library presented as Markdown files, with an index, a page per book and a page per author, linked to each other.

Listing 74. A library as files (volume/…​/CatalogVolume.java)
/**
 * A library presented as Markdown files: an index, a page per book and a page per author,
 * linked to each other. A browser, a WebDAV client or an agent with file tools reads it
 * like any folder.
 *
 * <p>
 * A read-only volume is the core of the SPI: stat, list, content, case sensitivity, and no
 * capabilities.
 */
public class CatalogVolume implements Volume {

	private final Map<String, byte[]> files = new TreeMap<>();
	private final Instant modified = Instant.now();

	public CatalogVolume(Library library) {
		files.put("index.md", bytes(index(library)));
		for (Book book: library.getBooks()) {
			files.put("books/" + slug(book.getName()) + ".md", bytes(book(book)));
		}
		for (Author author: library.getAuthors()) {
			files.put("authors/" + slug(author.getName()) + ".md", bytes(author(author)));
		}
	}

	@Override
	public Optional<Entry> stat(String path) {
		if (".".equals(path) || "books".equals(path) || "authors".equals(path)) {
			return Optional.of(new Entry(path, Entry.Kind.DIRECTORY, -1, null, modified));
		}
		byte[] bytes = files.get(path);
		if (bytes == null) {
			return Optional.empty();
		}
		Entry file = new Entry(path, Entry.Kind.FILE, bytes.length, hash(bytes), modified);
		return Optional.of(file);
	}

	@Override
	public List<Entry> list(String directory) throws IOException {
		if (".".equals(directory)) {
			return List.of(
					stat("authors").orElseThrow(),
					stat("books").orElseThrow(),
					stat("index.md").orElseThrow());
		}
		if (!"books".equals(directory) && !"authors".equals(directory)) {
			throw new NoSuchFileException(directory);
		}
		List<Entry> entries = new ArrayList<>();
		for (String path: files.keySet()) {
			if (path.startsWith(directory + "/")) {
				entries.add(stat(path).orElseThrow());
			}
		}
		return entries;
	}

	@Override
	public Content content(String path) {
		byte[] bytes = files.get(path);
		if (bytes == null) {
			return () -> {
				throw new NoSuchFileException(path); // Lazy: opening fails, asking does not
			};
		}
		return Content.of(bytes);
	}

	@Override
	public boolean caseSensitive() {
		return true;
	}

	@Override
	public <T> Optional<T> capability(Class<T> type) {
		return Optional.empty(); // Not writable, not watchable, not searchable
	}

Reading it is reading files:

Listing 75. Reading a volume
Volume catalog = new CatalogVolume(Samples.library());
assertThat(catalog.list("."))
	.extracting(Volume.Entry::path)
	.containsExactly("authors", "books", "index.md");
assertThat(catalog.stat("books/domain-driven-design.md")).hasValueSatisfying(entry -> {
	assertThat(entry.kind()).isEqualTo(Volume.Entry.Kind.FILE);
	assertThat(entry.hash()).isNotNull();                                (1)
});
try (InputStream in = catalog.content("books/design-patterns.md").openStream()) {
	assertThat(new String(in.readAllBytes(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8))
		.contains("* Cited by: [Domain-Driven Design](domain-driven-design.md)");
}
1 The hash is known without reading the file. The HTTP handler turns it into an ETag.

Book pages link to their authors and to the books that cite them. A Markdown viewer renders the catalog as a small site, and an agent with file tools navigates the model by following links without knowing that EMF exists. That is the point of presenting a model as files: every tool that understands files understands the model, at the level of detail the presentation chooses.

14.3. Capabilities

Everything beyond reading is optional, and discovered by asking for it:

Capability Adds Status

Writable

write(path, content), delete, move (atomic where the backend supports it) and createDirectory

AVAILABLE

Watchable

changes(), a Flow.Publisher of change batches: how a backend reports changes underneath it

SKETCH

Transactional

begin(), then commit(message) or rollback()

SKETCH

Searchable

glob(pattern) and grep(regex, glob), pushed down to a backend that can do better than a walk

SKETCH

Linked

readLink(path): in a model presented as files, non-containment references are links

SKETCH

The interfaces of all five are in the runtime. "Available" means that a volume in the runtime implements the capability; the others are declared so that the volumes to come, and the code that will use them, agree on the shape.

A read-only volume implements the core and answers empty to every capability. A volume over a Git repository will implement the core, Writable, Transactional and Watchable, and nothing forces it to implement the rest.

14.4. Volumes over directories

Volume.of(path) is a writable volume over a directory of any NIO file system: the default one, a zip file system, an in-memory one. It validates paths so that they cannot escape the root, and probes the file system for case sensitivity instead of guessing it from the operating system. It keeps file system semantics: writing into a missing directory fails, and so does deleting a non-empty one.

GenericVolume<C> is the same SPI with the type of content as a parameter, and Volume is the flavor whose content is bytes. adapt turns a volume of one content type into a volume of another, which is how the TypeScript generator of the runtime writes text without converting it to bytes itself:

Listing 76. A text volume over a directory
GenericVolume<String> text = Volume.of(directory).adapt(
		content -> {                                                     (1)
			try (InputStream in = content.openStream()) {
				return new String(in.readAllBytes(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
			} catch (IOException e) {
				throw new UncheckedIOException(e);
			}
		},
		string -> Content.of(string, StandardCharsets.UTF_8));           (2)

@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
GenericVolume.Writable<String> writable = text.capability(GenericVolume.Writable.class)
		.orElseThrow();
writable.write("hello.md", "# Hello");
assertThat(text.content("hello.md")).isEqualTo("# Hello");
assertThat(directory.resolve("hello.md")).hasContent("# Hello");
1 Reading maps bytes to text. The mapping runs when content is asked for, so a text volume reads eagerly.
2 Writing maps text to bytes, encoded when the target volume reads the content.

14.5. Content

A file’s state is a Content: a re-readable source of bytes, in the spirit of Guava’s ByteSource and of the JDK HTTP client’s BodyPublishers.ofInputStream(Supplier). An InputStream is one-shot and has unclear ownership. A content can be read more than once, for a hash, then for a write, then by each subscriber, and owns nothing until it is opened.

  • Getting content does no I/O. Opening it does.

  • Assigning content does not move bytes. Bytes move when a consumer reads the content: a commit, an HTTP response, a hash. An I/O failure surfaces when the bytes move, not at assignment.

  • Consumers push when they can. They call writeTo(out) for a response, a file, a digest or an upload; openStream() only when an input stream is required; and publisher() for the JDK HTTP client’s BodyPublishers.fromPublisher.

Factory Content

Content.of(bytes)

In memory, with a known length

Content.of(text, charset)

Text, encoded when read

Content.of(supplier)

From a stream supplier, called on every open

Content.of(uri)

At a URI, requested on every open: HTTP and HTTPS through the JDK HTTP client, file through NIO, other schemes through URL. A 404 is a NoSuchFileException

Content.once(stream)

A stream someone handed over. Not repeatable

Content.ofWriter(writer)

Produced by a closure that writes to an output stream, when the content is read

A content may also know its length and its hash without reading, and says whether it is repeatable. A consumer that needs to read a one-shot content twice buffers it first.

Content produced by a writer

Much content in the runtime is produced by code that writes to an output stream: saving a resource, generating a page, encoding text. Content.ofWriter turns such a closure into content without running it:

  • writeTo(out) runs the writer on the consumer’s stream, with no pipe and no thread. This is the arrangement of JAX-RS’s StreamingOutput.

  • openStream() returns a lazy pipe. The writer starts on a virtual thread at the first read and writes bounded chunks into a queue that the reader drains. A failure of the writer is rethrown to the reader, and a reader that closes early cancels the writer.

  • Each read runs the writer again, so the content is repeatable as long as the writer is.

The pipe is deliberately not PipedInputStream, which detects a dead writer or reader from thread liveness and has a 1 KB buffer.

Copying a model to another volume takes three lines, and the model is serialized straight into the target’s stream:

Listing 77. A model as content (volume/…​/Shelves.java)
/**
 * Copies a model as content produced by a writer: nothing is serialized until the target
 * volume reads the content, and it is serialized straight into the target's stream.
 */
public static void copy(Resource resource, Volume target, String path) throws IOException {
	Content content = Content.ofWriter(out -> resource.save(out, null));      (1)
	Volume.Writable writable = target.capability(Volume.Writable.class)       (2)
			.orElseThrow(() -> new IOException("Read-only volume"));
	writable.write(path, content);                                             (3)
}
1 Nothing is serialized here. The content is a promise to save the resource when it is read.
2 Writing is a capability: a read-only volume refuses it by not having it.
3 The volume reads the content, which runs the save on the volume’s own stream.

14.6. Models in volumes

A path is where the bytes of a model are; a URI is what the model is. VolumeURIHandler bridges the two for EMF: URIs below a base URI are paths in a volume, so a resource set loads and saves resources through the volume.

Listing 78. A resource set over a volume (volume/…​/Shelves.java)
public static final URI BASE = URI.createURI("library://shelves/");

/**
 * A resource set whose library:// URIs are paths in the volume.
 */
public static ResourceSet resourceSet(Volume volume) {
	ResourceSet resourceSet = NasdanikaResourceSet.createAndConfigure();
	URIConverter converter = resourceSet.getURIConverter();
	converter.getURIHandlers().add(0, new VolumeURIHandler(volume, BASE));    (1)
	TelemetryURIHandler.wrapAll(converter, () -> Telemetry.of(resourceSet)); (2)
	return resourceSet;
}

public static void save(Library library, Volume volume, String path) throws IOException {
	URI uri = BASE.appendSegments(path.split("/"));                           (3)
	Resource resource = resourceSet(volume).createResource(uri);
	resource.getContents().add(library);
	resource.save(null);                                                      (4)
}

public static Library load(Volume volume, String path) {
	URI uri = BASE.appendSegments(path.split("/"));
	Resource resource = resourceSet(volume).getResource(uri, true);
	return (Library) resource.getContents().getFirst();
}
1 URIs below library://shelves/ are paths in the volume. The handler goes first, before EMF’s default handlers.
2 A configured resource set has every handler instrumented, but this one was added later, so it is wrapped too. Reads and writes become URIHandler.read and URIHandler.write spans.
3 library://shelves/2026/shelf.library is the path 2026/shelf.library. Segments are decoded, and a query and a fragment are ignored, so the URI of an object maps to the path of its resource.
4 The bytes are buffered and written as one content when the stream is closed, so a failed save writes nothing. Missing parent directories are created first.
Listing 79. Saving and loading through a volume
Volume volume = Volume.of(directory);                                    (1)
Shelves.save(Samples.library(), volume, "2026/shelf.library");           (2)
assertThat(directory.resolve("2026").resolve("shelf.library")).exists(); (3)
Library loaded = Shelves.load(volume, "2026/shelf.library");
assertThat(loaded.getBooks()).hasSize(8);
1 A writable volume over a temporary directory.
2 The resource’s URI is library://shelves/2026/shelf.library, whatever the directory is.
3 The handler created the missing directory 2026 before writing.

The model never mentions where it is stored. Moving models from a working tree to an in-memory volume, a Git overlay or a volume over a remote system changes one handler, not the models and not the references between them.

The handler answers EMF’s attribute queries from stat: the time stamp, the length, whether a path is a directory, whether it is read-only (no Writable capability), and the hash.

14.7. Telemetry of transfers

Moving bytes is work, and it is reported to the unit of work’s OpenTelemetry instance:

Span When

Content.writeTo

Content pushed to a stream, with the byte count, unless the content is in memory

Content.pipe

Content produced by a writer and read as a stream: from the first read to the end of the writer. The writer runs in it, so the spans the writer starts are its children

GET (client)

Content at an HTTP URI, from the request to the close of the body, with the HTTP semantic convention attributes and the trace context in the request headers

Content.read

Content at another URI, from opening to closing

URIHandler.read, URIHandler.write

A stream opened through an instrumented URI handler, from opening to closing

All of them emit progress log records at most once a second while bytes move, so a long download shows in a live tree (Chapter 12) while it happens. Crossing to the writer’s virtual thread carries the OpenTelemetry instance and the parent span along, as the rules of Chapter 11 require. The URL recorded on a client span has no user info and no query string, which may carry credentials.

14.8. What comes next

The volume is the bottom layer of a larger design SKETCH:

  • The file model. Files and directories as an Xcore model over volumes: File, Directory, TextFile and types specialized by content type, with operations such as view, replace and insert that are also an agent’s file tools. Views decode content on get and encode it lazily on set, so two views of one file cannot diverge. The model and its generated code are in the runtime, in models/file; its behavior is being attached.

  • More volumes. An in-memory volume for tests and sandboxes. An overlay that keeps writes in memory over a read-only base until commit. A Git volume whose commit is a Git commit, locally or over the GitHub and GitLab APIs without a clone. A model volume that presents a resource set as folders, files and links.

  • A reactive file system. Processors, deterministic or agentic, react to file changes and change files in turn until nothing changes, and then one commit records the run. The hash in every entry is what lets such loops converge.

Chapter 26 places these in the roadmap.

Chapter 15. Serving over HTTP and WebDAV

Anything presented as a volume can be served: to a browser over HTTP, and to anything that mounts drives over WebDAV. A model becomes a folder in Finder or Explorer, a preview of a generated site is one URL away, and an agent reads a running system with the file tools it already has.

The runtime serves volumes with the HTTP server the JDK has shipped for years, com.sun.net.httpserver in the module jdk.httpserver. With virtual threads it is enough for local tools, previews and agents, with no servlet container and no framework.

15.1. Serving a volume

VolumeHttpHandler serves a volume read-only, in the manner of the JDK’s SimpleFileServer:

  • Files are sent with a media type from their extension, a Last-Modified header from the entry, and an ETag from the entry’s hash. A conditional request whose If-None-Match matches gets a 304.

  • Directories are generated HTML listings. A directory requested without a trailing slash is redirected to it, so relative links in pages and listings resolve.

  • The request path below the context path is the volume path. Paths with empty, . or .. segments are refused.

  • GET and HEAD are served; other methods get a 405.

WebDavHandler extends it into a read-only WebDAV (RFC 4918) class 1 share:

  • OPTIONS answers DAV: 1 and the allowed methods.

  • PROPFIND answers a 207 Multi-Status with the resource type, display name, content length, content type, ETag and modification time, as far as the volume knows them. Depth: infinity is answered as 1, so that a client cannot make the server walk a large volume.

  • GET and HEAD work as in VolumeHttpHandler, listings included, so the share also browses in a web browser.

  • Methods that write or lock get a 405. Writing belongs behind the volume’s Writable capability, and is not implemented yet.

That is enough to mount a share in macOS Finder ("Connect to Server"), on Windows (net use), on Linux (davfs2) or with rclone, and to read it with any tool. Clients need the content length of files to read them reliably, so a volume served over WebDAV should know its file sizes.

Serving the catalog of Chapter 14 both ways takes a few lines:

Listing 80. Serving a volume (volume/…​/Serve.java)
public static HttpServer serve(Library library, OpenTelemetry openTelemetry, int port)
		throws IOException {
	Volume catalog = new CatalogVolume(library);
	var address = new InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), port);
	HttpServer server = HttpServer.create(address, 0);
	server.setExecutor(Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor());              (1)

	HttpHandler files = new VolumeHttpHandler(catalog);
	server.createContext("/catalog", new TelemetryHandler(files, openTelemetry)); (2)

	HttpHandler share = new WebDavHandler(catalog);
	server.createContext("/dav", new TelemetryHandler(share, openTelemetry));     (3)

	server.start();
	return server;
}
1 A virtual thread per request. Handlers block, and blocking is cheap.
2 Browsers read the catalog at /catalog/. Each request is a unit of work with a server span.
3 WebDAV clients mount the same volume at /dav/.

The server binds to the loopback address. The handlers do not authenticate, so serving beyond the local machine needs what the JDK server provides for it, an HttpsServer and an Authenticator on the context, or a proxy in front.

Running Serve prints the two URLs. Opening the first in a browser shows the listing of the catalog’s root; following index.md shows the Markdown of the library.

15.2. Reading over HTTP

On the client side, content at a URL is a Content like any other:

Listing 81. Content at a URL
Content index = Content.of(URI.create(root + "/catalog/index.md")); (1)
try (InputStream in = index.openStream()) {
	String markdown = new String(in.readAllBytes(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
	assertThat(markdown).startsWith("# A Modeler's Shelf");
}
1 Nothing is requested until the content is opened, and every open requests it again.

A WebDAV listing is a PROPFIND request, which the JDK HTTP client sends like any other method:

Listing 82. Listing a directory over WebDAV
HttpResponse<String> listing = HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(
		HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(root + "/dav/books/"))
			.method("PROPFIND", HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.noBody())
			.header("Depth", "1")
			.build(),
		HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
assertThat(listing.statusCode()).isEqualTo(207); // Multi-Status
assertThat(listing.body()).contains("domain-driven-design.md");

15.3. One trace across client and server

TelemetryHandler wraps a handler, or is added as a filter of a context, and makes each request a unit of work:

  • The trace context is extracted from the request headers with the propagators of the OpenTelemetry instance, so the client’s span is the parent of the server’s.

  • The server span is named <method> <route>, the route being the context path, and carries the HTTP semantic convention attributes: method, route, path, scheme, server and client address, protocol version, user agent, response status and response body size.

  • The instance and the span are current while the wrapped handler runs, so whatever it does, content transfers, resource loads, its own log records, reports to the request.

  • A failure of the handler is recorded on the span. If no response was sent yet, the client gets a 500; if one was, the connection is dropped instead of completing a response that would look successful.

  • A failure or a 5xx sets the error status. A 4xx is the client’s error, not the server’s, and leaves the status unset.

On the client side, Content.of(uri) starts a client span and propagates its context in the request headers. Together they make one trace:

Listing 83. A trace that crosses HTTP
InMemorySpanExporter exporter = InMemorySpanExporter.create();
var tracerProvider = SdkTracerProvider.builder()
		.addSpanProcessor(SimpleSpanProcessor.create(exporter))
		.build();
try (OpenTelemetrySdk sdk = OpenTelemetrySdk.builder()
		.setPropagators(Telemetry.w3cPropagators())                      (1)
		.setTracerProvider(tracerProvider)
		.build()) {
	HttpServer server = Serve.serve(Samples.library(), sdk, 0);          (2)
	String index = "http://127.0.0.1:" + server.getAddress().getPort() + "/catalog/index.md";
	try (Scope scope = Telemetry.makeCurrent(sdk);                       (3)
			InputStream in = Content.of(URI.create(index)).openStream()) {
		in.readAllBytes();
	} finally {
		server.stop(0);
	}
	SpanData client = await(exporter, SpanKind.CLIENT);
	SpanData handled = await(exporter, SpanKind.SERVER);
	assertThat(handled.getTraceId()).isEqualTo(client.getTraceId());     (4)
	assertThat(handled.getParentSpanId()).isEqualTo(client.getSpanId());
	assertThat(handled.getName()).isEqualTo("GET /catalog");
}
1 W3C trace context propagation, on both sides: the client injects, the server extracts.
2 The server’s instance. In a real deployment it is another process with its own instance; here both share one, so the test can see both spans.
3 The client’s unit of work. Opening the content is a GET client span.
4 The server span is a child of the client span, in the same trace.

This is the cross-process rule of Chapter 11 at work: the unit of work spans two processes, each with its own instance, and the trace connects them. When both sides save their telemetry as models (Chapter 13), the two halves of the trace are two files that reference the same trace id, and a query can join them.

15.4. A server for the length of a test

In a test the two sides are one process, and the setup above, a server, an executor, a filter on every context, a client that propagates, is the same every time. The harness module packages it in one method, shaped like Telemetry.inSpan:

  • Harness.inServer(name, routes, body) starts a JDK HTTP server on the loopback address and a free port, on virtual threads; lets routes create its contexts, each instrumented with TelemetryHandler as it is created; runs body in a span named name; and stops the server when the body returns or throws.

  • The body gets a Server: its base URI, a get and a send whose requests are client spans that propagate the trace, and the propagation headers for clients the harness does not own, such as a browser.

  • With a Recording (Chapter 13), the body’s span, its client spans, the server’s spans and whatever the handlers logged are one trace, saved as one model.

The runtime’s own tests serve generated applications this way, and the playwright module drives a browser against a harness server in the same trace (Chapter 23). The Zephyr Book Harness covers the module in depth.

15.5. What comes next

Serving is the first of several surfaces over volumes, and the others are planned PLANNED:

  • Writable WebDAV, behind the Writable capability, so that editing a mounted model is editing the model.

  • VS Code, through its FileSystemProvider API, which consumes the change batches of a Watchable volume directly.

  • FUSE, for a native mount on Linux and macOS.

  • The polymorphic UI in React: a browser application that renders any model, and live telemetry, from the same server (Chapter 26).

Part V: The Command Line

Commands contributed by modules, found as capabilities and wired to their parents by generic type, and the launcher that runs them as units of work with their telemetry saved as models.

Chapter 16. Commands as capabilities

The command line is the runtime’s first user interface, for people, for build steps and for agents. An agent that can run a command and read a file can use everything the command line offers, with no protocol to implement.

Three decisions shape it:

  • Commands are contributed. A module that adds a command declares a factory in its module descriptor. Nothing lists all the commands: the command tree is whatever the module path contributes.

  • The tree is resolved. Commands find their parents and their sub-commands by capability resolution (Chapter 10), matched by the generic types they declare (Chapter 17).

  • A command execution is a unit of work. Every command runs in a span, and the launcher saves the telemetry of each launch as models (Chapter 18).

16.1. Picocli

The commands are picocli commands: annotated classes with options, parameters, mix-ins, generated help and completion. Picocli is mature, small and dependency-free, and a picocli command is a plain object that the runtime can create, inspect and wire. Created by Remko Popma, it expresses the domain of command lines in Java’s own constructs, annotations on typed fields, so well that a Java developer reads a command without learning anything new; the runtime adds to it what a contributed command line needs, assembly through capabilities and wiring by generic types. The Zephyr Book Declarative Command Lines covers the cli module in depth.

The runtime bundles picocli in its own module, org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.picocli, until a picocli release includes the changes the runtime contributed. Commands import picocli.CommandLine as usual.

16.2. A first command

Listing 84. A command (cli/…​/HelloCommand.java)
@Command(
		name = "hello",
		description = "Says hello",
		mixinStandardHelpOptions = true)
public class HelloCommand extends CommandBase {                         (1)

	@Parent
	private RootCommand root;                                           (2)

	@Option(names = "--name", defaultValue = "World", description = "Whom to greet")
	private String name;

	@Override
	protected Integer execute(Span span, Logger logger, Meter meter) { (3)
		span.setAttribute("greeting.name", name);
		Telemetry.log(logger, Severity.INFO, null, "Greeting " + name, null);
		spec.commandLine().getOut().println("Hello, " + name + "!");
		return 0;
	}

}
1 CommandBase runs the command in a span named after it, with the command’s qualified name, class, module and module version as attributes.
2 The command goes under the root command. How a declaration decides the parent is the subject of Chapter 17.
3 The execution gets the span and the logger and meter of the unit of work. Whatever the command does reports to them.

A command is contributed by a factory:

Listing 85. Its factory (cli/…​/HelloCommandFactory.java)
/**
 * Contributes the hello command. The factory is asked once per candidate parent; it creates the
 * command where the declarations of the command and the parent match.
 */
public class HelloCommandFactory extends SubCommandCapabilityFactory<HelloCommand> {

	@Override
	protected Class<HelloCommand> getCommandType() {
		return HelloCommand.class;                                          (1)
	}

	@Override
	protected Flow.Publisher<HelloCommand> doCreateCommand(
			List<CommandLine> parentPath,
			Loader loader,
			Span span,
			Logger logger,
			Meter meter) {
		return Flows.of(new HelloCommand());                                (2)
	}

}
1 The command’s class. The base factory matches it against each candidate parent before creating anything.
2 A new command for each parent it matches. A factory can also create several commands, or none, depending on the parent path and on what the loader resolves.

The module declares the factory, and opens the command package:

Listing 86. The module of the example commands (cli/…​/module-info.java)
import org.example.cli.BooksCommandFactory;
import org.example.cli.CsvExporterFactory;
import org.example.cli.ExportCommandFactory;
import org.example.cli.HelloCommandFactory;
import org.example.cli.LibraryCommandFactory;
import org.example.cli.LimitMixInFactory;
import org.example.cli.MarkdownExporterFactory;
import org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.common.capability.CapabilityFactory;

module org.example.cli {

	requires transitive org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.cli;
	requires transitive org.example.library;

	exports org.example.cli;

	opens org.example.cli; (1)

	provides CapabilityFactory with (2)
		HelloCommandFactory,
		LibraryCommandFactory,
		BooksCommandFactory,
		ExportCommandFactory,
		MarkdownExporterFactory,
		CsvExporterFactory,
		LimitMixInFactory;

}
1 Picocli sets option fields reflectively, and the wiring injects parents and sub-commands, so the package is open.
2 Each factory is a capability factory, found by the service loader in the module layer.

16.3. How the tree is built

The command tree is built by resolving one requirement: a CommandLine with a SubCommandRequirement payload whose parent path is empty. The runtime’s RootCommandFactory answers it with the root command, nsdk.

Every factory that creates a command then asks for the command’s own sub-commands, with the command appended to the parent path, and for its mix-ins. The tree grows within the same resolution until no factory matches a new parent path. A factory emits its command line only when the command’s sub-commands and mix-ins are attached, so a command line always arrives with its subtree, and a blocking load returns the whole tree. Two limits stop a runaway contribution: a parent path of at most 15 commands and at most 2,000 commands in a tree, set with the system properties org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.cli.maxCommandPath and org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.cli.maxCommands.

Listing 87. Assembling the command line (cli/…​/Assembly.java)
/**
 * The root command line with every command and mix-in contributed on the module path.
 */
public static CommandLine root(CapabilityLoader loader) {
	Requirement requirement = Requirement.of(
			CommandLine.class,
			new SubCommandRequirement(List.of(), new AtomicInteger())); (1)
	List<CommandLine> roots = loader.loadAll(requirement);              (2)
	return roots.getFirst();
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
	System.exit(root(CapabilityLoader.getInstance()).execute(args));
}
1 The requirement for root commands: an empty parent path and a counter shared by the whole tree.
2 A blocking load, pumping the resolution on the calling thread until it completes. The root it returns carries the whole tree.

With the example module on the module path, the tree is:

nsdk
  launcher
  hello
  library
    books
    export
      csv
      markdown
    save

launcher is the root command’s own sub-command, declared statically and therefore first (Chapter 18), and save is the runtime’s, which found its way under library by itself (Chapter 17). Running a command is picocli’s execute:

Listing 88. Running a command
Run run = run("hello", "--name", "Reader");
assertThat(run.exitCode()).isZero();
assertThat(run.out()).isEqualTo("Hello, Reader!\n");

The test prints the tree by walking the command lines:

static void tree(CommandLine commandLine, String indent, List<String> lines) {
	lines.add(indent + commandLine.getCommandName());
	commandLine.getSubcommands().values().stream()
		.filter(sub -> !sub.getCommandSpec().usageMessage().hidden())
		.forEach(sub -> tree(sub, indent + "  ", lines));
}

16.4. Groups

A group is a command that does nothing itself. It organizes sub-commands under a name and gives them something to work on, from its options.

Listing 89. A group (cli/…​/LibraryCommand.java)
/**
 * A group: it does nothing itself, and gives its sub-commands a library to work on. What
 * it gives is declared by the generic return types of its adapters.
 */
@Command(
		name = "library",
		description = "Works with a library of books",
		mixinStandardHelpOptions = true)
public class LibraryCommand extends CommandGroup {

	@Parent
	private RootCommand root;

	@Option(names = "--file", description = "Library file, the sample library if not set")
	private File file;                                                          (1)

	@Adapter
	public ExecutionSupplier<Library> library() {                             (2)
		return (span, logger, meter) -> load(span);
	}

	@Adapter
	public ExecutionSupplier<List<EObject>> contents() {                      (3)
		return (span, logger, meter) -> List.of(load(span));
	}

	private Library load(Span span) {
		if (file == null) {
			span.setAttribute("library.source", "sample");
			return Samples.library();
		}
		span.setAttribute("library.source", file.getPath());
		URI uri = URI.createFileURI(file.getAbsolutePath());
		ResourceSet resourceSet = NasdanikaResourceSet.createAndConfigure();
		return (Library) resourceSet.getResource(uri, true).getContents().getFirst(); (4)
	}

}
1 The group’s option, parsed before any of its sub-commands run.
2 What the group gives: a library, produced when a sub-command asks for it. The generic return type is the declaration that commands match.
3 The same library as a list of objects, for commands that work on any model.
4 Loading through a configured resource set, so the file can be in any format the runtime reads.

CommandGroup fails with "Missing required subcommand" when it is run alone, which picocli reports with the usage help. nsdk library --file shelf.yml books parses --file for the group and runs books, which asks the group for its library.

16.5. Mix-ins

A picocli mix-in contributes options to a command. In the runtime, mix-ins are contributed like commands, by factories, and a command asks for them by type:

Listing 90. A mix-in (cli/…​/LimitMixIn.java)
/**
 * An option contributed to commands that ask for it with @MixIns, or that a mix-in declares it
 * wants with a @Parent member.
 */
public class LimitMixIn {

	@Option(names = "--limit", description = "At most this many items")
	private Integer limit;

	public <T> List<T> apply(List<T> items) {
		return limit == null || items.size() <= limit ? items : items.subList(0, limit);
	}

}
Listing 91. Its factory (cli/…​/LimitMixInFactory.java)
public class LimitMixInFactory extends MixInCapabilityFactory<LimitMixIn> {

	@Override
	protected String getName() {
		return "limit";
	}

	@Override
	protected Class<LimitMixIn> getMixInType() {
		return LimitMixIn.class;
	}

	@Override
	protected Flow.Publisher<LimitMixIn> doCreateMixIn(
			List<CommandLine> commandPath,
			Loader loader,
			Span span,
			Logger logger,
			Meter meter) {
		return Flows.of(new LimitMixIn());
	}

}

A mix-in is added to a command when the mix-in takes the command through a @Parent member, when the command accepts it through a @MixIns field or method, by generic type, as @SubCommand accepts sub-commands, or when the command’s class is annotated with @MixIns listing a type of the mix-in. The books command of Chapter 17 asks for LimitMixIn and finds it among its mix-ins at execution, so nsdk library books --limit 2 prints two books.

The runtime’s mix-ins add common options without a factory, as picocli @Mixin fields:

Mix-in Options

ResourceSetMixIn

--extension-resource-factory, --protocol-resource-factory and --content-type-resource-factory, which map an extension, a protocol or a content type to a resource factory class, and createResourceSet()

PropertiesMixIn

-p for one property and -P for a properties resource, in YAML, JSON or properties format, loaded in order

16.6. Overriding

Several modules may contribute a command with the same name under the same parent. The runtime keeps one when it can tell which one overrides the others:

  • A command whose class is annotated with @Overrides overrides commands of the listed types.

  • A command implementing Overrider decides, for each other command, whether it overrides it.

  • A command whose class is a subclass of another command’s class overrides it.

Commands that do not override each other are all kept, and picocli reports the duplicate name. The same rules apply to mix-ins with the same name.

16.7. Commands in the runtime

Command What it does

nsdk

The root command, with version information from the module descriptors

launcher

Generates a Java command line, or an options file, from directories of modules and jars (Chapter 18)

save

Saves its parent’s model contents to a file, in any format the runtime writes (Chapter 17)

ecore

A group that narrows its parent’s objects to Ecore model elements

shell

Added by the launcher: an interactive shell over the root command, with exit

16.8. Commands and telemetry

Each executed command is a span named after the command, a child of the launcher’s root span. Spans the command starts, resource loads and saves, capability resolution, content transfers, are its children, and log records it emits are in it.

A parent’s work done for a child, loading the library in the example, runs in the child’s span when the child asks for it through an ExecutionSupplier, so the cost is attributed to the command that needed it (Chapter 17). The launcher saves all of it as models in a directory per launch (Chapter 18), which makes every command run an inspectable record.

Chapter 17. Wiring commands with generic types

Commands contributed by different modules have to find each other. The runtime’s save command should work under any command that has model contents to save; a books command should work under anything that supplies a library; an export command should run whatever exporters other modules contribute. None of these modules knows the others.

The runtime wires commands by declarations: a command declares, with generic types, what it needs from its parent and what it accepts as sub-commands, and a parent declares what it offers. Matching the declarations decides where commands go. Injecting adapted values just before execution connects them.

17.1. What a command needs from its parent

A @Parent member, a field or a method taking one parameter, declares what a command needs from its parent:

Listing 92. A command that needs a library (cli/…​/BooksCommand.java)
@Command(
		name = "books",
		description = "Lists books",
		mixinStandardHelpOptions = true)
@MixIns(LimitMixIn.class)                                                        (1)
public class BooksCommand extends CommandBase {

	@Parent
	private ExecutionSupplier<? extends Library> library;                        (2)

	@Option(names = "--before", description = "Only books published before this year")
	private Integer before;

	@Override
	protected Integer execute(Span span, Logger logger, Meter meter) throws Exception {
		Library theLibrary = library.get(span, logger, meter);                    (3)
		List<Book> books = before == null
				? theLibrary.getBooks()
				: theLibrary.publishedBefore(before);
		for (Book book: limit(books)) {
			spec.commandLine().getOut().println(book.getName() + " (" + book.getYear() + ")");
		}
		span.setAttribute("library.books", (long) books.size());
		return 0;
	}

	private <T> List<T> limit(List<T> items) {
		for (CommandSpec mixIn: spec.mixins().values()) {                          (4)
			if (mixIn.userObject() instanceof LimitMixIn limit) {
				return limit.apply(items);
			}
		}
		return items;
	}

}
1 The command asks for the LimitMixIn of Chapter 16.
2 What the command needs from its parent: something that produces a library while the command executes. ? extends widens what answers: a parent producing a subclass of Library matches too.
3 The library is produced now, inside this command’s span, with its logger and meter. If the command does not run, the library is never loaded.
4 The mix-in, found among the command’s mix-ins.

The parent declares what it offers with @Adapter methods, whose generic return types are the declarations matched. The library group of Chapter 16 offers ExecutionSupplier<Library> and ExecutionSupplier<List<EObject>>, and ExecutionSupplier<Library> is assignable to ExecutionSupplier<? extends Library>, so books goes under library.

A parent member is used twice:

  • Matching, before the command exists. A factory creates the command under a parent whose class is adaptable to the type of any of the command’s parent members (Chapter 8). Declarations decide, because the parent’s options are not parsed while the tree is built.

  • Injection, after parsing and before execution. The parent is adapted to the member types, most specific first, and the first value obtained is injected. A command has one parent, so several parent members are alternative ways to take it, and one is injected. A command whose parent provides none of them fails to execute, with a message naming what it needed.

17.2. ExecutionSupplier

What a parent hands a child is often not cheap: a model to load, a service to call, a repository to clone. ExecutionSupplier<T> is the shape for such values: a function from the executing command’s span, logger and meter to a value.

@FunctionalInterface
public interface ExecutionSupplier<T> {

	T get(Span span, Logger logger, Meter meter) throws Exception;

}

The work happens only if the command runs, and it happens inside the command’s span, so its cost, its log records and its failures are attributed to the command that needed it. A cheap value is better asked for directly: adapting the parent is then all it takes.

17.3. The runtime’s save command

The save command is in the runtime’s cli module. It has never heard of libraries:

@Parent
private ExecutionSupplier<? extends Collection<? extends EObject>> contentsSupplier;

@Parent
private EObjectSupplier<? extends EObject> eObjectSupplier;

ExecutionSupplier<List<EObject>>, the second adapter of the library group, is assignable to the first member’s type, so save goes under library and saves the library:

Listing 93. The runtime’s command under the example’s group
Path file = directory.resolve("shelf.xmi");
assertThat(run("library", "save", file.toString()).exitCode()).isZero();
assertThat(Files.readString(file)).contains("Domain-Driven Design");

// And the saved file is a library a later command can load
assertThat(run("library", "--file", file.toString(), "books", "--before", "1900").out())
	.contains("War and Peace (1869)");

The second member is the older shape, a parent implementing EObjectSupplier. Both work, and only one is injected.

17.4. What a command accepts as sub-commands

A @SubCommand member declares what a command accepts as sub-commands. A member typed as an array, a List, a Collection, an Iterable or a Set takes many sub-commands, and its element type is what is accepted; any other member takes one.

Listing 94. A command that runs what it is given (cli/…​/ExportCommand.java)
@Command(
		name = "export",
		description = "Exports the library. Without a format, lists the formats",
		mixinStandardHelpOptions = true)
public class ExportCommand extends CommandBase {

	@Parent
	private ExecutionSupplier<? extends Library> library;                    (1)

	@SubCommand
	private List<Exporter> exporters;                                       (2)

	/**
	 * For the exporters, which take this command as their parent. Not an adapter: an
	 * adapter would offer the library to every command that needs one, and they would
	 * all appear under export.
	 */
	public ExecutionSupplier<? extends Library> library() {                 (3)
		return library;
	}

	@Override
	protected Integer execute(Span span, Logger logger, Meter meter) {
		PrintWriter out = spec.commandLine().getOut();
		exporters.stream().map(Exporter::format).sorted().forEach(out::println);
		return 0;
	}

}
1 The export command needs a library from its parent, like books.
2 It accepts every sub-command adaptable to Exporter. Without a sub-command on the command line, it lists their formats.
3 It hands its library down to its exporters with a plain method, deliberately not an adapter.

Sub-command members are also used twice. A sub-command is created under a command whose sub-command members accept its class. After parsing, every member gets the sub-commands adaptable to what it accepts: all of them for a many-valued member, possibly none, and the first for a single-valued one. Sub-commands that are not on the command line have not had their options parsed, so a command uses them for what they are, not for their options.

An exporter takes its parent by class:

Listing 95. An exporter (cli/…​/MarkdownExporter.java)
@Command(
		name = "markdown",
		description = "Exports the library as Markdown",
		mixinStandardHelpOptions = true)
public class MarkdownExporter extends CommandBase implements Exporter {

	@Parent
	private ExportCommand parent; // A parent typed by its class

	@Override
	public String format() {
		return "markdown";
	}

	@Override
	public String export(Library library) {
		StringBuilder markdown = new StringBuilder("# ").append(library.getName());
		markdown.append("\n\n");
		for (Book book: library.getBooks()) {
			markdown.append("* _").append(book.getName()).append("_ (")
				.append(book.getYear()).append(")\n");
		}
		return markdown.toString();
	}

	@Override
	protected Integer execute(Span span, Logger logger, Meter meter) throws Exception {
		Library library = parent.library().get(span, logger, meter);
		spec.commandLine().getOut().print(export(library));
		return 0;
	}

}

nsdk library export prints csv and markdown, and nsdk library export markdown prints the library as Markdown. A module that contributes a JsonExporter adds a format without touching the export command.

17.5. Why export hides its library

Had ExportCommand.library() been an @Adapter, every command that needs a library, books included, would have appeared under export as well as under library. Adapters are offers to every command that might match. A plain method is an offer only to commands that take the export command by class, which is what the exporters do.

The test of the example asserts it: books is under library, and not under export.

Offer with @Adapter what any child may use. Hand down with plain methods what only children written for this parent should use.

17.6. When wiring happens

WiringExecutionStrategy injects @Parent and @SubCommand members of the commands on the command line, and the @Parent members of their mix-ins, and then executes as its delegate does, picocli’s RunLast by default.

  • After parsing. A parent’s options are parsed by then. Adapting the parent while the tree is being built would see their defaults.

  • From the root to the executed command. A parent’s own members are in place before it is adapted for its child, so a value can flow down several levels.

  • Not for help. Help and version requests skip wiring, so asking for help never fails on a parent that cannot provide.

SubCommandCapabilityFactory sets the strategy on the root commands it creates. A command line assembled otherwise needs commandLine.setExecutionStrategy(new WiringExecutionStrategy()).

17.7. Rules

  • Members are found once per class, on the class and its superclasses, and must be accessible to the cli module: in a package opened to it, as picocli needs command packages to be anyway. An inaccessible member fails with a message that says which package to open.

  • A parent member is a field or an instance method taking one parameter, never static. The same holds for sub-command members.

  • Ask with wildcards. ? extends at every level that is only read from, so that more parents answer.

  • Ask for an ExecutionSupplier for whatever is expensive to produce.

  • Most specific first. Of alternative parent members, the one with the most specific type is tried first, which is subject to the tie described in the editor’s note of Chapter 8.

17.8. Why declarations

Wiring by declarations, rather than by names or by registration, has three consequences that matter:

  • The tree is known before anything runs. Help lists exactly the commands that will work, because a command is only placed where its declared needs are met.

  • The compiler checks the contract. A parent’s adapter returns a type, a child’s member has a type, and both are checked where they are written. Nothing is matched by a string.

  • Modules stay independent. The runtime’s save and the example’s library have no dependency on each other, and an assistant generating a new command needs to know only the type it consumes.

Chapter 18. Distributions and launching

A command line is only useful when it can be installed and run. This chapter describes what a distribution of the runtime’s command line is, how it starts from any directory on any operating system, and how each launch becomes a unit of work whose telemetry is saved as models.

18.1. What a distribution is

The cli-launcher module builds a distribution of the runtime’s command line, and the same machinery builds a distribution of yours. A distribution is a directory, also packaged as nsdk.zip:

dist/
  lib/              (1)
  modules           (2)
  options           (3)
  nsdk  nsdk.bat    (4)
  nsdk-debug  nsdk-debug.bat
1 The jars, in the Maven repository layout: about fifty for the runtime’s own command line, the bootstrap jar among them.
2 The names of the modules in the launcher’s module layer, recorded at build time.
3 The Java options of the launch: the module path, the class path and the main module, with paths relative to the distribution root.
4 Wrapper scripts. The debug variants start the JVM with a debugger listening on port 8998.

The wrapper scripts are one line each, broken here to fit the page:

#!/bin/bash
exec java -jar \
  "$(dirname "$0")/lib/org/nasdanika/sdk/runtime/bootstrap/2026.10.0/bootstrap-2026.10.0.jar" \
  "$@"

A Windows variant of the distribution calls a JDK bundled under jdk/ instead of the java on the path, for machines where installing Java is a project of its own.

18.2. Module path and class path

The runtime is a set of named modules, and so are its direct dependencies: EMF, OpenTelemetry, Jackson. Some of the libraries further down are not modules, or are automatic modules whose names and requirements are guesses.

The launch puts on the module path the named modules and the modules they require, and everything else on the class path, where it is part of the unnamed module. The split is computed once, at build time, from the launcher’s module layer, by the launcher command, and written to options:

-p "lib/.../jackson-core-2.22.3.jar;lib/.../opentelemetry-api-1.67.0.jar;..."
--add-modules ALL-SYSTEM
-classpath "lib/.../guava-33.6.0-jre.jar;..."
-m org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.cli.launcher/org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.cli.launcher.Launcher

The launcher command can also be run by hand, for an assembly of your own: it scans directories of jars (lib by default) and prints, or writes to a file, a Java command line or just its options. Root modules can be given with patterns, . for the modules in a package and .* for those below it, and the Java command can carry extra options such as system properties.

18.3. Starting from any directory

Java resolves the relative paths of an argument file against the current directory, and scripts cannot expand their own location inside one. The bootstrap closes that gap. It is a small jar with no dependencies, and it:

  1. Finds the distribution root from its own location, walking up to the nearest lib directory.

  2. Reads options and rewrites every relative lib/…​ entry to an absolute path under the root.

  3. Writes a temporary argument file with the absolute paths. A file, not a command line, because a distribution with many jars exceeds the Windows limit of 32 KB for a command line.

  4. Launches a child JVM with that file and the user’s arguments, with standard input, output and error inherited and the exit code propagated.

The child runs in the user’s working directory, so relative file arguments of commands work as expected.

The bootstrap chooses the Java executable in this order: the BOOTSTRAP_JAVA environment variable, a java property in an optional bootstrap.conf in the distribution root, the executable that launched the bootstrap, java.home, a bundled jdk/bin/java, and finally java on the path. BOOTSTRAP_HOME forces the distribution root, and BOOTSTRAP_JAVA_OPTIONS adds JVM options to one invocation, which is how the debug scripts work. bootstrap.conf can also override the options file, the main module and class, the module path and the class path, and add JVM options.

18.4. A launch is a unit of work

Launcher is the main class of the distribution. It follows the rule of Chapter 11, one OpenTelemetry instance per unit of work, with the launch as the unit:

  1. It finds the home directory: the nsdk.home system property, the NSDK_HOME environment variable, or the parent of the lib directory it was loaded from.

  2. It creates a telemetry directory for the launch, <home>/telemetry/<year>/<month>/<day>-<hour>-<minute>-<second>-<millisecond>, and three telemetry resources in it, in the format of nsdk.telemetry.format or NSDK_TELEMETRY_FORMAT (Chapter 13).

  3. It builds an OpenTelemetry SDK whose exporters write to those resources, with the service name launcher, its version, and the working directory as resource attributes, and W3C propagators.

  4. It makes the instance current, continuing the trace in the TRACEPARENT, TRACESTATE and BAGGAGE environment variables if they are set.

  5. It resolves the command tree (Chapter 16), adds the shell command to the root, and executes the command line in a span named "Executing the root command".
