  6. It closes the SDK, which exports what is pending and saves traces, logs and metrics, and exits with the command’s exit code.

The environment variables connect a launch to whatever started it. A build step, a scheduler or another program that sets TRACEPARENT makes the launch a part of its trace, so a pipeline of command runs is one trace across processes, each saved where it ran.

18.5. Building a distribution

A distribution is built by a Maven module with three pieces:

  • Dependencies. The bootstrap jar, org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime:bootstrap, and the modules of the assembly: the runtime’s all aggregate and the modules that contribute commands.

  • Copying. maven-dependency-plugin:copy-dependencies with useRepositoryLayout copies the runtime dependencies into target/dist/lib in the prepare-package phase.

  • Generating. An integration test runs DistributionBuilder, which copies the module’s own jar, records the module layer, computes options and writes the scripts. maven-assembly-plugin packages the directory.

The runtime’s own integration test is the template:

@Test
public void generateLauncher() throws IOException {
	new DistributionBuilder(new File("target/dist")).build();
}

@Test
public void generateWindowsLauncher() throws IOException {
	// The Windows-specific distribution ships a bundled JDK under jdk/.
	new DistributionBuilder(new File("target/dist-win")) {

		@Override
		protected String getBatJava() {
			return "@\"%~dp0jdk\\bin\\java.exe\"";
		}

	}.build();
}

DistributionBuilder launches Launcher from the launcher module. An assembly with its own commands overrides getModuleName to return its own module, whose requires and provides bring in its commands and their dependencies, while the main class stays Launcher. The script name, the debug options, the path separator of the options file and the Java invocation are protected methods as well.

18.6. Running it

With the distribution unpacked and its directory on the path:

nsdk --help
nsdk shell

A distribution assembled with the example module of Chapter 16 also runs its commands, for example nsdk library --file shelf.yml books --before 2000.

nsdk shell starts an interactive shell over the root command, with history and line editing from JLine; exit leaves it. Every command run in the shell is executed by the same root command line, in the same launch, so the telemetry of a shell session is one trace.

After each launch, the telemetry directory holds the record of the run: the command’s span with the spans of everything it did, log records in the spans that emitted them, and recorded model changes where a command recorded them (Chapter 13).

Part VI: Models in the Runtime

The models that ship with the runtime: a Groovy DSL to author any of them, the core model of identity, documentation and provenance, Meta, the JVM model, the models that make the web a generation target, user interfaces assembled from views chosen by the class of what they show, and diagrams as sources of models and as drawings of them.

Chapter 19. Authoring models with the Groovy DSL

XMI, JSON and YAML are good formats for saving models and poor ones for writing them. Xcore is the language for metamodels (Chapter 7), and there is no equivalent for instances: a library, an architecture, a backlog.

The runtime’s groovy module fills the gap with a Groovy DSL that is driven by the metamodel. Nothing in it is written for a particular class or feature: every keyword, every nesting and every attribute is read reflectively from the packages the DSL is bound to. Bind it to a different metamodel and you get a different DSL, for free.

Groovy brings what a home-made language would have to build: nesting, variables, loops, string interpolation, and code where code is the clearest way to say something.

This chapter shows the DSL at the level of the rest of this book: what it is for, its rules, and how it is bound to a metamodel. The Groovy DSL Zephyr Book (The Nasdanika Zephyr Books) is its manual, with every call form, selector and option, the patterns for saving scripts, and the handlers you write for a metamodel of your own.

19.1. A library as a script

Listing 96. A library as a Groovy script (dsl/src/test/resources/reading-group.library.groovy)
library {
    name 'Reading Group'

    def evans = author { name 'Eric Evans' }         (1)
    def fowler = author { name 'Martin Fowler' }

    book {                                            (2)
        name 'Domain-Driven Design'                   (3)
        year 2003                                     (4)
        genre 'TECHNOLOGY'
        authors evans                                 (5)
        cites "../books[name='Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture']" (6)
        documentation '''
            Named the *Ubiquitous Language* and the *Published Language*.
            '''                                       (7)
    }

    book {
        name 'Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture'
        year 2002
        genre 'TECHNOLOGY'
        authors fowler
    }
}
1 Type dispatch. author names the class Author, so the call creates an author and puts it into the one containment feature of the library that accepts authors. The call returns the object, so it can be kept in a variable.
2 A book, into Library.books by the same rule.
3 Feature dispatch. name names a feature of the book, inherited from the core model’s NamedElement, so the call sets it. Feature dispatch is tried before type dispatch.
4 Values are coerced to the feature’s type: 2003 to int, 'TECHNOLOGY' to the enumeration literal.
5 A reference to an object the script holds.
6 A reference by path, to a book defined further down. Paths are resolved after the whole script has run, so forward references work.
7 The core model’s documentation feature, in Markdown.

The file name selects the language. It is read as qualifiers from right to left (Chapter 10): groovy compiles the text to a script, and library binds the DSL to the library metamodel and evaluates it. Loading the script is loading a resource:

Listing 97. Loading a script
Library library = (Library) NasdanikaResourceSet.createAndConfigure()
		.getResource(uri("reading-group.library.groovy"), true) (1)
		.getContents()
		.getFirst();

Book ddd = library.getBooks().getFirst();
assertThat(ddd.getAuthors()).extracting(a -> a.getName()).containsExactly("Eric Evans");
assertThat(ddd.getCites()).containsExactly(library.getBooks().get(1));
assertThat(ddd.getDocumentation()).contains("Published Language");
1 A configured resource set has the Groovy resource factory, and the qualifiers select the handlers.

The model is an ordinary model: it can be saved in any format, validated, transformed, served or generated from. The script is the source; the model is what it means.

19.2. The rules of the language

Entry points. At the top level, every concrete class of the bound packages whose uncapitalized simple name is unambiguous is a keyword: library, ePackage.

Dispatch. Inside a builder closure, a call whose name is a feature of the current object sets the feature; otherwise a call whose name is a class creates an object of that class in the one containment feature that accepts it. When a class fits more than one containment feature, or the feature is typed by an abstract class, the feature is named and the class given explicitly: eStructuralFeatures('EReference') { …​ }.

Built-in keywords. ref, dsl, onSave, loadResource, copy and eObject at the top level, and global, proxy, loadResource, copy and eObject in a closure, win over both kinds of dispatch.

Setting features. year 2003, year(2003) and year = 2003 all set the feature. One form is a trap: upperBound -1 is the expression upperBound - 1 in Groovy, which reads the feature, subtracts one and discards the result. Whenever a value starts with a minus or a plus sign, use the assignment or the parenthesized form.

References take one of three values:

  • An object the script holds, in a variable.

  • A path in the style of EMF URI fragments, resolved after the script has run: / anchors it at the root, .. goes to the container, and predicates select by attribute, as in ../books[name='Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture']. A path containing # is a URI, resolved against the script’s own URI, possibly in another resource.

  • A closure, evaluated after the script with the referencing object as its delegate, which returns an object or a path.

Names of classes can be simple (Book), uncapitalized (book), qualified by a package path (library.Book) or a namespace URI with a fragment (<nsURI>#Book). When a simple name matches several classes and one is a subclass of another, the more specific class wins, which is what makes refinements of a metamodel work in the same script as the metamodel itself. A name that is still ambiguous is an error that lists the qualified alternatives.

Results. The contents of the resource are the script’s last expression, if it is an object or a collection of objects, and otherwise the roots created by entry points.

19.3. Metamodels too

The runtime binds the DSL to Ecore itself, under the qualifier ecore, so a metamodel can be a script as well:

Listing 98. A metamodel as a script (dsl/src/test/resources/catalog.ecore.groovy)
ePackage {
    name 'catalog'
    nsURI 'https://example.org/catalog'
    nsPrefix 'catalog'

    def entry = eClass {                                            (1)
        name 'Entry'
        eAttribute { name 'title'; eType 'EString'; lowerBound 1 }  (2)
    }

    eClass {
        name 'Catalog'
        eStructuralFeatures('EReference') {                         (3)
            name 'entries'
            eType entry
            containment true
            upperBound = -1                                         (4)
        }
    }
}
1 A class, kept in a variable for the reference below.
2 Several features on one line, separated by semicolons. eType 'EString' is resolved as a class name.
3 eStructuralFeatures accepts attributes and references, so the class is named.
4 The assignment form, because the value is negative.
Listing 99. Loading a metamodel script
EPackage catalog = (EPackage) NasdanikaResourceSet.createAndConfigure()
		.getResource(uri("catalog.ecore.groovy"), true)
		.getContents()
		.getFirst();
EClass entry = (EClass) catalog.getEClassifier("Entry");
EClass catalogClass = (EClass) catalog.getEClassifier("Catalog");
assertThat(catalogClass.getEStructuralFeature("entries").getEType()).isSameAs(entry);
assertThat(catalogClass.getEStructuralFeature("entries").isMany()).isTrue();

Xcore remains the way to define a metamodel that has generated code. An Ecore script is the quick way to sketch one, or to derive one from something else.

19.4. Binding the DSL to a metamodel

Binding the DSL to a metamodel takes a handler that names the packages:

Listing 100. The library DSL (dsl/…​/LibraryDslHandler.java)
/**
 * The whole DSL for libraries: the metamodel is the language.
 */
public class LibraryDslHandler extends DslResourceContentsHandler {

	public LibraryDslHandler(
			Resource resource,
			ResourceContentsHandler<CompiledScript> sourceHandler) {
		super(resource, sourceHandler, LibraryPackage.eINSTANCE);
	}

}

and a capability factory that decides which qualifier it serves and connects it to the source handler on its right:

Listing 101. The qualifier (dsl/…​/LibraryDsl.java)
/**
 * Serves files named *.library.groovy: the library qualifier, with the groovy source to its
 * right.
 */
public class LibraryDsl extends ReflectiveCapabilityFactory {

	public LibraryDsl() {
		super(MethodHandles.lookup());
	}

	@Capability
	public Flow.Publisher<ResourceContentsHandler<EObject[]>> library(
			ResourceContentsHandler.Requirement requirement,
			Loader loader) {
		int index = requirement.getQualifierIndex();
		if (!EObject[].class.equals(requirement.getContentsType())
				|| index <= 0 // A source must be to the right
				|| !"library".equalsIgnoreCase(requirement.getQualifiers()[index])) {
			return null;                                                        (1)
		}

		Resource resource = requirement.getResource();
		var source = ResourceContentsHandler.createRequirement(                 (2)
				resource,
				CompiledScript.class,
				requirement.getQualifiers(),
				index - 1);
		CompletableFuture<List<ResourceContentsHandler<CompiledScript>>> sources =
				loader.loadAll(Requirement.of(ResourceContentsHandler.class, source));

		CompletableFuture<List<ResourceContentsHandler<EObject[]>>> handlers = sources
				.thenApply(list -> list.stream().map(s -> dsl(resource, s)).toList()); (3)
		return Flows.concatMap(Flows.fromFuture(handlers), Flows::fromIterable);
	}

	private static ResourceContentsHandler<EObject[]> dsl(
			Resource resource,
			ResourceContentsHandler<CompiledScript> source) {
		return new LibraryDslHandler(resource, source);
	}

}
1 Not a library script: some other factory’s business.
2 The handler of the qualifier to the right, groovy, which compiles the source.
3 One library handler per source handler.
Listing 102. The module (dsl/…​/module-info.java)
import org.example.dsl.LibraryDsl;
import org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.common.capability.CapabilityFactory;

module org.example.dsl {

	requires transitive org.example.library;
	requires transitive org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.groovy;

	exports org.example.dsl;

	provides CapabilityFactory with LibraryDsl;

}

A handler can do more than name packages: provide bindings to the script, a short form that creates an element from a plain value for a containment reference, and source locations for the elements it creates.

19.5. Scripts that derive models

A script is not limited to transcribing a model:

  • loadResource 'payments.drawio' loads another resource through the script’s resource set, relative to the script, with every handler and factory the set has. A script can iterate a diagram, a spreadsheet or another model and emit a model from it, which turns a transcription into a derivation. The Draw.io Zephyr Book shows the diagram’s side of this (The Nasdanika Zephyr Books).

  • copy '<uri>#<fragment>' { …​ } deep-copies an element as a prototype and then populates the copy like a new element: structure from a diagram, details from code. A copy is a snapshot, not a live link.

  • global '<uri>' registers the current element under a URI, so that other resources in the same resource set can reference it.

A DSL resource is read-only by default, because the script, not the model, is the source of truth and there is no general way to write a model back as a script. An onSave callback in the script decides what saving means when it should mean something: writing the model elsewhere, or rewriting the script.

19.6. Errors and telemetry

Failures are reported with the script’s URI and line, including failures of references resolved after the script has run, which report the line where the reference was written.

Loading a script is traced, and the spans nest the way the script does. This test collects the spans of loading the library script, with the script lines from the code.line.number attribute:

Listing 103. Collecting the spans of loading a script
List<String> spans = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
var provider = new PublishingTracerProvider(TracerProvider.noop(), Runnable::run, 4096);
try (var openTelemetry = new PublishingOpenTelemetry(OpenTelemetry.noop(), provider);
		Scope scope = Telemetry.makeCurrent(openTelemetry)) {
	openTelemetry.subscribe(new DslSpans(spans));                              (1)
	NasdanikaResourceSet.createAndConfigure()
		.getResource(uri("reading-group.library.groovy"), true);
}
assertThat(spans).containsSubsequence(
		"      Setting books, line 7",
		"        Loading Book, line 7",                                         (2)
		"          Setting cites, line 12",
		"      Resolving cites, line 12");                                      (3)
1 A subscriber that records started spans with their line numbers, indented by nesting.
2 The first book, from line 7, created in Library.books.
3 Its forward reference, resolved after the script ran, reported with the line where it was written.

The complete tree:

Resource.load
  Compiling script
  Evaluating script
    Loading Library, line 1
      Setting name, line 2
      Setting authors, line 4
        Loading Author, line 4
          Setting name, line 4
      Setting authors, line 5
        Loading Author, line 5
          Setting name, line 5
      Setting books, line 7
        Loading Book, line 7
          Setting name, line 8
          Setting year, line 9
          Setting genre, line 10
          Setting authors, line 11
          Setting cites, line 12
          Setting documentation, line 13
      Setting books, line 18
        Loading Book, line 18
          Setting name, line 19
          Setting year, line 20
          Setting genre, line 21
          Setting authors, line 22
    Resolving references
      Resolving cites, line 12

Spans carry locations, never loaded values: the script URI, the line, and the identities of classes and features as <nsURI>#<name>. A long script that fails, or that is slow, says where.

19.7. What comes next

The DSL is built on the JDK’s scripting API, javax.script, so the same pipeline can serve other JVM languages SKETCH. Kotlin scripts are designed, with the same qualifiers, so reading-group.library.kts would load like the Groovy script. Validation rules expressed in the DSL, and a path from a sketched metamodel script to Xcore and generated code, are part of the same design.

Chapter 20. The core model

Every model needs the same few things: elements that can be identified, named and documented, that know where they came from, and that can be found by whatever refers to them. Written once, these are a foundation; written in every model, they are a source of small, incompatible differences.

The runtime’s core model, in models/core, is that foundation. The library of this book extends it, and so do the runtime’s own models and the models of the tower to come (Chapter 26). In one sentence: model elements that are named, documented, identifiable, referrable, and that know where they came from.

20.1. The element hierarchy

Figure 7. The core hierarchy, and the library’s Book

ModelElement combines identity, documentation and provenance, and adds an icon and alias URIs. NamedElement adds a name. A model extends NamedElement, or ModelElement for elements without a name, and its elements get the rest by inheritance, along with everything built on top: documentation generation, sites, the polymorphic UI.

20.2. Identity and references

StringIdentity gives an element an id: a stable, human-readable identifier for URIs and cross-references. A name is for people and may change; an id is for references and should not.

ModelElement.uris are alias URIs, which may be absolute or opaque, such as actors://john-smith. They act as merge anchors: several teams may maintain elements with the same URI, for example myorg://capabilities/developer-productivity, and when their models are assembled into one, those elements are one logical element.

Referrable.getReferrers(reference) is inverse navigation without opposite references. It finds the objects in the element’s containment tree, resource or resource set that reference the element through a given reference:

Listing 104. Who refers to this element
Library library = Samples.library();
Book patterns = book(library, "Design Patterns");

// Book.cites has no opposite. Who cites Design Patterns?
assertThat(patterns.getReferrers(LibraryPackage.Literals.BOOK__CITES))
	.extracting(referrer -> ((Book) referrer).getName())
	.containsExactlyInAnyOrder("Domain-Driven Design", "EMF: Eclipse Modeling Framework");

An opposite reference is the right choice when both directions are part of the model’s meaning, and it has a cost: both ends must be in memory and kept consistent, which fails across resources loaded on demand. getReferrers costs a walk of what is loaded, and nothing when it is not called. The catalog volume of Chapter 14 uses it for the "Cited by" line of each book.

20.3. Documentation

Documented gives every element documentation that can be as short or as long as it needs to be:

Listing 105. Documenting an element
Book ddd = book(Samples.library(), "Domain-Driven Design");
ddd.setDocumentation("""
		Introduced the *Ubiquitous Language* and the *Published Language*:
		a vocabulary shared by a team, and its documented form shared with others.
		""");                                 (1)
ddd.setDocRef("ddd/review.md");               (2)
ddd.setId("ddd");                             (3)
ddd.setIcon("fas fa-book");                   (4)
1 Inline documentation, in Markdown unless docFormat says otherwise.
2 Long-form documentation in a resource, resolved relative to the element’s resource, with its format derived from the extension.
3 An identity for URIs and references.
4 An icon: a URL if it contains a slash, a CSS class otherwise, such as a Font Awesome icon.

Beyond the documentation and its reference, docContents adds a list of contents, inline or by reference, each with a content type, and docSections adds a tree of titled sections. Documentation can be written where it belongs, a sentence inline, a chapter in a Markdown file next to the model, and still be assembled into one site.

Micro-wikis

Documentation anchored to model elements grows into a way of sharing knowledge of its own: the micro-wiki. Every element of a model anchors its own documentation space, a Markdown page referenced by docRef, with sections and contents beside it.

A wiki has depth and is easy to contribute to, and it has no structure: pages multiply, links rot, and nobody knows which page is the one about a given thing. A model has structure, and it is a poor place for long prose. A micro-wiki takes the depth and the ease of contribution of the wiki, and gives it what it never had: the model as its site map. Navigation, cross-references and diagrams are generated from the model, and the pages are where people write.

Two properties make micro-wikis worth the name:

  • Documentation cannot drift away from what it describes, because it lives at it. Rename an element and its page moves with it; remove the element and the page goes too, in the same change.

  • Generated stubs say which file documents what. A documentation stub per element tells people, and assistants, which file to edit when they learn something about that element. An assistant asked to map a set of guidelines onto a model edits the stub of each element with the paragraphs that govern it, and the published site shows, for every element, the rules that apply to it.

Micro-models decompose meaning (Chapter 2); micro-wikis decompose the documentation of that meaning, along the same lines. The core model provides the structure today. Generating micro-wiki sites, with stubs and a site map, was part of the previous generation of Nasdanika’s tools and is planned for the runtime PLANNED.

20.4. Provenance

Marked elements carry markers that record where an element, or one feature of it, came from:

Listing 106. Recording where an element came from
Book ddd = book(Samples.library(), "Domain-Driven Design");
Marker marker = CoreFactory.eINSTANCE.createMarker();
marker.setLocation("https://example.org/catalogs/2026/books.csv"); (1)
marker.setPosition("42");                                          (2)
marker.setDate(new Date());
marker.setComment("Imported from the acquisitions spreadsheet");
ddd.getMarkers().add(marker);
1 The location of the source, typically the URI of the file the element was loaded from.
2 A position in the source: a line, a cell, a page.

A marker can name the feature it is about, carry a digest of its source, a hash of a file or of a model, and have child markers, for a value computed from other values that have markers of their own. GitMarker adds the path in a repository, its remotes, the branch, the head commit and the refs on it: with the position, enough to build a permalink to the exact line in the exact commit.

Markers make what is generated from models traceable. Every element on a generated page can point back to the file, the line and the version it came from, and a derived value can be traced through its inputs.

20.5. Attributes

Attributed is a mixin for elements that carry attributes: string keys and string values. They hold what a source format carries and a model does not name, such as the properties of a Draw.io shape or the block attributes of Markdown and AsciiDoc, and conventions of one’s own, such as layout options of a diagram element. The diagram model’s elements are Attributed, and so are, through them, the Draw.io model’s (Chapter 25).

They are called attributes, not properties, so that a model with properties of its own can mix in Attributed without a clash.

20.6. Evaluators

An evaluator is a documented, marked expression or script, evaluated against bindings and coerced to a result type. It is the core model’s way of putting computed values and conditions into models: a rule, a derived property, a filter.

Listing 107. A rule in the model
ScriptEvaluator classic = CoreFactory.eINSTANCE.createScriptEvaluator();
classic.setLanguage("groovy");                                           (1)
classic.setScript("book.year < 1980 && book.authors.size() == 1");
classic.setDocumentation("A classic: older than 1980, with a single author.");

Library library = Samples.library();
for (Book book: library.getBooks()) {
	Boolean result = classic.evaluate(Boolean.class, Map.of("book", book)); (2)
	if (result) {
		System.out.println(book.getName());
	}
}
1 A JSR-223 script. The language names the engine, here Groovy, which the dsl example module has on its module path.
2 The bindings are the script’s variables, and the evaluator itself is bound as self.

It prints "The Art of Computer Programming", "On the Origin of Species" and "War and Peace".

Evaluator Source Status

ScriptEvaluator

A script in any JSR-223 language, inline or by reference. A referenced script selects its engine by extension when no language is given

AVAILABLE

GroovyEvaluator

A Groovy script, inline or by reference

PLANNED

SpelEvaluator

A Spring Expression Language expression

PLANNED

XPathEvaluator

An XPath expression over the model

PLANNED

The planned evaluators are declared in the model, so that models can contain them today, and throw UnsupportedOperationException when evaluated. Their implementations are to be loaded as services, which keeps the core model free of the engines' dependencies.

20.7. Why a shared core matters

The benefits of the core model compound with the number of models that extend it.

  • One generator for many models. A documentation generator that knows NamedElement, Documented and Marked documents any model in the tower, including ones written after it.

  • One UI for many models. The polymorphic UI’s views of the core model show names, icons, documentation and provenance for any element, whatever its class.

  • Merging across teams. Alias URIs let independently maintained models be assembled into one.

  • Traceability by default. Markers are there to fill, by loaders, by importers, by agents recording where a change came from.

The library of this book got all of it by writing extends NamedElement.

Chapter 21. Meta: a language-neutral type system

A class with named, typed, possibly multi-valued features is one of the most stable ideas in computing, and every ecosystem spells it its own way: Ecore, Java, XML Schema, JSON Schema, a database schema, TypeScript, a table on a wiki page, a spreadsheet. The differences are real and small, and most are about the host language, not about the domain.

The cost is not the spelling. It is that one definition, of a customer, of a book, of a service, lives in many formats at once and nothing relates them. Each is a projection of a domain model that was never written down.

Meta, in models/meta, is a place to write it down once and project. It is a micro-model of typed domain models, about twenty classifiers, positioned directly on the core model (Chapter 20). In the terms of Domain-Driven Design it is a Published Language: a documented, shared vocabulary that bounded contexts translate into and out of, with the part that was out of reach when the term was coined: the vocabulary is machine-checkable, because the types and the documentation are generated from it.

21.1. What it models

Area Classifiers

Base

ModelElement, on the core model’s NamedElement, and Annotation

Structure

Package, Classifier, Class, DataType, Enum, EnumLiteral

Members

TypedElement, Feature, Attribute, Reference, Operation, Parameter

Types

TypeParameter, TypeReference, ClassifierReference, TypeParameterReference, PrimitiveTypeReference, UnionTypeReference, IntersectionTypeReference, WildcardTypeReference, OpaqueTypeReference, PrimitiveKind

Instances

Object, IncomingReference

Attribute.identifying marks the attributes that identify an instance, which is how a reference cites a target, and how a Domain-Driven Design entity is told from a value object. Reference.containment separates tree edges from graph edges; opposite and keys carry bidirectionality and identity within a list. A Package is the unit of publication: one package becomes one Maven artifact or one npm package.

The model is metacircular: a package containing classes describes Package and Class, so a runtime can bootstrap from it alone.

21.2. What it leaves out

The rule is that what a class-based type system cannot express is not a class in Meta. That keeps it at about twenty classifiers, against Ecore’s fifty-three:

  • No volatile, transient, unsettable or resolveProxies: implementation concerns of EMF with no meaning in a browser.

  • No feature maps, no factories, no generic type algebra. Unions, intersections and wildcards are carried, so that a Java or TypeScript signature can be written down without loss, but nothing computes subtyping or substitution with them.

  • No subpackages, which neither TypeScript modules nor npm packages need. A loader flattens and records the original path.

  • No interface flag. Whether a class becomes an interface, a type alias or a class is the projection’s decision.

What a source expresses and Meta does not goes into an Annotation, keyed by a source URI, the bargain Ecore’s EAnnotation makes. Loaders record what they cannot map instead of dropping it, so a round trip to the source stays possible.

21.3. Documentation as structure

Most formats carry documentation as one string: an Ecore annotation detail, a JSON Schema description, a database column remark. XML Schema, OpenAPI and OWL do better. None of them treats documentation as structure: a string cannot be divided into sections, point to a resource elsewhere, declare its format, or say who owns it.

Meta elements are core model elements, so they have all of that, and markers that say where each element came from: this class from that sheet of that spreadsheet, at that commit; this feature from that schema element. When two sources disagree about what a term means, the model shows both, and where each came from.

21.4. A vocabulary

Here is the library’s vocabulary in Meta, written with small builders:

Listing 108. Builders (meta/…​/Vocabulary.java)
static Class type(Package vocabulary, String name, String definition) {
	Class type = META.createClass();
	type.setName(name);
	type.setDocumentation(definition);                      (1)
	vocabulary.getClassifiers().add(type);
	return type;
}

static Attribute attribute(
		Class owner,
		String name,
		PrimitiveKind kind,
		boolean identifying,
		String definition) {
	Attribute attribute = META.createAttribute();
	attribute.setName(name);
	attribute.setDocumentation(definition);
	attribute.setIdentifying(identifying);                  (2)
	attribute.setLowerBound(identifying ? 1 : 0);
	PrimitiveTypeReference type = META.createPrimitiveTypeReference();
	type.setKind(kind);
	attribute.setType(type);
	owner.getFeatures().add(attribute);
	return attribute;
}

static Reference reference(Class owner, String name, Class target, String definition) {
	Reference reference = META.createReference();
	reference.setName(name);
	reference.setDocumentation(definition);
	reference.setUpperBound(-1);
	ClassifierReference type = META.createClassifierReference();
	type.setTarget(target);
	reference.setType(type);
	owner.getFeatures().add(reference);
	return reference;
}
1 Documentation is the core model’s structure, not a string attribute of Meta.
2 Identity of instances, as for entities in Domain-Driven Design.
Listing 109. The vocabulary (meta/…​/Vocabulary.java)
public static Package library() {
	Package vocabulary = META.createPackage();
	vocabulary.setName("library");
	vocabulary.setNamespace("https://example.org/vocabulary/library");
	vocabulary.setDocumentation("The words a library uses, and what they mean here.");

	Class person = type(vocabulary, "Person",
			"Someone who wrote, edited or translated a book.");
	attribute(person, "name", PrimitiveKind.STRING, true,
			"The name as printed on the title page.");

	Class book = type(vocabulary, "Book",
			"A published work, identified by its ISBN.");
	attribute(book, "isbn", PrimitiveKind.STRING, true,
			"International Standard Book Number, 13 digits.");
	attribute(book, "title", PrimitiveKind.STRING, false,
			"The title as printed, subtitle excluded.");
	attribute(book, "published", PrimitiveKind.DATE, false,
			"The date of the first edition.");
	reference(book, "authors", person,
			"The people credited as authors, in the order printed.");
	return vocabulary;
}

A vocabulary is a model, so it is saved, versioned, diffed and reviewed like any other:

Listing 110. Saving a vocabulary
ResourceSet resourceSet = NasdanikaResourceSet.createAndConfigure();
URI uri = URI.createFileURI(directory.resolve("library.meta.yml").toString());
Resource resource = resourceSet.createResource(uri);
resource.getContents().add(Vocabulary.library());
resource.save(null);                                            (1)
1 A YAML file in a repository. A change to what a term means is a pull request whose diff shows which features moved.

21.5. The text syntax

A vocabulary built in Java is a program that builds a vocabulary, which is how a harvester or a projection makes one, and not how a person should write one. A vocabulary written in Meta’s text syntax is the vocabulary itself: a file a developer reads top to bottom, diffs in a pull request, and edits in any editor.

The syntax writes metamodels the way Xcore writes Ecore models (Chapter 7). Files have the extension .nmeta, one file is one package, and they are parsed by the ANTLR runtime alone, with no Xtext and no Eclipse. The grammar, models/meta/model/src/main/grammar/Meta.g4, documents every construct and how it maps to the model.

Here is the library again:

Listing 111. The library’s vocabulary as text (meta/src/main/meta/library.nmeta)
/** The words a library uses, and what they mean here. */
package library namespace "https://example.org/vocabulary/library"

/** Someone who wrote, edited or translated a book. */
class Person {
    /** The name as printed on the title page. */
    id string[1] name
}

/** A published work, identified by its ISBN. */
class Book {
    /** International Standard Book Number, 13 digits. */
    id string[1] isbn

    /** The title as printed, subtitle excluded. */
    string title

    /** The date of the first edition. */
    date published

    /** The people credited as authors, in the order printed. */
    refers Person[*] authors
}

A documentation comment, /** ... */, is the Markdown documentation of the element that follows it, and other comments are ignored.

A second file shows the rest of the notation. Lending is a vocabulary of its own, kept by the circulation desk, which refers to the library’s books without owning them:

Listing 112. A package and its imports (meta/src/main/meta/lending.nmeta)
/** What the circulation desk lends, to whom and for how long. */
package lending namespace "https://example.org/vocabulary/lending" version "2026.10.0"

import "https://example.org/vocabulary/library" as library
import "https://runtime.sdk.nasdanika.org/models/occupancy" as occupancy
annotation "urn:org.nasdanika" as Nasdanika

  • The namespace URI is the package’s identity: what other packages import, and what a reference to one of its classes resolves against. The prefix and the version are optional.

  • import names another package by its namespace, under an alias. library.Book is then the class Book of that package. A namespace is a name, not an address: nothing is fetched from it.

  • annotation declares an alias for an annotation source, so that @Nasdanika(icon = "bi-person") is an annotation with the source urn:org.nasdanika and a detail icon.

Listing 113. Data types and enumerations (meta/src/main/meta/lending.nmeta)
/** An amount of money, a decimal string so that no cent is lost. */
type Amount as string wraps java.math.BigDecimal

/** Where a loan stands. */
enum LoanStatus {
    ACTIVE,
    RETURNED,
    WRITTEN_OFF as "written-off"
}

A data type has a name of its own and says how it crosses the wire: an Amount is a string, so that no projection turns money into a floating-point number. wraps records the type it stands for in a source language, as provenance. An enumeration’s literals may have a serialized form, as "written-off", and an ordinal, = 3; without one, a literal’s ordinal is one more than the previous literal’s.

Listing 114. Classes (meta/src/main/meta/lending.nmeta)
/** Someone entitled to borrow, with a card to show for it. */
@Nasdanika(icon = "bi-person")
class Member {
    /** Identifies the member, and is printed on the card. */
    id string[1] cardNumber

    /** The loans made to the member, addressed by their identifiers. */
    contains Loan[*] loans opposite member keys loanId
}

/** A book in a member's hands, until it comes back. */
class Loan {
    /** Identifies the loan among the member's loans. */
    id string[1] loanId

    /** The member who borrowed the book. */
    refers Member[1] member opposite loans

    /** The book on loan. Defined by the library's vocabulary, not here. */
    refers library.Book[1] book

    /** The day the book is due back. */
    date[1] due

    /** Where the loan stands. */
    LoanStatus[1] status = "ACTIVE"

    /** The fine so far, computed rather than stored. Not every jurisdiction allows one. */
    @occupancy.Presence { jurisdiction: "CA-ON" }
    derived readonly Amount fine

    /** The fine as it would stand at the end of a day. */
    op Amount fineOn(date day)
}

A feature is a type followed by a name, as in Xcore:

  • With refers or contains it is a reference, and contains makes the target part of this object: a loan belongs to its member, a book does not.

  • Otherwise it is an attribute, of a primitive kind, such as string and date, or of a data type or enumeration.

  • id marks an attribute that identifies its instance.

  • opposite pairs two references, keys names the attributes that identify a contained object within its list, and = "ACTIVE" is a default value.

  • derived and readonly say that a feature is computed rather than stored, and op declares the signature of an operation. Meta carries no bodies.

The multiplicity follows the type:

Written Bounds Meaning

string name

0..1

Optional, single-valued

string[1] name

1..1

Required

string[?] name

0..1

Optional, said explicitly

Loan[*] loans, Loan[] loans

0..*

Any number

Author[+] authors

1..*

At least one

string[2..5] names, string[2..*] names

2..5, 2..*

A range

Types also combine. string | number is a union, A & B an intersection, Repository<Loan, string> a class with type arguments, ? extends T a wildcard, and text in backticks an opaque type, for what nothing else covers, such as TypeScript’s Record<string, unknown>. They are rarely needed in a business vocabulary, and they are what lets a Java or TypeScript signature be written down without loss.

An annotation is a bag of strings keyed by its source. A facet is typed: @occupancy.Presence { jurisdiction: "CA-ON" } says where the fine applies, with a class of an occupancy model as the type of what it says. A facet is checked against its type when the type is available, and a property the class has no feature for is a warning. The occupancy model is PLANNED, so here the facet is read without checking, and the warning says so. Until the core model has facets, a facet is recorded as an annotation whose source is the URI of its type SKETCH.

21.6. Reading and writing text

A vocabulary in text loads like any other model:

Listing 115. A resource set for vocabularies (meta/…​/TestMeta.java)
static ResourceSet vocabularies() {
	ResourceSet resourceSet = NasdanikaResourceSet.createAndConfigure();    (1)
	resourceSet.getURIConverter().getURIMap().put(                          (2)
			URI.createURI("https://example.org/vocabulary/library"),
			URI.createFileURI(TEXT.resolve("library.nmeta").toString()));
	return resourceSet;
}
1 The module’s resource set contributor registers the text syntax for .nmeta files.
2 The library is another team’s vocabulary. The URI map says where its namespace is found here: a file next to this one.
Listing 116. Loading the lending vocabulary (meta/…​/TestMeta.java)
Resource resource = vocabularies().getResource(LENDING, true);
Package lending = (Package) resource.getContents().getFirst();

Class loan = (Class) classifier(lending, "Loan");
ClassifierReference book = (ClassifierReference) feature(loan, "book").getType();
assertThat(book.getTarget().getName()).isEqualTo("Book");                 (1)
assertThat(book.getTarget().eResource().getURI().lastSegment())
	.isEqualTo("library.nmeta");

Reference loans = (Reference) feature((Class) classifier(lending, "Member"), "loans");
assertThat(loans.isContainment()).isTrue();                               (2)
assertThat(loans.getOpposite()).isSameAs(feature(loan, "member"));
assertThat(loans.getKeys()).extracting(Feature::getName).containsExactly("loanId");

assertThat(resource.getWarnings()).extracting(Resource.Diagnostic::getMessage)  (3)
	.containsExactly("Facet type occupancy.Presence is not available, "
			+ "its properties are not checked");
1 library.Book resolves to a class of another resource, loaded on demand from where the URI map says.
2 The target is part of this object, its opposite is the member, and loanId identifies it within the list.
3 The occupancy facet’s type is not available. That is a warning, not an error.

A name qualified with an alias becomes a classifier reference with the imported namespace and the class name. Its target is set when the package of that namespace is available: loaded in the resource set already, or loadable because the URI converter maps the namespace to a location. Otherwise the reference keeps the namespace and the name, and the package is read on its own, which is what lets a team publish its vocabulary without the vocabularies it refers to.

The reader collects what is wrong in the resource’s getErrors() and getWarnings(), each with its file, line and column, and loading fails with the first error, as EMF’s XML resources do. Every package, classifier, feature, operation, parameter and enum literal it reads gets a core model marker with the file’s URI and the line:column where its declaration starts. When a generated page or a projected schema says something surprising, the marker says which line of which file it came from.

A vocabulary read from text is the same model as one built in code, so it is saved in any format a resource set supports, and the projections below work on it unchanged. The other direction is MetaWriter, which writes a package as text, and which the resource uses to save a .nmeta file:

Listing 117. Writing a vocabulary as text (meta/…​/TestMeta.java)
Package library = Vocabulary.library();                                 (1)
String text = MetaWriter.write(library);

URI uri = URI.createFileURI(directory.resolve("library.nmeta").toString());
Resource resource = vocabularies().createResource(uri);
resource.getContents().add(library);
resource.save(null);                                                    (2)
1 The vocabulary built with the builders above. The text is library.nmeta, which the test checks.
2 The same text, as a file.

The text is canonical, not a copy of a source: comments other than documentation and the layout of the source are not kept, and the imports and annotation aliases are derived from the namespaces and sources the package uses. Reading what was written and writing it again gives the same text. That makes the text syntax a target as well as a source: a vocabulary harvested from a database or authored in a spreadsheet can be written as text, reviewed as text, and compared with last month’s as text.

The Zephyr Book Meta Model (The Nasdanika Zephyr Books) writes a bank’s whole vocabulary in the text syntax, from the first line of a file to the glossary the business reads.

21.7. Projections

A vocabulary is worth writing down once because of what is projected from it. The runtime has the first projection below, a glossary; the others are planned, and the example sketches the second to show the idea.

The first is for people: a glossary that cannot drift from the types, because both come from one source.

Listing 118. A glossary (meta/…​/TestMeta.java)
String glossary = MetaGlossary.write(Vocabulary.library());             (1)

List<Path> written = MetaGlossary.generate(                             (2)
		Path.of("src/main/meta"),
		directory.resolve("glossary"));
1 One package, as Markdown.
2 A glossary for each .nmeta file under a directory.

It is for people who do not read the notation, so its Rule column states what the structure says, and the types are in plain words. For the library vocabulary, the section on books reads:

Listing 119. The books of the library’s glossary (meta/src/test/resources/library.md)
## Book

A published work, identified by its ISBN.

| Term | Type | Rule | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| isbn | text | required, identifies it | International Standard Book Number, 13 digits. |
| title | text | optional | The title as printed, subtitle excluded. |
| published | date | optional | The date of the first edition. |
| authors | Person | any number | The people credited as authors, in the order printed. |

The second is for tools: a dynamic Ecore package, so that every EMF tool works on a vocabulary without generated Java.

Listing 120. An Ecore projection (meta/…​/Projections.java)
/**
 * A sketch of the projection to Ecore: classes, attributes and references, enough for EMF to
 * create, validate and serialize instances without generated code.
 */
public static EPackage ecore(Package vocabulary) {
	EcoreFactory ecore = EcoreFactory.eINSTANCE;
	EPackage ePackage = ecore.createEPackage();
	ePackage.setName(vocabulary.getName());
	ePackage.setNsURI(vocabulary.getNamespace());
	ePackage.setNsPrefix(vocabulary.getName());

	Map<Class, EClass> classes = new HashMap<>();
	for (Classifier classifier: vocabulary.getClassifiers()) {
		if (classifier instanceof Class type) {
			EClass eClass = ecore.createEClass();
			eClass.setName(type.getName());
			ePackage.getEClassifiers().add(eClass);
			classes.put(type, eClass);
		}
	}
	classes.forEach((type, eClass) -> {
		for (Feature feature: type.getFeatures()) {
			if (feature instanceof Attribute attribute
					&& attribute.getType() instanceof PrimitiveTypeReference primitive) {
				EAttribute eAttribute = ecore.createEAttribute();
				eAttribute.setName(attribute.getName());
				eAttribute.setEType(dataType(primitive.getKind()));
				eAttribute.setLowerBound(attribute.getLowerBound());
				eAttribute.setUpperBound(attribute.getUpperBound());
				eAttribute.setID(attribute.isIdentifying());
				eClass.getEStructuralFeatures().add(eAttribute);
			} else if (feature instanceof Reference reference
					&& reference.getType() instanceof ClassifierReference target) {
				EReference eReference = ecore.createEReference();
				eReference.setName(reference.getName());
				eReference.setEType(classes.get((Class) target.getTarget()));
				eReference.setContainment(reference.isContainment());
				eReference.setLowerBound(reference.getLowerBound());
				eReference.setUpperBound(reference.getUpperBound());
				eClass.getEStructuralFeatures().add(eReference);
			}
		}
	});
	new ResourceImpl(URI.createURI(ePackage.getNsURI())).getContents().add(ePackage);
	return ePackage;
}

private static EDataType dataType(PrimitiveKind kind) {
	return switch (kind) {
		case NUMBER -> EcorePackage.Literals.EDOUBLE;
		case BOOLEAN -> EcorePackage.Literals.EBOOLEAN;
		case DATE, DATE_TIME -> EcorePackage.Literals.EDATE;
		default -> EcorePackage.Literals.ESTRING;
	};
}
Listing 121. Instances of a projected vocabulary
EPackage library = Projections.ecore(Vocabulary.library());
EClass bookClass = (EClass) library.getEClassifier("Book");
EObject book = EcoreUtil.create(bookClass);                     (1)
book.eSet(bookClass.getEStructuralFeature("isbn"), "978-0321125217");
book.eSet(bookClass.getEStructuralFeature("title"), "Domain-Driven Design");

ResourceSet resourceSet = NasdanikaResourceSet.createAndConfigure();
resourceSet.getPackageRegistry().put(library.getNsURI(), library); (2)
URI uri = URI.createFileURI(directory.resolve("books.json").toString());
Resource resource = resourceSet.createResource(uri);
resource.getContents().add(book);
resource.save(null);
1 An instance of a class that has no Java class.
2 The package is registered with the resource set, so its instances can be saved and loaded in any format.

The Ecore projection is the quiet one, and possibly the most useful: a vocabulary captured in a spreadsheet can be validated, compared, diagrammed and serialized by tools that already exist.

21.8. Sources and targets

The text syntax works today, in both directions, and so do YAML and JSON. The design names the other surfaces through which a vocabulary comes in and goes out PLANNED:

Direction Formats

Authored in

Excel, for the people who already keep the vocabulary there; Draw.io diagrams, where the diagram is the source; Markdown, where the prose matters most; the Groovy DSL (Chapter 19)

Harvested from

Ecore, Java, XML Schema, JSON Schema, database metadata: most of a domain model is already written down somewhere, and asking people to retype it is how modeling efforts die

Projected to

TypeScript packages with runtime type information (Chapter 23), JSON Schema, for validation and for the tool schemas of agents, Ecore, documentation sites with diagrams, and on demand SQL, Java or Python

The rule that makes many formats affordable is that every format reads into Meta and every output is projected from Meta. Nothing converts from one format to another directly, so a new input format works with every output there is, and a new output with every input.

The incumbent for a shared vocabulary is a spreadsheet and a wiki table, which win because they are free and ask nobody to adopt anything. Meta treats them as inputs, not as competitors.

21.9. AI-assisted domain design

Until those inputs are here, there is another way in for the people who know what the words mean. A librarian knows what makes a loan overdue, can spot a wrong definition of it in a second, and has no reason to learn a grammar. An assistant can write the notation for them: they describe the domain in their own words, or hand over a glossary, a spreadsheet extract or meeting notes, the assistant drafts a .nmeta file, and they correct what it says about their business.

An assistant also writes a plausible definition of a term it has never heard as easily as a correct one, and that gets past a reader who does not know the domain. So review only works where the reviewer can judge what is reviewed, and this way of working gives each check to whoever can:

  • The validator judges the structure, which the subject-matter expert cannot and does not have to: the syntax, that every type exists, that opposites and keys exist, that imports within the project resolve. It says nothing about whether a definition is right.

  • The subject-matter expert judges the meaning, which neither the assistant nor the validator can. The definitions are prose. The rules are in the structure, often guessed, so the assistant reads them back as questions, the guessed ones first: refers Member[1] member asks whether a loan can exist without a member, and contains Loan[*] loans whether a loan exists apart from its member. The generated glossary states the same rules for the whole vocabulary, in its Rule column.

  • A developer or an architect sets the project up once, and reviews the pull request for how the vocabulary fits with others.

The validator is what lets an assistant correct its own drafts before anyone reads them. MetaValidator reads the .nmeta files of a directory together, and reports problems in the format of compilers:

Listing 122. Validating a directory (meta/…​/TestMeta.java)
List<Problem> problems = MetaValidator.validate(TEXT, TEXT);            (1)
assertThat(problems).extracting(Problem::toString).containsExactly(     (2)
		"lending.nmeta:51:6: warning: Facet type occupancy.Presence "
		+ "is not available, its properties are not checked");
assertThat(MetaValidator.hasErrors(problems)).isFalse();
1 The directory to search, and the directory the reported file names are relative to. lending.nmeta imports library.nmeta, and no URI map is needed.
2 file:line:column: severity: message, which a person can read, an assistant can act on, and an editor can show.

What teaches an assistant all this is an agent skill: a directory of instructions it loads when a task calls for them. The skill nasdanika-meta is in the runtime’s repository, at models/meta/model/src/main/skill/nasdanika-meta, and holds the workflow, with the read-back as a step of it, the syntax, tested examples, and the conventions a language reference would not give: a definition for a business reader for every term, a multiplicity that says the business rule, and terms other teams own imported rather than copied. It comes with a starter project, whose whole build is one test that runs the validator and writes the glossary to target/glossary, so mvn -q test is what the assistant runs on a laptop and what stops a broken vocabulary from being merged. The runtime’s tests check what an assistant learns from the skill, and do not test an assistant: what it writes is checked by the validator and by the people who own the words.

The first half of the corresponding chapter of the Zephyr Book Meta Model (The Nasdanika Zephyr Books) needs no code, and can be handed to a subject-matter expert: how a session goes, how to read a vocabulary without learning the notation, and what to watch for.

21.10. Instances whose type is a reference

Object is the reflective instance of a Meta class: no generated interface, no implementation class, no factory. It knows its type by reference, and answers about itself through a dozen operations: get, whole or by range, set, add, remove, unset, size, invoke, its container and containment feature, and its incoming references, filtered, paged and counted. An agent gets an interaction surface that can be taught in a paragraph.

Because the type is a reference, an object can exist before it is classified, and be classified later. That is the shape elicitation has: a thing is named before anyone knows what kind of thing it is, an agent proposes a classification, and a person corrects it. Values without a typed home wait in annotations, and classification promotes what fits into features:

Change Example Safety

Specialization

Person to Author

Safe: every feature stays in scope

Generalization

Author to Person

Loses a distinction

Reclassification

Person to Publisher

Arbitrary: names may coincide while meanings do not

Values are never silently dropped: a value whose feature falls out of scope moves to an annotation, with its feature name and the type that declared it. Identity is intrinsic, not derived from an identifying attribute, so it survives retyping, and a marker records who classified an object and when, which separates confirmed facts from unreviewed machine guesses.

The obvious implementation is dynamic EMF behind this interface, through the Ecore projection. In the runtime as of this edition, the operations of Object are declared and have no implementation SKETCH.

21.11. Federated by design

There is no server and no central repository. A vocabulary is files in Git, or an artifact published to Maven Central or npm, and packages reference each other by namespace URI, as lending.nmeta refers to the library. A team owns its vocabulary and refers to another team’s without coordinating a release, and gets what a catalog cannot give:

  • Branching. A proposed change to a term, reviewed as a pull request.

  • History. The same history the code has, with the same tools.

  • Ownership at the edges. Nobody administers the whole graph.

  • Immutable snapshots. What a term meant last year is an install, not an investigation.

Chapter 22. The JVM model

A running Java virtual machine knows a great deal about itself. ModuleLayer.boot() gives the module graph, Configuration reports what resolution actually produced, and reflection has exposed types and members since Java 1.1. The information was never the problem. Getting an answer meant writing a program, so only questions worth a program were ever asked, and that is a small set.

I have written such programs more than once (Prior art, first-hand). The largest, in 2012, was for a monolith of about fifteen thousand classes, in which two hundred packages formed a single dependency cycle; on our diagrams those packages were red, and we called them the black hole. Its model of the code held about two million objects on a 32-bit JVM. The questions it answered were worth it, because the monolith had to be taken apart. Most questions are smaller than that, and they went unasked.

The JVM model, in models/jvm, is a model of what a JVM can name: layers, class loaders, modules, packages, types, methods, fields and parameters. With the JVM as a model, a question costs what it costs to ask it, and the answer can be saved, compared and published like any other model.

22.1. What your assembly became

There is a gap between what a build declares and what runs, and nothing reports it. A dependency tree describes what could be on the path, test scope, optional dependencies and libraries nothing loads included. The resolved module graph is shorter and truer.

Its clearest instance is readability: modules that read something they never required. Usually that is correct and by design, because requires transitive propagates readability and service binding pulls providers into the resolved graph that no dependency declaration mentions. It is a property of resolution, not of the build, so it is absent from every POM and every bill of materials, and no dependency tool can report it.

Non-modular code is as visible as modular code. Code on the class path lives in a class loader’s unnamed module, which is a value with packages and types in it, not an absence, so the model is useful for an application that has never heard of the module system.

22.2. Identity

Elements are named the way the JVM names them: binary names and method descriptors, such as java.util.List, [I and get(I)Ljava/lang/Object;.

That is not a local convention. It is the form in the constant pool, in stack traces, in jdeps output, in JFR events and in profilers and coverage tools, and OpenTelemetry’s code attributes carry its two halves. A build scan, a coverage report, a profile and a span name the same method the same way, and models produced independently merge on URIs with no translation:

Element URI

Module

jvm:module/<module name>

Package

jvm:package/<binary package name>

Type

jvm:type/<binary name>

Method

jvm:method/<owner binary name>#<name><descriptor>

Field

jvm:field/<owner binary name>#<name>:<descriptor>

Parameter

jvm:parameter/<owner method>#<index>

Joining static structure to runtime observation is then mechanical, not a project. A JaCoCo report already keys classes by binary name and methods by name and descriptor, so coverage attaches to these elements with no mapping layer.

22.3. What it models

Area Types

Root

JavaVirtualMachine: whether it is live, the VM’s name, version, vendor and specification version; it contains modules, layers and class loaders

Runtime structure

Layer, with its parents and modules; ClassLoader, with its parent and unnamed module

Modules

Module, with its version, modifiers, main class, uses and reads, the resolved readability; Requires, Exports and Opens with their targets; Provides with the service and its providers

Types

Package; Type, with its kind, access level, binary name, descriptor, signature, supertype, interfaces and class file version

Members

Method, constructors and static initializers included; Field, with its constant value; Parameter

Three decisions shape it:

  • Modules are contained by the root, not by a layer. A named module belongs to a layer and an unnamed module to a class loader, and one containment cannot express both, so layers and loaders reference modules.

  • Constructors are methods, named <init>, and static initializers are <clinit>, as in bytecode, where the identity scheme comes from.

  • Access flags are booleans, not a packed integer, so that a query language without bitwise operators can ask about them.

Generic types are carried as data: the class file’s Signature attribute, verbatim, on types and members. Identity uses erased descriptors, because that is how the JVM tells overloads apart. Annotations, source positions and instructions are out of scope for the first version; annotations are the most likely next addition.

The JVM model extends the core model, not Meta (Chapter 21). Bridge methods, synthetic accessors and overloads that differ only in erased parameter types are realities of the JVM that Meta deliberately does not hold, so the JVM model projects to Meta instead of extending it.

22.4. A snapshot of a running JVM

The runtime’s live loader is planned PLANNED. A minimal one fits in a page, and shows the shape:

Listing 123. A snapshot of a module layer (jvm/…​/Snapshot.java)
public static JavaVirtualMachine of(ModuleLayer layer) {
	JvmFactory factory = JvmFactory.eINSTANCE;
	JavaVirtualMachine vm = factory.createJavaVirtualMachine();
	vm.setLive(true);                                                       (1)
	vm.setVmName(System.getProperty("java.vm.name"));
	vm.setVmVersion(System.getProperty("java.vm.version"));
	vm.setSpecificationVersion(System.getProperty("java.specification.version"));

	Layer boot = factory.createLayer();
	boot.setName("boot");
	boot.setBoot(true);
	vm.getLayers().add(boot);

	Map<String, Module> modules = new TreeMap<>();
	for (java.lang.Module running: layer.modules()) {                       (2)
		ModuleDescriptor descriptor = running.getDescriptor();
		Module module = factory.createModule();
		module.setName(running.getName());
		module.setId("jvm:module/" + running.getName());                   (3)
		module.setNamed(true);
		descriptor.rawVersion().ifPresent(module::setVersion);
		if (descriptor.isAutomatic()) {
			module.getModifiers().add(ModuleModifier.AUTOMATIC);
		}
		module.getUses().addAll(new TreeSet<>(descriptor.uses()));
		for (ModuleDescriptor.Provides service: descriptor.provides()) {
			Provides provides = factory.createProvides();
			provides.setServiceName(service.service());
			provides.getProviderNames().addAll(service.providers());
			module.getProvides().add(provides);
		}
		modules.put(module.getName(), module);
	}
	vm.getModules().addAll(modules.values());
	boot.getModules().addAll(modules.values());

	Configuration configuration = layer.configuration();
	for (Module module: modules.values()) {
		ModuleDescriptor descriptor = layer.findModule(module.getName())
				.orElseThrow()
				.getDescriptor();
		for (ModuleDescriptor.Requires declared: descriptor.requires()) {
			Requires requires = factory.createRequires();
			requires.setName(declared.name());
			for (ModuleDescriptor.Requires.Modifier modifier: declared.modifiers()) {
				requires.getModifiers().add(RequiresModifier.valueOf(modifier.name()));
			}
			requires.setModule(modules.get(declared.name()));               (4)
			module.getRequires().add(requires);
		}
		configuration.findModule(module.getName()).ifPresent(resolved -> {  (5)
			for (ResolvedModule read: resolved.reads()) {
				Module target = modules.get(read.name());
				if (target != null) {
					module.getReads().add(target);
				}
			}
		});
	}
	return vm;
}
1 Observed in a running VM, not scanned from jars.
2 What each module declares, from its descriptor.
3 The JVM’s own naming, as the identity of the element.
4 A required module that was not resolved stays unresolved: the declaration is kept, with no target.
5 What resolution made of the declarations: the modules each module reads.

A snapshot is a model, so it is saved as evidence of what ran:

Listing 124. Saving a snapshot and asking it a question
JavaVirtualMachine vm = Snapshot.of(ModuleLayer.boot());

URI uri = URI.createFileURI(directory.resolve("jvm.yml").toString());
Resource resource = NasdanikaResourceSet.createAndConfigure().createResource(uri);
resource.getContents().add(vm);
resource.save(null);                                                    (1)

Map<String, List<String>> implicit = Snapshot.readsWithoutRequires(vm);
assertThat(implicit.get("org.example.jvm")).contains("org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.models.core");
1 A YAML file, next to the build or the release it describes.

The question is ordinary code over the model:

Listing 125. Modules that read what they never required (jvm/…​/Snapshot.java)
/**
 * Modules that read something they never required: by requires transitive, usually.
 */
public static Map<String, List<String>> readsWithoutRequires(JavaVirtualMachine vm) {
	Map<String, List<String>> answer = new TreeMap<>();
	for (Module module: vm.getModules()) {
		Set<Module> required = module.getRequires().stream()
				.map(Requires::getModule)
				.filter(Objects::nonNull)
				.collect(Collectors.toSet());
		List<String> implicit = module.getReads().stream()
				.filter(read -> !required.contains(read))
				.map(Module::getName)
				.sorted()
				.toList();
		if (!implicit.isEmpty()) {
			answer.put(module.getName(), implicit);
		}
	}
	return answer;
}

For the test’s own module layer, the answer includes:

Module Reads without requiring

org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.models.core

emfjson.jackson, io.opentelemetry.api, io.opentelemetry.context, org.eclipse.emf.ecore.xmi

org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.common

emfjson.jackson

org.example.jvm

emfjson.jackson, io.opentelemetry.api, io.opentelemetry.context, org.eclipse.emf.common, org.eclipse.emf.ecore, org.eclipse.emf.ecore.xmi, org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.models.core

Some of this is requires transitive at work: the example requires the JVM model, which requires the core model and EMF transitively. The first row is more interesting. The core model requires only EMF and java.scripting, and yet it reads OpenTelemetry and a JSON library. EMF, OpenTelemetry and emfjson-jackson are automatic modules, jars without a module descriptor, and the module system gives a module that reads one automatic module readability of all of them. No build file says so, and the snapshot shows it in the first query anyone runs.

22.5. Loading

A live loader comes first, before any scanner of jars, because it is smaller and produces a real graph to ask questions of: it walks the boot layer and its parents, reads each module descriptor, takes readability from the configuration, and reflects over loaded types. Where reflection does not reach, as for a field’s constant value, it reads the loaded type’s class file through the JDK’s class file API, which is final since Java 24 and needs no dependency.

A build-time scanner over class files follows, and adds what a running VM cannot show: types that were never loaded. It has to record which release of a multi-release jar it modeled, and take automatic module names from manifests and file names.

22.6. Applications

  • Ask a running process what it is. Logs, metrics, traces and profiles describe behavior over time; none describes composition. The JVM model is the missing view.

  • Deployed versus running. The difference between the dependency tree and the resolved graph, computed rather than argued.

  • Reports that are expensive today. Which class file versions are present, which modules are automatic, which packages are opened for deep reflection and to whom.

  • A join point for telemetry. A stack trace, a JFR event and a span resolve to model elements without a mapping, so a slow span resolves to a method, in a module, from an artifact, owned by a team.

  • Coverage that knows what runs. With a live loader recording what was loaded and coverage attached from builds, two lists appear that a coverage tool alone cannot produce: covered but never loaded, and loaded but not covered.

  • The JVM as files. A snapshot presented as a volume (Chapter 14) and served over WebDAV (Chapter 15) is a running system that an agent reads with the file tools it already has.

Documentation of JVM concepts is meant to be generated, and the specifications and the JDK’s Javadoc are under licenses that do not permit republishing derived text under the runtime’s license. Concepts are not copyrightable and expression is: generated documentation must be original prose, and an assistant describing requires transitive must not reproduce Javadoc it remembers.

Chapter 23. From models to the web

A model that the people who own it cannot read is a private notation. The web is where they read, so the runtime treats web pages and web applications as generation targets, and generates them the way it does everything else: from models, into models, and only then into text.

The whole browser side is generated or served from Java: HTML and Bootstrap for pages, TypeScript and React for applications. A Java developer builds them with Java APIs and models, with no npm, no Node.js and no build step, and with little knowledge of how React works. What runs in the browser can be deployed as static files with no JVM behind it, and still be an application, because React provides the dynamic behavior.

23.1. Pages are models too

Generating HTML by concatenating strings is easy to start and hard to keep correct: escaping, nesting, attribute order, the one closing tag that went missing. The runtime’s generators build a model of the page and let a generator write the text.

Model What it covers

models/html

HTML elements, attributes, text and comments, with a generator that writes HTML text

models/html/bootstrap

Bootstrap 5 semantics: documents with themes, containers, grids, and components for content, navigation, overlays and forms

models/typescript

The declaration surface of TypeScript: packages, modules, declarations and type references, with a generator that writes sources and manages imports

models/react

React components, hooks, contexts and JSX, on top of the TypeScript model

models/react/bootstrap, models/react/flow

Bootstrap components in React, and React Flow diagrams with a simple layered layout

The Bootstrap model describes semantics, not markup: a modal has a title, a size and whether it is centered and scrollable. How that becomes elements, classes, ARIA and data attributes, and ids that Bootstrap’s JavaScript connects, is the business of BootstrapStructure, used by the HTML generator for static pages and by the React generator for components. One model of a page renders both ways.

23.2. A catalog site

The example generates a small site from the library: an index with a table of books, and a page per book with a breadcrumb and its facts.

Listing 126. Generating the site (web/…​/CatalogSite.java)
public static void generate(Library library, Volume volume) throws IOException {
	Volume.Writable site = volume.capability(Volume.Writable.class)
			.orElseThrow(() -> new IOException("Read-only volume"));
	String name = library.getName();
	site.write("index.html", html(page(name, heading(name), table(library)))); (1)
	if (volume.stat("books").isEmpty()) {
		site.createDirectory("books");                                     (2)
	}
	for (Book book: library.getBooks()) {
		site.write("books/" + slug(book.getName()) + ".html", html(page(
				book.getName(),
				breadcrumb(library, book),
				heading(book.getName()),
				facts(book))));
	}
}

private static Content html(BootstrapDocument document) {
	String html = BootstrapStructure.generate(document);                   (3)
	return Content.of(html, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
}
1 Each page is a model of a Bootstrap document, turned into content and written to the volume.
2 File system semantics: a directory is created before files are written into it.
3 The generator interprets the page model and writes HTML.

A page is a document with a theme, a head and a body:

Listing 127. A page (web/…​/CatalogSite.java)
static BootstrapDocument page(String title, Node... contents) {
	BootstrapDocument document = BOOTSTRAP.createBootstrapDocument();
	document.setTheme(Theme.FLATLY);                                       (1)
	document.setLang("en");

	Head head = HTML.createHead();
	head.setTitle(title);
	document.setHead(head);

	Container container = BOOTSTRAP.createContainer();
	container.getClasses().add("my-4");
	container.getContents().addAll(List.of(contents));
	Body body = HTML.createBody();
	body.getContents().add(container);
	document.setBody(body);
	return document;
}
1 A Bootswatch theme, applied by the generator.

The table is a Bootstrap table with badges, built from the library:

Listing 128. A table of books (web/…​/CatalogSite.java)
static Table table(Library library) {
	Table table = CONTENT.createTable();
	table.setStriped(true);
	table.setHover(true);

	TableHead head = HTML.createTableHead();
	head.getRows().add(row(true, text("Title"), text("Year"), text("Genre"), text("Authors")));
	table.setHead(head);

	TableBody body = HTML.createTableBody();
	for (Book book: library.getBooks()) {
		Anchor link = HTML.createAnchor();
		link.setHref("books/" + slug(book.getName()) + ".html");
		link.getContents().add(text(book.getName()));

		Badge genre = CONTENT.createBadge();
		genre.setBg(book.getGenre() == Genre.TECHNOLOGY ? Variant.PRIMARY : Variant.SECONDARY);
		genre.setContent(book.getGenre().getLiteral());

		String authors = book.getAuthors().stream()
				.map(Author::getName)
				.collect(Collectors.joining(", "));
		body.getRows().add(row(
				false,
				link,
				text(String.valueOf(book.getYear())),
				genre,
				text(authors)));
	}
	table.getBodies().add(body);
	return table;
}

The site is written to any writable volume (Chapter 14):

CatalogSite.generate(Samples.library(), Volume.of(directory));

A directory today, an in-memory volume for a test, a Git overlay for a publishing pipeline, or a volume served over HTTP for a preview (Chapter 15): the generator does not know and does not need to.

Writing the page as a model has consequences beyond correctness. The page model can be checked before it is written, by a test or an agent; it can carry markers that point back to the model elements each part was generated from (Chapter 20); and it can be transformed, for example by adding a navigation panel to every page of a site after the pages were generated.

23.3. Navigation

Documentation sites of models need navigation that works for people, crawlers and agents alike. The Bootstrap module’s NavigationTree builds a side panel as nested details and summary elements, which work without JavaScript, so crawlers and agents read the tree as plain links. Branches on the path to the current page are open, and the current item is marked with aria-current="page". For large models, a local tree renders the branches off the path as links without their children, so a page of a model with thousands of elements stays small.

23.4. Applications without npm

A React application is usually a Node.js project: a package manifest, hundreds of packages in node_modules, a bundler and a build. None of it is needed to run React in a browser. Browsers load ES modules natively, an import map in the page resolves bare specifiers such as react to URLs, and a CDN such as esm.sh serves npm packages as ES modules. What remains is the application’s own code, and the runtime generates that from a model.

The example renders the library’s books as a table with a filter:

Listing 129. A component as a model (ui/…​/BookTable.java)
/**
 * A table of books with a filter. The module is not a TSX module, so the generator writes
 * createElement calls that a browser runs as they are.
 */
public static Module module() {
	ComponentDeclaration table = REACT.createComponentDeclaration();
	table.setName("BookTable");
	table.setExported(true);
	table.getParameters().add(parameter("props"));
	table.getHooks().add(state("rows", "setRows", "null"));                       (1)
	table.getHooks().add(state("query", "setQuery", "\"\""));
	table.getHooks().add(effect(                                                 (2)
			"fetch(props.dataUrl).then(response => response.json()).then(setRows);",
			"props.dataUrl"));
	table.getHooks().add(memo("shown",                                           (3)
			"(rows || []).filter(row => matches(row, query))",
			"rows", "query"));

	Input search = HTML.createInput();                                           (4)
	search.setType("search");
	search.setPlaceholder("Filter by title");
	search.getClasses().addAll(List.of("form-control", "mb-3"));
	JsxNode filter = intrinsic(search,
			attribute("value", "query"),
			event("onChange", "event => setQuery(event.target.value)"));

	JsxNode spinner = element(external("Spinner", "react-bootstrap"),          (5)
			literal("animation", "border"));
	JsxNode books = children(
			element(external("Table", "react-bootstrap"), attribute("striped", "true")),
			intrinsic(head("Title", "Year", "Authors")),
			children(
					intrinsic(HTML.createTableBody()),
					iterator("shown", "row", "row.title",                            (6)
							intrinsic(row("row.title", "row.year", "row.authors")))));
	table.setRender(children(tag("div"), filter, conditional("!rows", spinner, books)));

	Module module = TS.createModule();
	module.setName("books");
	module.setPath("modules/books");
	module.setHeader("// Generated from a React model. Do not edit.");
	module.getImports().add(Jsx.namedImport("react-dom/client", "createRoot"));
	module.getDeclarations().add(matches());
	module.getDeclarations().add(table);
	module.getDeclarations().add(mount());
	return module;
}
1 State: the rows once they are loaded, and the text of the filter.
2 An effect that loads the rows from a URL when the component mounts.
3 The rows that match the filter, recomputed only when the rows or the filter change. The test itself is a function of the module, matches.
4 An input of the HTML model, used as a JSX intrinsic, with its value and its change handler as JSX attributes.
5 React Bootstrap components, referenced by name and module. The generator imports them.
6 A row per matching book, keyed by title.

Jsx is a small helper of the example: each of its methods creates one object of the React, TypeScript or HTML model and sets what the call passes. The generator writes this module:
