Listing 130. The generated module (modules/books.js)
// Generated from a React model. Do not edit.

import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client";
import { Spinner, Table } from "react-bootstrap";
import { createElement, useState, useEffect, useMemo } from "react";

function matches(row, query) {
  return row.title.toLowerCase().includes(query.toLowerCase());
}

export function BookTable(props) {
  const [rows, setRows] = useState(null);
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
  useEffect(() => {
    fetch(props.dataUrl).then(response => response.json()).then(setRows);
  }, [props.dataUrl]);
  const shown = useMemo(() => ((rows || []).filter(row => matches(row, query))), [rows, query]);
  return createElement("div", null,
    createElement("input", {
      className: "form-control mb-3",
      type: "search",
      placeholder: "Filter by title",
      value: query,
      onChange: event => setQuery(event.target.value)
    }),
    !rows
      ? createElement(Spinner, { animation: "border" })
      : createElement(Table, { striped: true },
        createElement("thead", null,
          createElement("tr", null,
            createElement("th", null, "Title"),
            createElement("th", null, "Year"),
            createElement("th", null, "Authors"))),
        createElement("tbody", null,
          shown.map(row => createElement("tr", { key: row.title },
            createElement("td", null, row.title),
            createElement("td", null, row.year),
            createElement("td", null, row.authors))))));
}

export function mount(element, dataUrl) {
  createRoot(element).render(createElement(BookTable, { dataUrl }));
}

The imports are computed from the model: createElement and the hooks from react, Spinner and Table from react-bootstrap. Only createRoot, which is used in opaque code, was declared by hand. A module without type annotations is plain JavaScript, so the browser runs what the generator wrote, as it is. The test of the example compares the generated module with the listing above, so the listing is what the generator writes.

The page is a model too:

Listing 131. The page (ui/…​/BookTable.java)
/**
 * The page: Bootstrap's stylesheet, an import map resolving React and React Bootstrap to a
 * CDN, a mount point and a module script. Relative URLs only, so the page works at any
 * address, static or served.
 */
public static Document page() {
	ImportMap importMap = HTML.createImportMap();                               (1)
	importMap.getImports().put("react", ESM + "react@" + REACT_VERSION);
	importMap.getImports().put("react/jsx-runtime",
			ESM + "react@" + REACT_VERSION + "/jsx-runtime");
	importMap.getImports().put("react-dom",
			ESM + "react-dom@" + REACT_VERSION + "?external=react");
	importMap.getImports().put("react-dom/client",
			ESM + "react-dom@" + REACT_VERSION + "/client?external=react");
	importMap.getImports().put("react-bootstrap",
			ESM + "react-bootstrap@2.10.10?external=react,react-dom");

	Head head = HTML.createHead();
	head.setTitle("Books");
	head.getMetas().add(viewport());
	head.getStylesheets().add(stylesheet(BOOTSTRAP_CSS));
	head.setImportMap(importMap);

	Div root = HTML.createDiv();
	root.setId("root");
	Script script = HTML.createScript();                                        (2)
	script.setModule(true);
	script.setContent("""

			import { mount } from "./%s";
			mount(document.getElementById("root"), "%s");
			""".formatted(MODULE, DATA));

	Main main = HTML.createMain();
	main.getClasses().addAll(List.of("container", "py-4"));
	main.getContents().add(heading("Books"));
	main.getContents().add(root);
	Body body = HTML.createBody();
	body.getContents().add(main);
	body.getContents().add(script);

	Document page = HTML.createDocument();
	page.setLang("en");
	page.setHead(head);
	page.setBody(body);
	return page;
}
1 The import map resolves bare specifiers to the CDN. It is the only place where the CDN is named.
2 A module script that mounts the component, with the URL of the data.

The generated page, without the stylesheet link and the import map, which are long lines in the file:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <title>Books</title>
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  </head>
  <body>
    <main class="container py-4">
      <h1>Books</h1>
      <div id="root"></div>
    </main>
    <script type="module">
import { mount } from "./modules/books.js";
mount(document.getElementById("root"), "data/books.json");
</script>
  </body>
</html>

23.5. Static or served

The application is three files, written to any writable volume (Chapter 14):

Listing 132. Writing the application (ui/…​/BookTable.java)
/**
 * Writes the application to a writable volume: a directory to copy to a static host, or
 * a volume that the runtime serves. The same bytes either way.
 */
public static void write(Library library, Volume volume) throws IOException {
	Volume.Writable site = volume.capability(Volume.Writable.class)
			.orElseThrow(() -> new IOException("Read-only volume"));
	String html = new Generator().generate(page()) + "\n";
	String javaScript = new ReactGenerator().generate(module());
	site.write(PAGE, Content.of(html, UTF_8));
	createDirectory(volume, site, "modules");
	site.write(MODULE, Content.of(javaScript, UTF_8));
	createDirectory(volume, site, "data");
	site.write(DATA, Content.of(data(library).toString(2), UTF_8));
}

Written to a directory, it is a static site:

Listing 133. A static deployment
BookTable.write(Samples.library(), Volume.of(directory));                    (1)

assertThat(directory.resolve("index.html")).content()
	.contains("<script type=\"importmap\">");
assertThat(directory.resolve("modules/books.js")).content()
	.contains("export function BookTable(props)");
JSONArray books = new JSONArray(Files.readString(directory.resolve("data/books.json")));
assertThat(books.length()).isEqualTo(8);
1 Any directory: copy it to any static host.

When a browser opens the page, React loads from the CDN, the component fetches data/books.json, and filtering happens in the browser. No JVM runs anywhere. ES modules do not load from file: URLs, so even on a laptop the files need an HTTP server, such as the JDK’s jwebserver, or the runtime’s own handler:

Listing 134. The same files, served
Volume site = Volume.of(directory);
BookTable.write(Samples.library(), site);

var address = new InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0);
HttpServer server = HttpServer.create(address, 0);
server.createContext("/", new VolumeHttpHandler(site));                       (1)
server.start();
try (HttpClient client = HttpClient.newHttpClient()) {
	URI base = URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:" + server.getAddress().getPort() + "/");
	assertThat(contentType(client, base.resolve(BookTable.PAGE))).startsWith("text/html");
	assertThat(contentType(client, base.resolve(BookTable.MODULE)))
		.startsWith("text/javascript");                                          (2)
	assertThat(contentType(client, base.resolve(BookTable.DATA)))
		.startsWith("application/json");
} finally {
	server.stop(0);
}
1 The volume the application was written to, served by the handler of Chapter 15.
2 Media types come from the extensions, as browsers require for modules.

The bytes are the same either way, so a preview is the deployment. Served with data computed for each request, the same kind of application shows live data: the runtime’s own tests serve a table of the properties of the running JVM that way.

23.6. The TypeScript and React models

The TypeScript model covers the declaration surface: packages, modules, interfaces, classes, functions, type aliases, and the type references between them. Bodies are opaque code blocks, which carry references to the declarations they use. Its generator writes sources to a volume of text (Chapter 14) and owns import management, the hardest part of emitting TypeScript correctly: it walks the type references reachable from each module, resolves each to the module that declares it, computes the module specifier, decides whether an import can be import type, and aliases names that would collide. The model is write-only by design; nothing in the runtime parses TypeScript.

The React model adds what the TypeScript model leaves opaque: components, hooks, contexts and JSX. ReactGenerator writes JSX into .tsx modules compiled with the automatic runtime, or, as in the example, createElement calls into plain JavaScript modules that a browser runs without a build step. HTML elements used in JSX are interpreted by the same structure the HTML generator uses, with attributes mapped to React props, so a page model and a component model mean the same markup. The React Bootstrap and React Flow models describe those libraries' components as annotated classes, so using a component library takes no generator code.

Generating through models, not templates, keeps three things that templates lose:

  • Imports, computed from references instead of maintained by hand.

  • Provenance, from a source element through every intermediate model to the generated code.

  • Structure: generated code that can be diffed, analyzed and reported on as a model, not compared as text.

23.7. Walking through an application

A generated application is checked the way a user checks it: in a browser. The playwright module drives one with Playwright for Java, against a server of the harness module (Chapter 15), in the server’s trace:

  • Browsing.inBrowser(server, session → …​) launches Chromium, an installed Chrome or Edge or Playwright’s own, with relative URLs resolving against the server, and runs the session in a Browser span.

  • session.step(name, () → …​) runs a step in a span, with screenshots before and after it, or of the failure, recorded as log records in the step with the image files' paths.

  • Every request the browser sends to the server carries the step’s span, so the server’s spans are children of the step that caused them; requests to content delivery networks get no trace context.

  • session.narrate(text), or a step’s narration, records what a person would say about the step as a log record, in order with the screenshots: the script of a video, the text of a guide.

  • Console messages and uncaught page errors are log records too.

  • With a video file in the options, the session is recorded as a video, and each step, screenshot and narration line carries its offset into it, so the video and the trace explain each other: in the video, a list changes at some second; the trace says which step was running then and which request the server was handling.

The runtime’s React model tests walk through a generated application, a table of the running JVM’s properties: generated from models, served by a harness server, opened and reloaded in Chrome, and recorded with a Recording as one model in which each step has its screenshots and the server’s spans for the page, the module and the data. A recorded walk-through is a user guide and a demo video in waiting: steps, pictures, and what the server did, regenerated with every build; with the steps narrated, the trace is also the script (Chapter 26). A session needs no server: the Draw.io rendering module runs Draw.io’s viewer in one, a page per step, to render diagrams as images and videos (Chapter 25). The Zephyr Book Walk-throughs with Playwright covers the module in depth.

23.8. JavaScript as another bytecode

With the TypeScript and React models in place, JavaScript is a generation target: the format a machine executes, written by a tool from a source people work in, as bytecode is written by a compiler. The idea is not new. Scott Hanselman called JavaScript the assembly language of the web in 2011, Google Web Toolkit compiled Java to JavaScript in 2006, and J2CL, TeaVM, Kotlin/JS and Scala.js do it today. The runtime’s route is different, generation from models into readable modules rather than compilation of Java code, but the destination is the same: people work on the JVM, and the browser gets JavaScript.

That raises a question of direction, and it deserves a careful answer. On the JVM, with these generators, a team can do most of what it would do with Node.js to build and serve a browser application: generate modules and pages, serve them, test them, and deploy them as static files. Not all of it: bundlers, server-side rendering of React, and the npm tool chain of linters and component test runners run on Node.js, and only some of them run on the JVM, through GraalJS. The other direction works as text, since a Node.js program can write Java source as easily as Java writes JavaScript. What it cannot do is be the JVM: it has no checked generic declarations to match at run time (Chapter 8), and it cannot load the JVM’s libraries, EMF, JDBC drivers and the rest of the enterprise ecosystem, into its own process. So the asymmetry is real but narrower than "the JVM can do everything Node.js can": the JVM can generate and host most of a browser application, while Node.js can generate Java but cannot host what Java runs on.

Verify Hanselman’s 2011 post, "JavaScript is Assembly Language for the Web", before publishing.

23.9. What comes next

The next chapter assembles user interfaces from views chosen by the class of what they show: the polymorphic UI (Chapter 24). On the roadmap PLANNED:

  • Vendored modules, copied into the application’s volume with an import map pointing at them, for offline and closed networks.

  • Documentation sites for models: a page per element with its documentation, its neighbors, provenance links and a diagram of its neighborhood, for any model built on the core model.

  • The polymorphic UI in React: a browser application that renders any model, and live telemetry, from the runtime’s HTTP server. Meta’s projection to TypeScript gives it runtime type information (Chapter 21).

The module models/typescript/ecore, which generates TypeScript packages from EMF packages, is commented out of the build and still uses the previous generation’s package org.nasdanika.models.typescript.ecore and module org.nasdanika.common.

Chapter 24. Polymorphic UI

A model with fifty classes should not need fifty screens. A polymorphic user interface renders each element with the view of its class, the way a method call dispatches on the class of its receiver. The benefit is the same as for methods: the general case is written once, and the specific cases only where they earn their place.

This chapter builds one from pieces the runtime already has: the capability framework finds the views, the class hierarchy of the model orders them, and the HTML and Bootstrap models of Chapter 23 are what they produce.

A user interface, in this book, is wherever a person or an agent exchanges information with a system, even in one direction: a page, a PDF, Markdown or AsciiDoc that an agent reads, a tool it calls. With more than one format, the dispatch has two dimensions, the class of the element and the format asked for, which makes it double dispatch, the job the visitor pattern does for code. This chapter works in one format, HTML.

24.1. Where the idea comes from

The idea is old, and its history is the best argument for it.

JFace. An Eclipse tree or table viewer does not know what it displays. A content provider tells it the children of an element; a label provider tells it the text and the icon. One viewer shows anything for which those two can answer.

EMF.Edit. For every class of a model, EMF generates an item provider that is both the content and the label provider of its instances, along with a property source for the property sheet. Adapter factories find the item provider of an object’s class, and a reflective item provider answers for classes without one. That is how a tree editor, generated in minutes, edits any Ecore model.

Naked Objects. Richard Pawson argued in the early 2000s that a user interface should be generated by reflection over the domain object model, and that a domain model from which no decent interface can be generated is probably the problem. I saw it presented at a conference at the time, and the idea stayed with me. It lives on as Apache Causeway, and the reflective interface has been rediscovered roughly once per platform generation since: Django’s admin, JSON Forms, the metadata-driven screens of the large business platforms.

Three things are different here:

  • The model is the source, and code is one of its outputs. Naked Objects derives the model from the classes; here the classes, the documentation, the schemas and the user interface all come from the model.

  • Views are contributions. A module adds views by declaring them, and the capability framework finds them, the way EMF.Edit finds item providers through adapter factories, with no registry to maintain.

  • The output is a page model, rendered to static HTML or to React components that run in a browser with no JVM behind them (Chapter 23).

24.2. Dispatch on the class of an element

Method dispatch looks for the most specific implementation along a class hierarchy. A model’s class hierarchy is explicit and reflective, and it has multiple inheritance: a library’s Book extends the core model’s NamedElement, which extends ModelElement, which mixes in identity, documentation and provenance. The order in which to ask is the class itself, then its superclasses, nearest first:

Listing 135. The lineage of a book
assertThat(Util.lineage(LibraryPackage.Literals.BOOK)).containsExactly(
		LibraryPackage.Literals.BOOK,
		CorePackage.Literals.NAMED_ELEMENT,
		CorePackage.Literals.MODEL_ELEMENT,
		CorePackage.Literals.STRING_IDENTITY,
		CorePackage.Literals.REFERRABLE, 
		CorePackage.Literals.DOCUMENTED,
		CorePackage.Literals.MARKED);

The lineage is breadth-first, and superclasses at the same distance keep their declaration order, so a mix-in declared first is asked first. The HTML model uses the same walk on a small scale: a Bootstrap element finds its tag name in the nearest class, along that order, whose annotation names one.

24.3. Views are capabilities

A view is asked for with a requirement naming exactly one class:

Listing 136. The requirement (ui/…​/ViewOf.java)
/**
 * A requirement for the view of exactly one class. Factories answer it only for their own
 * class, so a resolver can ask from the most specific class to the most general, and the
 * first answer is the most specific view.
 */
public record ViewOf(EClass eClass) {
}

A view is a capability factory that answers it for its own class and provides itself:

Listing 137. A view (ui/…​/View.java)
/**
 * The view of the instances of one class, contributed as a capability factory. It answers
 * the requirement for a view of its class, and the capability it provides is itself.
 */
public abstract class View<T extends EObject> implements CapabilityFactory<ViewOf, View<?>> {

	private final EClass eClass;

	protected View(EClass eClass) {
		this.eClass = eClass;
	}

	/**
	 * The page model of an element. Views of the elements it shows come from the resolver.
	 */
	protected abstract Node render(T element, Views views);

	@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
	public Node apply(EObject element, Views views) {
		return render((T) element, views);
	}

	@Override
	public boolean canHandle(Object requirement) {
		return requirement instanceof ViewOf viewOf && viewOf.eClass() == eClass; (1)
	}

	@Override
	public Flow.Publisher<CapabilityProvider<View<?>>> create(
			ViewOf requirement,
			Loader loader,
			Span span,
			Logger logger,
			Meter meter) {
		return Flows.of(CapabilityProvider.<View<?>>of(this));                    (2)
	}
1 Only the requirement for this exact class. A view of NamedElement does not answer for Book; the resolver asks for NamedElement itself when Book has no view.
2 The factory is its own capability.

Asking for exact classes is deliberate. A requirement matching every superclass at once, such as the generic type Function<? super Book, Node>, would leave the choice between the matching views to the order in which capabilities are returned, and that order compares erased types, as the editor’s note of Chapter 8 explains. With one class per requirement, the first answer along the lineage is the most specific view, by construction.

24.4. The resolver

Listing 138. Polymorphic rendering (ui/…​/Views.java)
/**
 * Renders model elements polymorphically: with the view of an element's class, or of its
 * nearest superclass that has one, or with the reflective view of last resort.
 */
public class Views {

	private final CapabilityLoader loader;
	private final Map<EClass, Optional<View<?>>> resolved = new HashMap<>();

	public Views(CapabilityLoader loader) {
		this.loader = loader;
	}

	public Node render(EObject element) {
		for (EClass eClass: Util.lineage(element.eClass())) {                   (1)
			Optional<View<?>> view = resolved.computeIfAbsent(                  (2)
					eClass,
					key -> Optional.ofNullable(loader.<View<?>>loadOne(new ViewOf(key))));
			if (view.isPresent()) {
				return view.get().apply(element, this);                         (3)
			}
		}
		return Properties.render(element, this);                               (4)
	}

}
1 The element’s class first, then its superclasses, nearest first.
2 One resolution per class, remembered: the view of a class does not change while a page is rendered.
3 The first view found renders the element. A view renders what the element shows, books in a library, by calling the resolver again.
4 No view anywhere along the lineage: the reflective view of last resort.

24.5. Views of the library

A library is rendered by its own view, which does not know what a book or an author looks like:

Listing 139. The library (ui/…​/LibraryView.java)
/**
 * A library: its name, a card per book, and its authors. What a book or an author looks like
 * is not this view's business: it asks the resolver.
 */
public class LibraryView extends View<Library> {

	public LibraryView() {
		super(LibraryPackage.Literals.LIBRARY);
	}

	@Override
	protected Node render(Library library, Views views) {
		Div page = HTML.createDiv();
		page.getContents().add(heading(1, library.getName()));

		Div books = HTML.createDiv();
		books.getClasses().addAll(List.of("d-grid", "gap-3", "mb-4"));
		for (Book book: library.getBooks()) {
			books.getContents().add(views.render(book));                         (1)
		}
		page.getContents().add(books);

		page.getContents().add(heading(2, "Authors"));
		for (Author author: library.getAuthors()) {
			page.getContents().add(views.render(author));                        (2)
		}
		return page;
	}
1 A book’s view comes from the resolver.
2 So does an author’s. The library model has no view of its own for authors, so the view of NamedElement renders them.
Listing 140. A book (ui/…​/BookCard.java)
/**
 * A book as a Bootstrap card.
 */
public class BookCard extends View<Book> {

	public BookCard() {
		super(LibraryPackage.Literals.BOOK);
	}

	@Override
	protected Node render(Book book, Views views) {
		CardTitle title = CONTENT.createCardTitle();
		title.setContent(book.getName());
		CardSubtitle subtitle = CONTENT.createCardSubtitle();
		subtitle.setContent(book.getYear() + ", " + book.getGenre().getLiteral().toLowerCase());
		CardText authors = CONTENT.createCardText();
		authors.setContent(book.getAuthors().stream()
				.map(Author::getName)
				.collect(Collectors.joining(", ")));

		CardBody body = CONTENT.createCardBody();
		body.setTitle(title);
		body.setSubtitle(subtitle);
		body.getTexts().add(authors);
		for (Marker marker: book.getMarkers()) {
			body.getContents().add(views.render(marker));                        (1)
		}

		Card card = CONTENT.createCard();
		card.getBodies().add(body);
		return card;
	}

}
1 A marker of the core model has no view at all; the reflective view renders it, inside the card.

The view of NamedElement is written once for the core model, and renders every named element of every model built on it, until a module contributes something more specific:

Listing 141. Anything with a name (ui/…​/NamedElementView.java)
/**
 * Anything with a name, in any model built on the core model: the name, and the
 * documentation if there is any. It renders every named element without a view of its own.
 */
public class NamedElementView extends View<NamedElement> {

	public NamedElementView() {
		super(CorePackage.Literals.NAMED_ELEMENT);
	}

	@Override
	protected Node render(NamedElement element, Views views) {
		Strong name = HTML.createStrong();
		name.getContents().add(text(element.getName()));
		Paragraph paragraph = HTML.createParagraph();
		paragraph.getClasses().add("named-element");
		paragraph.getContents().add(name);
		if (element.getDocumentation() != null) {
			paragraph.getContents().add(text(": " + element.getDocumentation()));
		}
		return paragraph;
	}

}

24.6. The reflective view of last resort

The last resort reads what the metamodel says about the element: its class, and the features it has values for. It is the equivalent of EMF.Edit’s reflective item provider and property sheet:

Listing 142. The reflective view (ui/…​/Properties.java)
/**
 * A table of the element's class and of the features it has values for.
 */
static Node render(EObject element, Views views) {
	TableBody body = HTML.createTableBody();
	body.getRows().add(row(text("Class"), text(element.eClass().getName())));
	for (EStructuralFeature feature: element.eClass().getEAllStructuralFeatures()) {
		if (element.eIsSet(feature)) {
			body.getRows().add(row(text(feature.getName()), value(element, feature, views)));
		}
	}
	Table table = CONTENT.createTable();
	table.setSize(Size.SM);
	table.getClasses().add("properties");
	table.getBodies().add(body);
	return table;
}

private static Node value(EObject element, EStructuralFeature feature, Views views) {
	Object value = element.eGet(feature);
	List<?> values = value instanceof Collection<?> many ? List.copyOf(many) : List.of(value);
	if (feature instanceof EReference reference && reference.isContainment()) {
		Div contents = HTML.createDiv();
		for (Object child: values) {
			contents.getContents().add(views.render((EObject) child));       (1)
		}
		return contents;
	}
	return text(values.stream().map(Properties::label).collect(Collectors.joining(", ")));
}
1 Contained objects are rendered polymorphically too, so a reflective view can contain specific ones, and the other way around.

24.7. Contributing views

Views are declared like any capability factory:

Listing 143. The module (ui/…​/module-info.java)
import org.example.ui.BookCard;
import org.example.ui.LibraryView;
import org.example.ui.NamedElementView;
import org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.common.capability.CapabilityFactory;

module org.example.ui {

	requires transitive org.example.library;
	requires transitive org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.models.html.bootstrap;
	requires transitive org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.models.react;
	requires transitive org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.volume;
	requires org.json;

	exports org.example.ui;

	provides CapabilityFactory with (1)
		LibraryView,
		BookCard,
		NamedElementView;

}
1 Declaration is registration (Chapter 2). Another module can contribute a view of Author, or a better view of Book, without changing this one or the pages that use it.

24.8. Putting it together

Listing 144. Rendering a library polymorphically
Library library = Samples.library();
Marker marker = CoreFactory.eINSTANCE.createMarker();
marker.setLocation("acquisitions.csv");
marker.setPosition("42");
book(library, "Domain-Driven Design").getMarkers().add(marker);

Views views = new Views(CapabilityLoader.getInstance());                    (1)
String html = BootstrapStructure.generate(views.render(library));

assertThat(html)
	.contains("<h1>A Modeler's Shelf</h1>")                                 (2)
	.contains("<h5 class=\"card-title\">Domain-Driven Design</h5>")         (3)
	.contains("<p class=\"named-element\"><strong>Eric Evans</strong></p>") (4)
	.contains("<th>location</th>")                                         (5)
	.contains("acquisitions.csv");
1 A resolver over the capability loader of the module path, which finds the views the module declares.
2 The library: its own view.
3 The books: their own view, a Bootstrap card.
4 The authors: the view of NamedElement, the nearest class along their lineage that has one.
5 The marker: the reflective view.

The book carrying the marker renders as:

<div class="card">

    <h6 class="card-subtitle mb-2 text-body-secondary">2003, technology</h6>
    <p class="card-text">Eric Evans</p>
    <table class="table table-sm properties">
      <tbody>
        <tr>
          <th>Class</th>
          <td>Marker</td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
          <th>location</th>
          <td>acquisitions.csv</td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
          <th>position</th>
          <td>42</td>
        </tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
  </div>
</div>

Objects of classes without generated code are rendered too, because the lineage is that of the class, not of a Java type:

Listing 145. A dynamic object
EClass note = EcoreFactory.eINSTANCE.createEClass();                        (1)
note.setName("Note");
EAttribute text = EcoreFactory.eINSTANCE.createEAttribute();
text.setName("text");
text.setEType(EcorePackage.Literals.ESTRING);
note.getEStructuralFeatures().add(text);
EPackage notes = EcoreFactory.eINSTANCE.createEPackage();
notes.setName("notes");
notes.setNsURI("https://example.org/notes");
notes.getEClassifiers().add(note);

EObject reminder = EcoreUtil.create(note);
reminder.eSet(text, "Return the book by Friday");

String html = BootstrapStructure.generate(
		new Views(CapabilityLoader.getInstance()).render(reminder));
assertThat(html)
	.contains("<td>Note</td>")                                                (2)
	.contains("<td>Return the book by Friday</td>");
1 A class defined at run time, as a vocabulary projected from Meta would be (Chapter 21).
2 No view along its lineage, so the reflective view shows it.

24.9. Mix-ins and sections

Because the lineage walks every superclass, a view can be contributed for a mix-in. A view of Documented renders the documentation of anything documented that has no nearer view; a view of Marked renders provenance.

The resolver above stops at the first view, which suits a card or a row. A page can instead collect a view from every level of the lineage, nearest first: the fields of the class itself, then the documentation section contributed for Documented, then the provenance section for Marked. Each class and each mix-in contributes what it knows, and a new mix-in brings its section to every page of every class that uses it. This is multiple inheritance applied to user interfaces, and it is a small change to the resolver: ask for all the views at each level instead of the first one.

24.10. Static pages, and the browser

The pages in this chapter are static HTML, generated once and served by anything. The same views can render inside React components: an Intrinsic places an element of the HTML model in a component, and JsxContent places JSX inside an HTML element, so the page model of a view becomes part of an application that runs in a browser (Chapter 23).

Every resolution is a capability resolution, so it is traced: the telemetry of a page generation says which view rendered which element.

24.11. What comes next

The pieces of this chapter are available in the runtime; the example assembles them. The roadmap turns them into a product PLANNED:

  • The polymorphic UI in a terminal. The same dispatch with views that draw in a terminal, so that any model element gets a tree and a property sheet where developers already work.

  • The polymorphic UI in React. A browser application that renders any model this way: a property sheet for every object, with categories from the annotations Xcore models already carry, and views resolved by class through the capability framework.

  • More formats. The same dispatch for Markdown and AsciiDoc, which agents read, and later for MCP and query languages. A normative document, such as a standard or a policy, then comes out as a PDF for people and AsciiDoc for agents from one source, so the two cannot disagree.

  • Telemetry and JVM browsing, with the generic views first and specific views, such as a timeline for spans, where the generic ones are visibly weak.

  • Documentation sites, where every element of every model gets a page assembled from the views and sections along its lineage, and from its micro-wiki (Chapter 20).

Chapter 25. Diagrams

Most diagrams in an organization are drawn once, looked at a few times, and left to drift away from what they describe. They do not have to be. A diagram drawn in a tool people already use is a structured document: shapes with names, properties, tooltips and links, joined by connections and nested in containers. The runtime treats it as one, in both directions: a diagram is a source that models are read from, and a target that models are drawn into.

I once moved a software delivery process of about a hundred activities from a drawing into a diagram editor backed by a model of what is done, by whom, in which phase and with what (Prior art, first-hand). The drawing and the editor showed the same boxes. Only the editor could say which activities a role performs or what a phase needs, and that difference is what this chapter is about.

This chapter introduces seven modules that do it, and an example that generates a diagram of the library’s citations, lays it out, saves it as a Draw.io file, reads it back as a diagram, checks it against the library, and draws it as SVG.

25.1. A continuum, not a choice

Between a picture and a model there is a continuum. At one end, a diagram is a picture: boxes and lines that mean something to the people who drew them. Add names and tooltips, and it is documentation. Add properties, and programs can read it: a property names the system a shape stands for, its owner, the class of model element it is. At the far end, a diagram is the source of a model, and the people who own the domain keep it in a tool they already know, while programs check it, generate from it and keep it in step with what it describes.

Each diagram should sit on the continuum where its structure pays for itself, and move right when it needs to. That is the principle of more structure with less effort applied to pictures (Chapter 2): nobody has to learn a modeling tool to contribute, and nothing has to be redrawn when a diagram starts to matter.

The other direction matters as much. A model that nobody can see is a private notation (Chapter 23), and a diagram generated from a model is the quickest way to show it, provided that it is laid out well enough to read without anyone moving a box.

25.2. What a good diagram is worth

A diagram is a message, and most of its cost is the reader’s time. An icon for a well-known element, a database, a queue, a person, is recognized before its label is read. A layout that keeps related things together and lines from crossing is understood in seconds; the same boxes placed at random take minutes, and some readers give up. Multiplied by every reader and every reading, a good diagram is one of the cheapest efficiencies an enterprise has (Chapter 1).

Many people say diagrams are not worth the trouble. Some of them are the fox in Aesop’s fable, who could not reach the grapes and decided they were sour. Good diagrams have been expensive to draw and more expensive to keep current, so dismissing them was cheaper than making them. Generated from models and laid out automatically, they are no longer out of reach.

25.3. Two layers, seven modules

The Draw.io API and its rendering. drawio reads, navigates, changes and writes Draw.io documents in plain Java: documents, pages, layers, nodes and connections, properties and placeholders, selectors, links across pages and documents, and styles. It reads and writes diagrams embedded in PNG images, which is how a figure can be its own source: a reader sees a picture, Draw.io opens the same file for editing, and a program loads it. drawio-playwright renders pages with Draw.io’s own viewer in a browser driven by the playwright module, in a session that needs no server (Chapter 23): PNG and SVG images with the page embedded, pages after a program has clicked their shapes to run custom actions, and videos of pages shown in sequence, each rendering in a span. It is a module of its own so that drawio stays light: Playwright and a browser come only with it.

The models. They form one family, and most of its value comes from the supertypes:

  • The diagram model, models/diagram, has what every notation has: elements with ids, names, documentation and attributes (Chapter 20); nodes with bounds and ports; connections with waypoints; layers; nesting; and the elements of other models that a shape depicts, its semantic elements.

  • Layout with ELK, models/diagram/elk, places the nodes and routes the connections of any diagram of the model with the Eclipse Layout Kernel: its layered, tree, force and radial algorithms, with options set in code or as attributes of the elements.

  • The presentation model, models/presentation SKETCH, extends the diagram model with decks: a presentation is a diagram of slides, and a slide is a diagram of shapes, text, images, tables and connectors.

  • The Draw.io model, models/drawio, extends both: a document is a presentation, a page is a slide, and its layers, nodes and connections are their diagram namesakes. A .drawio file, or a PNG or SVG image that Draw.io exported with the diagram in it, loads into any resource set as a model and saves back.

  • The SVG model, models/svg, is a subset of SVG as EMF, with SVG’s own namespace, so that a resource of it is an SVG file. It is the vector target for generated diagrams, the same in HTML, PDF and EPUB.

So a program written against the diagram model reads a Draw.io page without knowing it is one, and ELK lays out a Draw.io page because it lays out diagrams. The example shows both.

25.4. A diagram generated from a model

The example’s diagram shows which books of the library cite which: a node per book that cites or is cited, and a connection per citation. It is built as a Draw.io model from the start, because a Draw.io page is a diagram, so nothing has to be converted later:

Listing 146. The citations as a Draw.io document (diagram/…​/Citations.java)
/**
 * A Draw.io document with one page of the library's citations.
 */
public static Document diagram(Library library) {
	DrawioFactory factory = DrawioFactory.eINSTANCE;
	Document document = factory.createDocument();
	Page page = factory.createPage();
	page.setId("citations");
	page.setName("Citations");
	page.getAttributes().put("elk.direction", "DOWN");                   (1)
	document.getChildren().add(page);
	Layer layer = factory.createLayer();
	page.getChildren().add(layer);

	Map<Book, org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.models.drawio.Node> nodes = new LinkedHashMap<>();
	for (Book book : library.getBooks()) {
		if (book.getCites().isEmpty() && cited(library, book).isEmpty()) {
			continue;
		}
		var node = factory.createNode();
		node.setId("book-" + library.getBooks().indexOf(book));
		node.setName(book.getName());
		node.setDocumentation(book.getYear() + ", " + authors(book));      (2)
		node.getAttributes().put(BOOK, book.getName());                    (3)
		node.getSemanticElements().add(book);                              (4)
		node.getStyle().put("rounded", "1");
		node.getStyle().put("fillColor", "#dae8fc");
		node.getStyle().put("strokeColor", "#6c8ebf");
		layer.getChildren().add(node);
		nodes.put(book, node);
	}
	for (Book book : nodes.keySet()) {
		for (Book cited : book.getCites()) {
			var connection = factory.createConnection();
			connection.setId(nodes.get(book).getId() + "-cites-" + nodes.get(cited).getId());
			connection.setSource(nodes.get(book));
			connection.setTarget(nodes.get(cited));
			connection.getStyle().put("endArrow", "open");
			layer.getChildren().add(connection);
		}
	}
	return document;
}
1 A layout option of ELK, as an attribute of the page. Attributes of elements override the options set in code, so a diagram can carry its own layout preferences.
2 The documentation of an element is its tooltip in Draw.io.
3 An attribute that names the book. It is written to the file as a property of the shape, so it survives a round trip through Draw.io, where people can see and change it.
4 The book the node depicts, as a semantic element: a reference to an object of another model. It lives in memory and is not written to the Draw.io file; the attribute is how the reference is restored after loading.

The nodes have no bounds and the connections no routes. That is the layout’s job:

Listing 147. Laid out and saved (diagram/…​/TestCitations.java)
Document document = Citations.diagram(library);
Page page = document.getPages().getFirst();
new ElkLayout().layout(page);                                               (1)

ResourceSet resourceSet = NasdanikaResourceSet.createAndConfigure();
Resource drawio = resourceSet.createResource(uri("citations.drawio"));    (2)
drawio.getContents().add(document);
drawio.save(null);
1 ELK places the nodes, sizes them to fit their names, routes the connections, and writes bounds and waypoints back into the diagram, in an ELK Layout span with the numbers of nodes and edges.
2 The Draw.io model contributes a resource factory for .drawio files to every resource set, so saving a document is saving a resource (Chapter 7).

The file opens in Draw.io as a diagram anyone can edit, with the book of each shape among its properties.

25.5. Read back, and checked

A person rearranges the diagram, adds a citation, or reverses an arrow by mistake. The program reads the file back and checks it against the library. The check is written against the diagram model alone, so it works on a Draw.io page, and would work on any notation that maps to the diagram model:

Listing 148. Mapping nodes to books and checking connections (diagram/…​/Citations.java)
/**
 * Maps the nodes of a diagram to the books they depict, by the book attribute, and returns
 * the citations the diagram shows that the library does not have.
 */
public static List<String> check(DiagramElement diagram, Library library) {
	Map<String, Book> books = new LinkedHashMap<>();
	library.getBooks().forEach(book -> books.put(book.getName(), book));
	List<String> problems = new ArrayList<>();
	for (EObject element : contents(diagram)) {
		if (element instanceof Node node && node.getAttributes().containsKey(BOOK)) {
			Book book = books.get(node.getAttributes().get(BOOK));
			if (book == null) {
				problems.add("No book " + node.getAttributes().get(BOOK));
			} else {
				node.getSemanticElements().add(book);                      (1)
			}
		}
	}
	for (EObject element : contents(diagram)) {
		if (element instanceof Connection connection) {
			Book source = book(connection.getSource());
			Book target = book(connection.getTarget());
			if (source != null && target != null && !source.getCites().contains(target)) {
				problems.add(source.getName() + " does not cite " + target.getName()); (2)
			}
		}
	}
	return problems;
}
1 A node becomes a depiction of a book again: the attribute names it, and the book becomes the node’s semantic element.
2 A connection between two books must be a citation in the library. The check reports what the diagram shows and the model does not have.
Listing 149. Reading the file back as a diagram (diagram/…​/TestCitations.java)
Resource loaded = NasdanikaResourceSet.createAndConfigure()
	.getResource(uri("citations.drawio"), true);
DiagramElement diagram = (DiagramElement) loaded.getContents().getFirst(); (1)
assertThat(Citations.check(diagram, library)).isEmpty();

Connection connection = all(diagram, Connection.class).getFirst();
Connectable source = connection.getSource();
connection.setSource(connection.getTarget());                             (2)
connection.setTarget(source);
assertThat(Citations.check(diagram, library)).containsExactly(
		connection.getSource().getName() + " does not cite " + source.getName()); (3)
1 The loaded Draw.io document, used as a DiagramElement of the diagram model.
2 What a person might do in Draw.io: reverse an arrow.
3 The check names the citation that does not exist.

The direction can also be turned around. A diagram drawn first, with properties that name classes and features, becomes the source of a model; the Zephyr Book Diagram Model does that with the figure of its own model, drawn in Draw.io, mapped to the metamodel it depicts and checked against it.

25.6. Drawn as SVG

The same laid-out page draws as SVG through the SVG model. The drawing is written against the diagram model too, and short, because ELK has done the hard part:

Listing 150. A diagram drawn as SVG (diagram/…​/SvgDrawing.java)
public static Svg draw(DiagramElement diagram) {
	SvgFactory factory = SvgFactory.eINSTANCE;
	Svg svg = factory.createSvg();
	svg.setFontFamily("Noto Sans, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif");
	svg.setFontSize("12");
	svg.add(arrowhead());
	double width = 0;
	double height = 0;
	for (EObject element : (Iterable<EObject>) diagram::eAllContents) {
		if (element instanceof Node node && !(node instanceof Label)) {          (1)
			Bounds b = node.getBounds();
			width = Math.max(width, b.getX() + b.getWidth());
			height = Math.max(height, b.getY() + b.getHeight());
			G g = svg.add(factory.createG());
			if (node.getDocumentation() != null) {
				g.add(factory.createTitle()).setValue(node.getDocumentation());     (2)
			}
			Rect rect = g.add(factory.createRect());
			rect.setX(round(MARGIN + b.getX()));
			rect.setY(round(MARGIN + b.getY()));
			rect.setWidth(round(b.getWidth()));
			rect.setHeight(round(b.getHeight()));
			rect.setRx(6);
			rect.setFill("#dae8fc");
			rect.setStroke("#6c8ebf");
			Text text = g.add(factory.createText());
			text.setX(number(MARGIN + b.getX() + b.getWidth() / 2));
			text.setY(number(MARGIN + b.getY() + b.getHeight() / 2 + 4));
			text.setTextAnchor("middle");
			text.addText(node.getName());
		} else if (element instanceof Connection connection) {                   (3)
			Polyline line = svg.add(factory.createPolyline());
			line.setPoints(connection.getWaypoints()
				.stream()
				.map(p -> number(MARGIN + p.getX()) + "," + number(MARGIN + p.getY()))
				.collect(Collectors.joining(" ")));
			line.setFill("none");
			line.setStroke("#333333");
			line.setMarkerEnd("url(#arrow)");
		}
	}
	svg.setWidth(number(width + 2 * MARGIN));
	svg.setHeight(number(height + 2 * MARGIN));
	svg.setViewBox("0 0 " + svg.getWidth() + " " + svg.getHeight());
	return svg;
}
1 Every node has bounds, from ELK: a rounded rectangle with the name in the middle. A label of a connection is a node too, and is not drawn here.
2 The documentation becomes an SVG title, which browsers show as a tooltip.
3 The waypoints of a connection, from ELK, become a polyline with an arrowhead.
Listing 151. Saving the drawing (diagram/…​/TestCitations.java)
Svg svg = SvgDrawing.draw(page);
Resource image = resourceSet.createResource(uri("citations.svg"));       (1)
image.getContents().add(svg);
image.save(null);
1 The SVG model contributes a resource factory for .svg files, so an SVG drawing is saved, and loaded, like any other model.
Figure 8. The library’s citations, generated, laid out with ELK and drawn as SVG by the example

The figure is a copy of the drawing, kept with the example’s test resources. The test loads it back as an SVG model and fails if it no longer shows the books the diagram does, so a figure that no longer matches its example stops the build, like a listing. Opened on its own in a browser, the SVG file shows each book’s year and authors as a tooltip.

25.7. The Zephyr Books

Each of these modules is documented in depth in a Zephyr Book (The Nasdanika Zephyr Books):

  • Draw.io, for drawio and drawio-playwright: the visual communication continuum, the API, and rendering with Draw.io’s viewer.

  • Draw.io Model, for models/drawio: loading, saving and generating Draw.io documents as models, with a diagram of the running JVM’s modules generated, laid out with ELK and rendered by Draw.io’s viewer.

  • Diagram Model, for models/diagram: diagrams as data, stored as YAML, converted from Draw.io and mapped to the models they depict.

  • Diagram Layout with ELK, for models/diagram/elk: layout options, diagrams of Ecore models, and rendering with React Flow and Draw.io.

  • SVG Model, for models/svg: SVG as a model, and diagrams laid out with ELK drawn as SVG, every shape a link and every documented shape a tooltip.

  • Presentation Model, for models/presentation: decks, slides, masters, shapes, text, tables, connectors and speaker notes as a model on the diagram model, because a slide is a diagram.

25.8. What comes next

On the roadmap PLANNED, as the Zephyr Books describe it:

  • Mapping to models by properties, as Nasdanika core’s semantic mapping does: element properties that name classes and features, so that a diagram loaded into a resource set is a model without code like this chapter’s.

  • Merging generated and arranged diagrams: a diagram generated from a model and arranged by a person, regenerated when the model changes, with the changes merged into the person’s layout by id.

  • Custom actions and animations as objects, so that an animation is generated like a diagram, checked before it renders, and recorded as a video by drawio-playwright.

  • Documented diagrams: a documentation site generated from a diagram, a page per documented element, with the diagram embedded in the viewer and linked to the pages.

  • Executable diagrams: behavior bound to elements, wired along connections by the capability framework, with telemetry that records what the diagram did, the road to the executable graphs of Chapter 26.

  • Figures from Draw.io files: an Asciidoctor extension that renders a .drawio file referenced from a book as the book is built.

Models for Visio, PowerPoint and Excel are postponed.

Part VII: Looking Ahead

Where the runtime is going: what comes next, what is designed, and the North Star that orders the work.

Chapter 26. Roadmap and vision

The previous chapters describe what the runtime does in this edition. This one describes where it is going: the North Star that orders the work, the picture that the pieces fit into, and the increments planned next. Plans change as they meet code, and the runtime’s site and repository are the current record; this chapter is the plan as of November 2026, distilled from the roadmap described in Section 3.8.

26.1. The North Star

The North Star is agentic work on models: executable graphs whose activities include AI agents, operating on bounded, typed models, with transactional safety and state saved to Git, runnable on a laptop, in a container or in a CI pipeline as the same artifact.

Each part of that sentence is a constraint:

  • Executable graphs. Work is a graph of activities with transitions between them, drawn as a diagram and executed as it is drawn.

  • Activities include AI agents. An agent is an activity like any other, with inputs, outputs, tools and a record of what it did.

  • Bounded, typed models. Agents work on models with declared types and documented terms, not on unstructured text, so what they produce can be checked.

  • Transactional safety. An agent’s changes are a change set, reviewed before it is applied and reversible after.

  • State saved to Git. History, review and rollback come from the tool every developer already has.

  • The same artifact everywhere. No server to install and no platform to adopt: what runs on a laptop runs in a pipeline.

Executing a drawing is the oldest idea in this book. My first executable model, in the early 2000s, was XML that described mainframe screens and the flows between them, run by an interpreter; for years after that I built integrations that were drawn and deployed as drawn; and the last time I modeled an integration code base, the model became an engine that executed its processes directly (Prior art, first-hand). What is new is that some activities are agents, and the transactional, Git-backed state around them.

The minimum credible demonstration is one agentic workflow with Git-backed state and transactional rollback, runnable locally and in CI. Everything in this book is on the way there, and useful before it.

The work is ordered by a rule: an increment is admitted when it states the agentic capability it adds, the demonstration that shows it, what it pulls into the runtime, and that it builds green from a clean clone. Code that no increment needs does not move.

26.2. Three planes

The picture the pieces fit into has three planes, separated by volumes:

Figure 9. Three planes, separated by volumes

  • The data plane is where data sits: files, repositories, a running JVM, a Maven repository, an issue tracker, a cloud’s resource graph.

  • The semantic plane is models loaded from the data, with references resolved across sources.

  • The presentation plane is what people and agents read: Markdown, static HTML, JavaScript modules and React applications generated from models.

Reads flow up through volumes, which pull what is asked for. Writes flow down through commands, the control plane, as recorded change sets and commits.

Layer by layer, a stack built this way has data source volumes that serve one resource each, a mount that composes them under paths (jvm, maven, issues), a resource set that resolves references across the mount, and representations chosen by the type of the source object and the requested view, whose output is again a volume: served over HTTP, mounted over WebDAV, or copied into a zip for static hosting. A model object becomes a folder with a static page, an application page, its JSON and its JavaScript module.

26.3. Next: browsing and serving

PLANNED

  • The polymorphic UI in a terminal. The same dispatch (Chapter 24), with views for the terminal beside those for HTML, so that the reflective view gives any model element a tree and a property sheet where developers already work. How this divides into a format and a delivery channel is still to be refined: a terminal draws, and the same command piped to a file or read by an agent gets Markdown or text.

  • The polymorphic UI in React. A browser application over the JavaScript model, which is read-only facades over EMF JSON, with a property sheet per object, categories from the annotations Xcore models already carry, and custom views resolved by capability, with the class of the object as the requirement. It reaches the people a terminal does not.

  • Telemetry and JVM browsing in the React UI, the generic views first, and custom ones where they are visibly needed: spans want a timeline, not a property sheet.

  • Live telemetry in the browser. A subscriber that builds the telemetry model from span events as they happen, exposed as a watchable volume, delivered to the browser with server-sent events, so a running command and a recorded one look the same.

  • http, https and webdav commands over the handlers of Chapter 15, with safe defaults and token authentication.

  • The runtime’s site from its models: pages generated from the models themselves, beside the module pages and the Zephyr Books (The Nasdanika Zephyr Books).

  • Narrated videos from walk-throughs: browser walk-throughs already record narration as log records in their steps, beside the screenshots, so the trace is a storyboard, and can record a silent video of the session with each step’s offset into it (Chapter 23); planned is a narrated video rendered from the storyboard, each screenshot held for as long as its narration takes to speak, the narration spoken by a text-to-speech service, with subtitles; and a video model between the trace and the rendering, for people to trim and annotate (Chapter 23).

  • Documents from walk-throughs: user guides in AsciiDoc and Markdown with the narration as their text, slide decks through the presentation model, and a PowerPoint model when it is built, with the narration in the speaker notes, and sequence diagrams through the diagram model and ELK, generated from the same traces (Chapter 23, Chapter 25).

26.4. Next: more volumes

PLANNED

  • A JVM volume: the JVM model of Chapter 22 served one module per resource, references as proxies resolved on demand.

  • An Azure volume over the plain REST API, where resource ids are already paths and the resource graph reports changes.

  • A Git volume that commits without a clone, over the GitHub and GitLab APIs, and an overlay that keeps writes in memory over a read-only base until they are committed.

  • A caching volume, and a coalescing processor that folds queued changes into the net change per path.

  • Writes through change sets: a client submits a recorded change set to a command inbox, the command side of a CQRS split, and raw bytes remain plain PUT and DELETE.

26.5. Next: the command line

PLANNED

  • nsdk install: extend an installation from Maven coordinates, with profiles for rollback, so new models and commands arrive without rebuilding the distribution.

  • Command lines as models: a Groovy DSL for long command pipelines, and forms generated from command definitions, sub-commands as wizards and mix-ins as sections, with an assistant that proposes a command and a person who keeps or undoes it.

  • Nasdanika Commander: a two-panel file manager in the terminal, over mounted volumes, with the classic function keys and a key bar. View, edit, copy, move and delete across a directory, a running JVM or an organization’s own volumes, where WebDAV would be more than is needed. Contributed commands and syntax highlighting arrive through the capability framework.

  • Narrated video as a model: a video model whose narration and screen events are regenerated as build artifacts. The diagram models it builds on are in this edition (Chapter 25); the presentation model is a sketch, and Visio, PowerPoint and Excel models are postponed.

26.6. The agentic increments

The increments toward the North Star, in their planned order PLANNED:

Capability Demonstration

Conversations with tool calling, recorded as models

An agent loop against Anthropic and OpenAI models with file tools, view, create, replace, insert, glob and grep, over an in-memory volume: a seeded folder and a task in, a diff and a recorded session out

A sandbox

The agent writes to an overlay over a read-only base; the changes are reviewed as a diff, then committed or discarded

Model choice and portable sessions

A saved session is reloaded and continued with another provider, selected by requirement

Declarative tools

Tools from a tool model, with input schemas generated from Meta, and the same tools over the Model Context Protocol from the runtime’s own server

Provenance

Every element an agent produced says which turn and which model produced it, in its markers

Model and graph queries

XPath over models, then a read-only Cypher tool over the graph: the query side

Reviewable writes

A command tool that takes changes, returns a plan, applies and records them: the command side

Executable agentic graphs

A diagram’s transitions as Flow publishers and subscribers, one workflow with one agentic activity running until it settles

Git-backed state and rollback

Durable inboxes, one commit per settled step, a CI trigger, and a reply approved in a pull request, then replayed over the diagram from history

The last two rest on one idea: a commit is a message. Transitions of an executable graph are publishers and subscribers, and payloads are models that serialize to JSON. When an activity sends an event, the event is committed; the commit triggers a pipeline that runs nsdk, which loads the graph, finds the event and delivers it to the receiving activity. When the run settles, its changes are committed and pushed, which may trigger another run elsewhere. Execution is recorded as commits, so it can be inspected, replayed over the diagram, and reverted.

The reactive file system of Chapter 14 is the runner: processors, deterministic or agentic, react to file changes until nothing changes, and one commit records the run.

26.7. Humans at both ends of the line

Draw software development as a line from intent to operation. AI takes the middle, writing and testing code, and pushes people out to both ends.

To the left is intent: the big picture, the vocabulary, the specification. Meta (Chapter 21) and the core model’s documentation are tools for that end.

To the right is assurance: knowing what the system actually did. Telemetry per unit of work saved as models (Chapter 13), snapshots of running systems (Chapter 22), recorded changes in the spans that made them, and live observation (Chapter 12) are tools for that end. The runtime is built for both ends of the line, and for the agents in the middle to be checked from both.

26.8. An architecture method on Git

The same pieces compose into a lightweight architecture method, in the spirit of TOGAF without its ceremony:

  • Git is the architecture repository, with models in it, reviewed as pull requests.

  • Meta models the business concepts and the data, the vocabulary everything else uses.

  • Diagrams model processes and application architecture, as sources, not pictures, and processes may later be executed.

  • Technology stacks are managed as models, with coordinates for variants by region, tier or audience.

  • Agents are grounded in the models, code is generated from them, external systems are wired in through volumes, and snapshots are taken with a copy.

It is the answer to the question the first chapter asked: more structure, for less effort than the tools that make structure expensive.

26.9. The model tower

The runtime’s models are the lower floors of a tower of small models, each extending the ones below instead of reinventing them: the core model, then Meta, the JVM model, telemetry, the file model and the diagram models. Above them sit floors for work and roles, ownership and governance, accounting, kinds that configure, and occupancy, where elements are situated in coordinates such as time, jurisdiction and tier. Each floor enters the runtime when an increment needs it.

26.10. Following along

The runtime is developed in the open at github.com/Nasdanika-SDK/runtime, with its documentation at runtime.sdk.nasdanika.org. The stories behind the design are published at medium.com/nasdanika, and new capabilities are shown as short videos. This book is built with the runtime and versioned with it: when the runtime changes, the next edition’s examples are compiled and tested against it.
