Appendix C: Rules of thumb for people and assistants

This appendix collects the rules the chapters explain, as short imperatives. It is written to be pasted into the instructions of a coding assistant working on a Nasdanika project, and to be read by the people who review its work. Each rule names the chapter that explains it.

C.1. Foundations

  1. Depend on the JDK, EMF core and the OpenTelemetry API, and nothing else, in code meant to be reused. Anything that needs more goes into its own module (Chapter 2).

  2. Use the JDK where it can do the job: java.util.concurrent.Flow, not Reactor; the JDK HTTP client and server; virtual threads; the service loader (Chapter 2).

  3. Derive identities from the module’s path: the Java module org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.<path>, dropping a trailing model, and the nsURI https://runtime.sdk.nasdanika.org/<path> (Chapter 2).

  4. Register by declaring: provides in module-info.java, never registration code (Chapter 2).

  5. Register by type with Java services, such as EPackages and resource set contributors. Use capabilities only for lookups that have a requirement object (Chapter 2, Chapter 10).

  6. Say what is stuck. A failure names what it needed, what it found and what was waiting for what (Chapter 2).

C.2. Models

  1. Write metamodels in Xcore. Give the GenModel’s modelDirectory the Maven module’s directory as its first segment (Chapter 7).

  2. Contribute each package through an EPackage provider in the module’s services package, declared in module-info.java (Chapter 7).

  3. Create resource sets with NasdanikaResourceSet.createAndConfigure(), so that every contributed package, factory and handler is there and every load and save is traced (Chapter 7).

  4. Choose the format with the extension: xmi to interchange, yml and json to read and review, ebin and egz for size (Chapter 7).

  5. Extend the core model’s NamedElement, or ModelElement for elements without names, and get identity, documentation and provenance with it (Chapter 20).

  6. Prefer getReferrers to an opposite reference when the inverse is not part of the model’s meaning (Chapter 20).

  7. Fill markers. A loader, an importer and an agent record where an element came from (Chapter 20).

  8. Keep a vocabulary in Meta when it has to be projected to more than one language (Chapter 21).

  9. Give a model a module of its own, a micro-model, only for a dependency the others do not want, a different set of consumers or a different maturity; otherwise add a nano-model, an .xcore file, to the module it changes with (Chapter 2).

  10. Keep the core concepts of a model on one diagram that a newcomer understands in a quarter of an hour. A model that needs two diagrams is two models (Chapter 2).

  11. Anchor long documentation to the element it describes, a page per element with docRef: a micro-wiki (Chapter 20).

C.3. Types, flows and capabilities

  1. Ask with wildcards, ? extends, at every level that is only read from (Chapter 8, Chapter 17).

  2. Use ground types in requirements: classes, or parameterized types whose arguments are classes or wildcards (Chapter 10).

  3. Remember that objects carry no type arguments: what matches is always what was declared, a return type or a generic supertype (Chapter 8).

  4. Drive asynchronous work that must be ordered and settled with a Pump (Chapter 9).

  5. Emit only complete results from a capability factory: attach what a result needs before emitting it, so that a blocking load returns it whole (Chapter 10, Chapter 16).

  6. Do not return null from a first mapping to skip a source; distinguish sources by type, or use all (Chapter 9).

  7. Explain a resolution with a listener before guessing why a capability is missing (Chapter 10).

C.4. Telemetry

  1. Create one OpenTelemetry instance per unit of work and make it current. Never use GlobalOpenTelemetry (Chapter 11).

  2. Depend on the OpenTelemetry API in instrumented code; only the assembly that runs a unit of work depends on the SDK (Chapter 11, Chapter 13).

  3. Make an operation a span named Type.operation, and emit log records with the Logs API inside it. Do not use span events (Chapter 11).

  4. Put locations and identities in attributes: URIs, lines, names of types. Never put loaded values or credentials there (Chapter 11, Chapter 19).

  5. Report progress with progress log records, at most once a second (Chapter 11).

  6. Carry the context across threads; the pump does it for its subscribers (Chapter 11).

  7. Record changes to models with Changes.record inside the span that makes them, so the change lands in the span (Chapter 13).

  8. Keep the telemetry of units of work worth keeping, as models, next to what they describe (Chapter 13).

C.5. Files and serving

  1. Use string paths, slash-separated and relative to the root, and keep URIs at the edges (Chapter 14).

  2. Report hashes in entries when they are cheap to know (Chapter 14).

  3. Push content with writeTo when you can; pull with openStream only when an input stream is required (Chapter 14).

  4. Produce generated content with Content.ofWriter, so it is written when read, into the reader’s stream (Chapter 14).

  5. Ask a volume for capabilities instead of assuming them (Chapter 14).

  6. Keep model URIs independent of where the bytes are: map them to volumes with VolumeURIHandler (Chapter 14).

  7. Bind servers to the loopback address unless authentication is in front of them (Chapter 15).

C.6. Commands

  1. Extend CommandBase and implement execute(span, logger, meter); write output to spec.commandLine().getOut() (Chapter 16).

  2. Contribute a command with a factory and provides CapabilityFactory, and open the command’s package (Chapter 16).

  3. Declare what a command needs from its parent with @Parent and a generic type, and what it accepts with @SubCommand (Chapter 17).

  4. Ask for an ExecutionSupplier for anything expensive, so the work happens in the command’s span and only if it runs (Chapter 17).

  5. Offer with @Adapter what any child may use; hand down with plain methods what only children written for the parent should use (Chapter 17).

  6. Never let help fail. Wiring is skipped for help; keep constructors and option defaults free of work (Chapter 17).

C.7. User interfaces

  1. Build pages and components as models of HTML, Bootstrap and React, and let generators write the text (Chapter 23).

  2. Deliver applications as static files where you can, and serve the same bytes for previews and live data (Chapter 23).

  3. Resolve the view of an element by its class, nearest first along its lineage, with a reflective view of last resort (Chapter 24).

  4. Ask for the view of an exact class at each level; do not leave the choice between views to the order of capabilities (Chapter 24).

  5. Write the general view once, and specific views only where they earn their place (Chapter 24).

C.8. The Groovy DSL

  1. Set a negative number with upperBound = -1 or upperBound(-1), never upperBound -1 (Chapter 19).

  2. Reference forward with paths; they are resolved after the script has run (Chapter 19).

  3. Prefix a path with ./ when a local name clashes with a class name (Chapter 19).

C.9. Working with an assistant

  1. Record the binding of decisions: what was decided, by whom or by what, in the course of what work, and on what evidence, at design time and at run time (Chapter 3).

  2. Ask whether a task should exist before asking an assistant to do it faster (Chapter 4).

  3. Keep ownership with the people who will live with the result: they choose the language and the stack, and they review what an assistant binds (Chapter 4).

  4. Measure a system by what it does, not by its lines of code, services or boxes on a diagram (Chapter 4).

  5. Give each check to whoever can judge it. When an assistant drafts a vocabulary, the validator checks the structure and the people who own the words check the meaning; a draft that validates has not been reviewed (Section 21.9).

C.10. For assistants

  1. Ground answers in models and their documentation, and cite elements by their URIs.

  2. Check an API against the module reference (Appendix A) and the listings of this book and of the Zephyr Books, which compile and are tested, before using it. Do not invent methods.

  3. Go to a module’s Nasdanika Zephyr Book for what this book only outlines, and to the module’s test sources for the complete code behind a listing (The Nasdanika Zephyr Books).

  4. Respect the status labels. Present SKETCH and PLANNED features as designs, never as available.

  5. Propose changes as recorded change sets or diffs that a person reviews; do not apply them silently.

  6. Say which decisions you bound and why, so that the people who own the result can review them (Chapter 3).

  7. Write original prose when documenting the JDK and other licensed specifications; never reproduce their text (Chapter 22).

  8. Prefer the surfaces the runtime gives you, commands and files, to new integrations.

  9. When you learn something about a model element, write it into the element’s documentation page, its micro-wiki stub, so the next person or assistant finds it there (Chapter 20).

  10. Spend effort at the right altitude: change the model or the generator rather than the code it generates (Chapter 3).

  11. When you draft a vocabulary, read its rules back to the people who own the words as plain statements, and say which you guessed (Section 21.9).

Appendix D: Glossary

Adaptable

An object that can be asked for a view of itself as another type, through adapt(type). Its @Adapter methods declare, with their generic return types, what it can be adapted to (Chapter 8).

Adapter method

A method annotated with @Adapter whose return type declares a type the object can be adapted to. Command groups offer their sub-commands values this way (Chapter 17).

Agent skill

A directory of instructions that an AI assistant loads when a task calls for them. Meta’s, nasdanika-meta, teaches an assistant to write and validate vocabularies (Section 21.9).

Assembly

A set of modules on a module path, run together: a test, a command line distribution, an application. What an assembly became at run time is what the JVM model snapshots (Chapter 22).

Attributes

String keys and values on an Attributed element of the core model, for what a source format carries and a model does not name, such as the properties of a Draw.io shape (Chapter 20).

Automatic module

A jar without a module descriptor on the module path. Its name comes from its manifest or file name, it reads every module, and a module that reads one automatic module reads all of them (Chapter 22).

Bootstrap

The dependency-free jar that starts a distribution from any directory, by rewriting the distribution’s options to absolute paths and relaunching Java (Chapter 18).

Capability

Something a factory provides in answer to a requirement: an object, a function, a service (Chapter 10).

Capability factory

A class that answers requirements, declared as a service. A reflective factory answers with methods annotated @Capability, matched by their declared return types (Chapter 10).

Capability loader

The object that resolves a requirement against a source of factories, on a pump, and returns a publisher of providers (Chapter 10).

Change description

A record of changes to models, stored forward and detached from the models, contained by the span in which the changes were recorded (Chapter 13).

Command group

A command that does nothing itself and gives its sub-commands something to work on (Chapter 16).

Content

The state of a file in a volume: a re-readable source of bytes that does no I/O until it is opened (Chapter 14).

Core model

The model of identity, documentation, provenance and evaluators that the other models extend (Chapter 20).

Decision binding

Fixing an open question of a design so that it can be executed, at design time, build time, deployment or run time, by a person, a tool or an assistant. Software development is the process of binding decisions, and with assistants binding some of them, the record of who or what bound each one matters as much as the result (Chapter 3).

Distribution

A directory, or an archive of one, with the jars of a command line, its options file, the bootstrap and wrapper scripts (Chapter 18).

Ecore

The metamodel of EMF: the language of packages, classes, attributes and references in which EMF models are defined (Chapter 7).

EMF

The Eclipse Modeling Framework: a Java framework that generates code from a model and provides reflection, serialization, notifications and references across files. It does not need the Eclipse IDE (Chapter 7).

EPackage provider

A service that contributes a generated EMF package, so that a configured resource set knows it (Chapter 7).

ExecutionSupplier

A value that a parent produces for a child while the child executes, in the child’s span (Chapter 17).

Explaining listener

A listener that tells, line by line, which factories a capability loader asked about a requirement, which declined, and what each produced (Chapter 10).

Gradient ascent

Ordering the work by taking, at each point, the step with the most value per unit of time and effort, then measuring again from where the work stands; the best next action is picked from a roadmap of interconnected decisions that an assistant keeps consistent, with the North Star as the guard against climbing the wrong hill (Section 3.8).

Import map

A script in a web page that maps bare module specifiers, such as react, to URLs, so that a browser loads libraries as ES modules from a CDN with no build step (Chapter 23).

JPMS

The Java Platform Module System, part of Java since version 9. A module declares in module-info.java what it requires, what it exports and which services it provides (Chapter 6).

Marker

A record of where an element, or one of its features, came from: a location, a position, a date, a digest, or a commit (Chapter 20).

Meta

The language-neutral type system of the runtime: packages, classes, features, operations and type references, to write a vocabulary once and project it to many languages (Chapter 21).

Meta text syntax

Meta’s own notation, in .nmeta files: metamodels written the way Xcore writes Ecore models (Section 21.5).

Metamodel

A model of models: what a model may contain, such as a package of classes with typed features. A library of books is a model; the classes Library and Book are its metamodel (Chapter 7).

Micro-model

A small model with a single concern, explicit dependencies on other models and no knowledge of its consumers, in a module of its own (Chapter 2).

Micro-wiki

Documentation anchored to model elements: a page per element, with the model as the site map, so that documentation cannot drift from what it describes and everyone knows which file to edit (Chapter 20).

Mix-in

A set of options contributed to a command, by a factory or by a picocli @Mixin field (Chapter 16).

Model tower

The stack of small models, each extending the ones below: the core model at the bottom, then Meta, the JVM model, telemetry, the diagram models and the floors above (Chapter 26).

Nano-model

One of several small models in one module, because they are reused and changed together, such as the four telemetry models (Chapter 2).

Nasdanika Body of Knowledge (NBOK)

The books, stories and example code about Nasdanika, laid out by one convention and built so that every listing is tested code; every book in it ends with the same appendix on how it is organized (Appendix F).

Nasdanika Zephyr Book

An in-depth technical manual for one module of the runtime, or a small group of modules used together, in the manner of IBM Redbooks, with every listing included from the module’s tests. It is on the module’s page and attached to the module’s artifact with the classifier book, as PDF and HTML (The Nasdanika Zephyr Books).

nsURI

The namespace URI of an EMF package: its identity, under runtime.sdk.nasdanika.org/ for the runtime’s models (Chapter 2).

OpenTelemetry

A vendor-neutral standard and API for traces, log records and metrics. Code is instrumented once, and whoever runs it decides where the signals go (Chapter 11).

Planes

The data plane where data sits, the semantic plane of models with resolved references, and the presentation plane of what people and agents read, separated by volumes, with commands writing down (Chapter 26).

Polymorphic UI

A user interface that renders each element with the view of its class, or of its nearest superclass that has one, or with a reflective view of last resort, the way a method call dispatches on the class of its receiver. With several formats (HTML, React, Markdown, AsciiDoc), it dispatches on the format as well (Chapter 24).

Published Language

In Domain-Driven Design, a documented, shared vocabulary that bounded contexts translate into and out of. Meta is one that is machine-checkable (Chapter 21).

Pump

A serial work queue, drained by one thread at a time, that drives capability resolution, transformations and pumped publishers. A thread that waits on it runs queued work instead of sleeping, and it reports what is stuck when nothing can progress (Chapter 9).

Pure Nasdanika

Code that depends on the JDK, EMF core and the OpenTelemetry API and nothing else (Chapter 2).

Qualifier

A dot-separated part of a file name, read right to left, that selects a handler for a resource’s contents: reading-group.library.groovy has the qualifiers groovy and library (Chapter 10, Chapter 19).

Reflective view

The view of last resort in a polymorphic user interface: what the metamodel says about an element, its class and the features it has values for (Chapter 24).

Requirement

A type, possibly generic, and payloads that select and parameterize what is required (Chapter 10).

Resource set contributor

A service that configures resource sets: packages, factories, URI handlers, adapters (Chapter 7).

Semantic elements

The objects of other models that a diagram element depicts, such as the book a node of a diagram stands for. A diagram element is a model element in its own right, so a diagram is a model even when it depicts nothing (Chapter 25).

Snapshot

A model of a running system saved as a file, such as the JVM model of a module layer: evidence of what ran (Chapter 22).

Span

An operation in a trace, with a name, a start, an end, attributes and log records; in the runtime, one per operation worth seeing (Chapter 11).

Status label

AVAILABLE for what the runtime does in this edition, SKETCH for what is designed and partly built, PLANNED for what is designed and not built.

Telemetry model

Traces, logs and metrics as EMF models, faithful to OpenTelemetry’s data model, with nested spans, log records in their spans and recorded changes (Chapter 13).

Transformer

A function from sources to publishers of targets, with mappings declared by annotated methods and wiring of targets to each other (Chapter 9).

Type token

An object that captures a generic type at compile time, such as new TypeToken<Supplier<Library>>() {}, where erasure would lose it (Chapter 8).

UI

Wherever a person or an agent exchanges information with a system, even in one direction: a page, a PDF, Markdown or AsciiDoc that an agent reads, a tool it calls (Chapter 24).

Unit of work

A piece of work with its own OpenTelemetry instance and its own record: a command run, a request served, an agent session, a test (Chapter 11).

Volume

The runtime’s file abstraction: string paths, stat, list, content, declared case sensitivity and optional capabilities, implemented over NIO, models or remote systems (Chapter 14).

Wiring

Matching commands to parents and sub-commands by declared generic types, and injecting adapted values before execution (Chapter 17).

XMI

XML Metadata Interchange, a standard XML format for models and the one every EMF tool understands (Chapter 7).

Xcore

A textual syntax for Ecore models with operation bodies, from which EMF generates Java (Chapter 7).

Appendix E: Building and publishing this book

This book is written in AsciiDoc and built with the runtime, in the runtime’s repository. Its examples are Maven modules compiled and tested with every build, so a listing that no longer compiles, or a test that no longer passes, fails the build before it can mislead a reader.

E.1. Layout

doc/                       documentation parent, never deployed
  book/
    examples/              one Maven module per topic: start, library, generics, flow,
                           capability, telemetry, recording, volume, cli, dsl, meta,
                           jvm, web, ui
    manuscript/
      src/docs/asciidoc/   book.adoc, front matter, chapters, appendices, back matter, images
      src/docs/themes/     the PDF theme
      src/cover/           the cover generator
  zephyr/                  the PDF theme and the stylesheets of the Zephyr Books

The documentation parent sets maven.deploy.skip, so nothing under doc is deployed, as with test modules. The manuscript module does not depend on the examples through Maven; it includes their files.

E.2. Building

The book is built with the runtime:

mvn clean install                      # the runtime, the examples and the book
mvn clean install -Dasciidoctor.skip   # everything but the book

Or on its own, from doc/book/manuscript:

mvn verify                             # PDF, EPUB and HTML in target/book
mvn verify -Dbook.editor-notes=false   # without editor's notes, for publication
mvn verify -Dbook.media=prepress       # print: no cover, URLs after links, recto chapters

The build produces three editions, named after the runtime version:

  • PDF, at 189 by 246 mm (7.44 by 9.69 inches), a standard trim size for print on demand, with a theme that extends Asciidoctor PDF’s default: Noto Serif for text, Noto Sans for headings, and M+ 1mn for code.

  • EPUB, for readers.

  • HTML, one page with every image embedded: the whole book in one file, every term and every rule in it. Its markup, most of it the highlighting of listings, makes the file nearly three times the size of its text, so an assistant working in the repository is better served by the AsciiDoc sources and the examples, read in the parts it needs (Chapter 3).

Diagrams are PlantUML, rendered by Asciidoctor Diagram with PlantUML’s own layout engine, so no Graphviz installation is needed. The exception is the figure of Chapter 25, an SVG file that its example generates and checks.

E.3. Conventions of the manuscript

  • Listings are included, not copied. A listing is a tagged region of an example, included with include::{examplesdir}/...[tag=name,indent=0]. Callouts are comments of the form // <1> in the example’s source.

  • Listings fit the page. At the code font size of the PDF, a line holds 96 characters, and longer lines in tagged regions are wrapped in the source, not by the renderer.

  • Warnings fail the build. A missing tag, a broken cross-reference or an unknown attribute stops it.

  • Status labels mark what is not available yet: [.sketch]#SKETCH# and [.planned]#PLANNED#.

  • Editor’s notes are IMPORTANT blocks inside ifdef::editor-notes[], for the author and the runtime’s maintainers. They record inconsistencies between the runtime and its documentation found while writing, and are left out of published editions.

E.4. The cover

The cover is generated by a single-file Java program, src/cover/Cover.java, which draws the title, the subtitle and the logo with Java 2D, using the Noto Sans fonts bundled with Asciidoctor PDF:

java src/cover/Cover.java \
    <path to asciidoctorj-pdf jar> \
    src/docs/asciidoc/images/nasdanika-sdk-logo.jpg \
    src/docs/asciidoc/images/cover.png

E.5. Publishing

The book is published on Leanpub as a "Bring Your Own Book" title: Leanpub does not build it; each release uploads the PDF and the EPUB built here, and a sample if one is wanted. The minimum price is zero with a suggested price, so the book is free and readers can choose to pay. The text and figures are licensed under CC BY 4.0 and the examples under EPL-2.0, as the colophon states; the legal code of CC BY 4.0 is in doc/book/manuscript/LICENSE. A release of the book follows a release of the runtime, and has its version. The Zephyr Books with readers beyond the runtime are Leanpub titles too, released with each release of the runtime and offered with this book in a bundle (The Nasdanika Zephyr Books).

E.6. Building a Zephyr Book

A Nasdanika Zephyr Book (The Nasdanika Zephyr Books) is built with the same tool chain, in the module it documents. A module has one when it has src/docs/asciidoc/index.adoc: that file activates a profile in the runtime’s parent POM, so a module opts in without a change to its own POM. Its listings are tagged regions of the module’s tests and test resources, included as this book includes its examples, and the conventions above hold, warnings that fail the build included.

The profile renders two editions in the Zephyr look, a PDF with a theme of its own and a single HTML page with Bootswatch’s Zephyr stylesheet, both from doc/zephyr. It attaches them to the module’s artifact with the classifier book, and the module’s test sources with the classifier test-sources. The release build leaves the editor’s notes out, as it does for this book, because what is published to Maven Central cannot be withdrawn.

Appendix F: The Nasdanika Body of Knowledge

This book is part of the Nasdanika Body of Knowledge, NBOK for short: the books, stories and example code about Nasdanika, organized so that people and AI assistants can find what they need in it and rely on what they find. Every book in it ends with this appendix, word for word, so that whichever one you are reading, you know where the others are and how they fit together.

Bodies of knowledge such as SWEBOK for software engineering and PMBOK for project management are written guides. NBOK is built. Its listings are regions of code that is compiled and tested before a book is rendered, so a book whose code no longer does what it says does not build.

F.1. What it holds

  • The SDK book, Nasdanika SDK Runtime: More Structure with Less Effort: the overview, with the why, the key capabilities and the high-level how. Read it first.

  • Nasdanika Zephyr Books: one per module, or per small group of modules used together, each the detail for its modules, as user guide, developer guide and reference. Each stands on its own.

  • Readmes: one page on what a module is and why. A module with a Zephyr Book may have none.

  • Nasdanika SDK Stories PLANNED: one use case each, related to the Nasdanika SDK in some shape or form, written as a Maven module whose code, if it has any, is the source of its listings, and collected each year.

  • The International Banking System PLANNED: the practice of architecture as code, taught as a course on one example that grows with the platform. Inspired by the C4 Model "Internet Banking System".

  • Nasdanika Field Notes: short articles about the technologies and services Nasdanika is built and published with, such as EMF, each verified by a test where it can be, and recipes, such as publishing a book, collected in one book. Their tests use the third-party versions of the runtime’s BOM, so every runtime release checks the runtime’s assumptions about its dependencies. Unlike the rest of NBOK, they are about other projects' code, and useful without Nasdanika.

A story is à la carte; the International Banking System is the course; a field note is about the ground they stand on.

F.2. How it is laid out

Every repository of NBOK follows one layout, the Maven layout with a few additions:

pom.xml                          the reactor: its modules, their names and descriptions
doc/                             documentation about the repository as a whole
  book/manuscript/               a book about the repository, if it has one
  book/examples/<topic>/         that book's examples, one Maven module per topic
<module>/
  pom.xml                        the module's name and description
  readme.md                      what the module is and why, on one page
  src/main/java/                 the code, with module-info.java
  src/main/resources/            resources, and Xcore models under the package path
  src/test/java/                 the tests: the source of the book's listings
  src/test/resources/            test data: the source of the book's figures
  src/docs/asciidoc/index.adoc   the module's Zephyr Book, with front/, chapters/
                                 and appendices/ beside it

A module has a Zephyr Book when it has src/docs/asciidoc/index.adoc. A story PLANNED is a module at <year>/<topic>/ in the stories repository, with story.adoc and index.adoc in src/docs/asciidoc/ beside its code, and <year>/book/ builds the year’s collection from the stories next to it. A field note is a module at <technology>/<topic>/ in the field-notes repository, with article.adoc and index.adoc in src/docs/asciidoc/ beside its tests, and book/ builds the collection.

F.3. How it is published

  • Maven Central, per module and version: the jar, its sources and javadoc, and, for a module with a Zephyr Book, the book as PDF and HTML with the classifier book and the tests with the classifier test-sources, the complete source of every listing. Central is permanent, so the book of every released version stays available.

  • The runtime’s site, PLANNED runtime.sdk.nasdanika.org, with the latest books.

  • Leanpub: the SDK book, with the Zephyr Books that have readers beyond the runtime in a bundle, and the yearly collection of stories PLANNED, each free with a suggested price.

  • Zenodo, sources published by GitHub and books uploaded manually.

  • Lulu for print-on-demand copies of the books.

F.4. How to read it

People read the PDF or the HTML: the SDK book for the why and the big picture, then the Zephyr Book of the module at hand.

AI assistants are better served by the sources than by the renders. AsciiDoc is a fraction of the size of the HTML, whose markup and highlighting multiply it, and the sources lead to the code itself. In a repository of NBOK, an assistant finds its way as an engineer does:

  1. The root pom.xml lists the modules, with a name and a description each.

  2. A module’s readme.md, where it has one, says what the module is.

  3. A module’s src/docs/asciidoc/index.adoc includes the book’s files, and each listing’s include:: names the test file and the tagged region it comes from: follow it to the code.

  4. A term is in a book’s glossary appendix, and a convention in its rules or building appendix.

Two aids for assistants are planned PLANNED: each book and story also as one AsciiDoc file with its includes resolved, so that it is complete without the repository, and an index generated from the headers of the books and stories (title, description, keywords, version), so that an assistant can choose the few it needs instead of reading all of them.

F.5. Why it can be trusted, and for which version

  • Listings are code. Every listing is a tagged region of a test or an example that is compiled and run before the book is rendered, and a warning, such as a missing tag, fails the build.

  • Every book has a version. A book is built with a release of the runtime and carries its version, here 2026.11.0. It is true for that version; for another, read the book of that version.

  • Status labels mark what is not built yet: SKETCH for what is designed and partly built, PLANNED for what is designed and not built. Everything without a label is available.

  • Editor’s notes, the author’s notes on what is still to be checked, are left out of published editions.

  • Stories are built twice PLANNED: against the release each was published with, so that it reproduces, and against the next one, so that a story that no longer applies is marked before a reader finds out.

The source of this appendix is doc/nbok/nbok-appendix.adoc in github.com/Nasdanika-SDK/runtime, published with each release as org.nasdanika.sdk.runtime.doc:nbok.

About the author

I am Pavel Vlasov, the creator of Nasdanika and of the runtime this book describes. I have worked in information technology for more than thirty years, thirty of them in financial services, as a developer, an architect and an enterprise architect.

I hold a master’s degree in plasma physics from the Novosibirsk State University. I am certified as a Java developer and as a Java architect, and as a TOGAF Enterprise Architecture Practitioner.

I write about models, architecture and AI-assisted development at medium.com/nasdanika. My code is on GitHub, and I am on LinkedIn.
